#6104. It’s scary how watchable these stories are

A version of this story first appeared in The Swell, Salon's culture newsletter. Sign up for early access to articles like this, for more culture that's made to last.

Iâve never been great at the whole Halloween thing. By the time I remember itâs happening, all the good sweets are gone from grocery store shelves, so any visiting trick-or-treaters get butterscotch suckers, breath mints or candy corn. I donât do costume parties. I never got the point of carving pumpkins.

But movie and TV marathons? Sign me up â along with a lot of other homebodies. The horror genre is bigger than ever, according to a San Francisco Chronicle report that says this yearâs domestic box office reached nearly $1.3 billion as of the start of October.

Horrorâs surge has also yielded more films designed to play with our perception as opposed to the âSawâ-style torture porn dominating years past. Think âObsessionâ or âBackrooms,â both of which are among the 10 highest-earning movies of 2026 thus far. Thatâs good news for anyone who isnât partial to splatter flicks or slashers but still enjoys a creep show that makes you think, especially ones that are more thoughtful than scary. If thatâs your speed, the following options may be perfect for your reclusive Samhain.

I will bet good money the first bong-ripping undergrad to declare that all horror is metaphor cited George Romeroâs âNight of the Living Deadâ as a prime example. Thatâs not wrong; Romeroâs 1968 benchmark established the modern cinematic zombie as a stand-in for mindless capitalist consumption. But âBlack Zombieâ rewinds to the monsterâs Haitian roots to examine an even darker origin tied to that countryâs shared history with ours.

You may be wondering why Iâd recommend a documentary in a horror roundup, let alone one that explains how the modern movie flesh gobbler began as a manifestation of white fear. The answer is that Maya Annik Bedwardâs film doubles as an impressive cinematic syllabus.

By braiding Americaâs media history with its national history, Bedward and her assemblage of academics, creatives, authors and Vodou practitioners invite us to think differently about the prejudices driving movies like, say, Victor Halperinâs 1932 effort âWhite Zombie,â or 1943âs âI Walked with a Zombie.â

âBlack Zombieâ opens with a truth that has long escaped those fascinated by the shambling undead. To some, theyâre simply mindless hunters. But Haitians understand the horror of zombies to be one of dispossession, a curse enacted by enslavers that binds victims to mindless servitude, denying them liberation in the afterlife. But long after Romero transformed them from blank-eyed puppets to ravenous murder machines, Bedwardâs film demonstrates how Hollywoodâs version of the zombie impacts Americaâs perception of Vodou, Haitians and immigration.

âBlack Zombieâ not only asks us to think differently about an overexposed subgenre, but also thoughtfully examines Vodouâs central role in the revolution that drove out French colonizers, and Franceâs imposition of debt to punish Haitians for winning their freedom.

All of this informs the zombieâs continued proliferation across popular culture, in films like âWorld War Zâ and shows such as âThe Last of Usâ and âThe Walking Dead.â Theyâre terrific entertainment, certainly. But each is, in its own way, built upon decadesâ worth of misrepresenting Haitiâs syncretic faith to the detriment and demonization of a people. At the same time, âBlack Zombieâ recognizes this subgenreâs cultural resilience, arguing that recognizing the zombieâs true roots broadens its narrative possibilities.

Proving that point, one of Bedwardâs subjects, a Vodou priest, says he grew up loving Wes Cravenâs âThe Serpent and the Rainbow,â despite its message that visitors to his country risk having their nuts nailed to a chair. Â âItâs a fantastical world to scare children,â he says, before adding that his main problem is its inaccurate messaging about his faith. âWe say, âWow â Haitians are devils.â Thatâs what weâre taught.â

Iâd nearly forgotten about that movie. Now I might rewatch it for the first time in decades and expect to be horrified for entirely different reasons.

Available to rent on Prime Video, Apple TV, and Fandango.

Stephen Kingâs classic may be more than half a century old and has undergone multiple adaptations, but it endures because its central moral that high school is hell never ages. Still, Mike Flanaganâs interpretation has divided the audience. Some, including King, appreciate Flanaganâs kinder portrait of Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) as an innocent unjustly sequestered from the world by fundamentalist parents who repudiate her extraordinary power. Others disagree with Flanaganâs alteration to the storyâs climactic scene, which shifts culpability for the prom massacre from Carrie to a character created expressly for the series.

Pretty much everyone questions the season finale, which hints at taking an âX-Menâ-style turn for its recently greenlit second season.

As someone who accepts nothing is sacrosanct now, not to mention a fan of the creatorâs other adaptations, including âThe Fall of the House of Usher,â I appreciated Flanagan using Carrieâs story to critique ignorance, knowledge suppression, and the dehumanizing effect of social media.

Besides, nearly all the key elements of âCarrieâ remain. The bullies are still awful, and the famous âplug it upâ shower scene in Brian DePalmaâs 1976 standard-setter is worsened by her tormentors posting Carrieâs frightened sobs on social media.

Some changes retain the spirit of past performances. Carrieâs mother Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) is still an abusive religious zealot fond of locking her daughter in a prayer closet, for instance. But after the law forces her homeschooled girl to join the festering sin den that is their local public school, Margaret throws herself into advocating for parentsâ rights, entirely disregarding her teenâs desire for a ânormalâ adolescence.

Part of the additional fun Flanagan has with this marquee property is strewing cultural Easter Eggs throughout. Some nod to whatâs happening in America, such as when Carrie discovers the school library and gravitates straight to books that have been banned from classrooms and community libraries across the country. Another winks at âArmy of Darknessâ fans; look for the logo on Margaretâs work uniform.

By the time we reach Carrieâs bloodbath, we may be left to question whether sheâs simply a bullied victim pushed beyond her limit or some version of a Final Girl empowered to vanquish tormentors who earn their reckoning. Even if you donât ultimately see Howellâs Carrie that way, itâs a fine dance with one of horrorâs oldest friends.

âCarrieâ is streaming on Prime Video.

For adults, Halloween is an excuse to mingle sensuality with morbid themes. Why cosplay as a grizzled cop when you can be a flirty detective? Why settle for pretending to be a humpbacked wiccan when you can troll for hookups as a sexy witch?

âYagaâ has it all ways, resplendent with softcore interludes dangled between clue-finding excursions and unexpected chicken violence. The latest infatuation bait from Crave, the Canadian streamer that brought us âHeated Rivalry,â also gives us a new view of Hudson Williams and his naked hindquarters.

Only now, theyâre humping away in a mystery taking place in a verdant seaside community called Whittock. There, dirtbag P.I. Charlie Rapp (Noah Reid) is drawn into a tense partnership with Carson (Clark Backo), a no-nonsense cop fatigued with her colleaguesâ disrespect.

At first, Carson is repulsed by Rappâs slimy overstepping, but she slowly learns not to loathe him. Implied in this, perhaps, is that a spell has ensnared the two as they probe the disappearance of rich playboy Henry Park (Williams). This pursuit leads them to encounter free-range poultry in odd places, along with strange symbols, a variety of nubile temptresses and a roommate, Logan (also Williams), who resembles Henry to an unsettling degree.

The showâs title has nothing to do with John Wick. It refers to the mythical Slavic crone, Baba Yaga, who either gives heroes a boon or lures wayward children to a forest hut that moves around on bird legs. Playwright Kat Chandlerâs interpretation leaves open the question of whether our impressions of its witch are unwarranted or dead right, further muddling our judgment with the introduction of Carrie-Anne Mossâ university professor, Katherine Hargrove.

Katherine announces herself by cozying up to Rapp over the manuscript for her new book titled âSexy Bones,â thrilling him with her mature lady erotic energy. As she flirts with and antagonizes the private dick, along with other townies, it grows increasingly baffling as whether sheâs friend or foe. Much like our titular enchantress.

This adaptation of Chandlerâs play looks like a cop drama tangled with witchy murder, but from a longer TV perspective itâs really a haunting by the ghosts of erotic TV shows past. Remember âRed Shoe Diariesâ and its moaning sax riffs? Like that anthology once did, âYagaâ banks on the power of smut to compel you. Itâs a cheap indulgence, but what Halloween candy isnât?

âYagaâ is streaming in the U.S. on AMC+.

Sometimes, simplicity is king. And that's certainly the case with the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

The Venture Rewards is a card I frequently recommend to beginners who want to earn rewards they can maximize for travel.

Why? Because for a reasonable $95 annual fee, the card earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, making it easy to build a rewards balance without keeping track of bonus categories. Plus, it offers valuable travel perks and flexible redemption options, whether you want to keep things simple or explore more advanced strategies.

Whether you're new to earning travel rewards or recently picked up the card yourself, here are six beginner-friendly ways to make the most of the Venture Rewards.

Earning a welcome bonus is one of the easiest ways for beginners to kick-start their points and miles journey.

Currently, new Venture Rewards cardholders can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, they'll also receive a $300 credit for Capital One Travel hotel and vacation rentals upon account opening.

According to TPG's October 2026 valuations, Capital One miles are worth 1.85 cents per mile. When including the credit, the total value of this welcome offer comes to $1,688. That makes this offer the most valuable we've seen in over two years.

Those 75,000 Capital One miles can be a great starting point for anyone new to maximizing points and miles.

And as for the $300 Capital One Travel credit, it's a great way to dip your toe into the world of travel portals. You could use it to cover a weekend hotel stay, save on a vacation rental or offset the cost of a more expensive trip.

Just remember that the credit must be used toward eligible hotel or vacation rental bookings through Capital One Travel within your first cardholder year.

Related: Credit cards 101: The beginner’s guide

One of the Venture Rewards' best perks is that it earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase.

With some travel rewards cards, you earn more points when spending in certain everyday categories. But with the Venture Rewards, you'll earn 2 miles per dollar whether you're filling up your tank, furnishing your apartment or stocking your fridge.

The card also earns 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel.

TPG lead writer Katie Genter has held the Venture Rewards for more than a decade and still finds it useful for everyday purchases: "I like the Venture's straightforward earning structure and the fact that it earns versatile yet valuable Capital One miles."

She often uses her Venture Rewards for purchases that would earn just 1 point or mile per dollar with another rewards card.

If you're new to the world of points and miles, the Venture Rewards can be a great place to start, given how simple it is to earn rewards that can then be used for travel, which we'll cover below.

Related: The best credit cards for everyday spending

Another way to maximize your Venture Rewards as a beginner is to book eligible travel through Capital One Travel, the issuer's online travel booking platform.

As mentioned above, Venture Rewards cardholders earn 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through the portal, compared to the standard 2 miles per dollar on other purchases.

For example, booking a $1,000 hotel stay through Capital One Travel would earn you 5,000 miles (compared to 2,000 miles if you booked directly with the hotel). That's an additional 3,000 miles, worth approximately $56 according to TPG's valuations.

Plus, Venture Rewards cardholders can access Capital One's Lifestyle Collection, which offers benefits such as a $50 experience credit for each eligible hotel stay and potential room upgrades (when available).

However, I don't recommend using the portal as your default method of booking travel. You usually won't earn hotel loyalty points or receive elite status benefits when booking through a third party, so it's worth comparing prices and benefits before making a reservation.

Still, for beginners looking to earn more miles without changing their spending habits, Capital One Travel can be a useful tool.

Related: Should I book flights through a travel portal?

Beyond earning miles, the Venture Rewards comes with several travel perks that can help you save money and make your trips a little easier.

One of the most useful is a statement credit of up to $120 (every four years) for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee. All you need to do is pay the application fee with your card, and you'll receive a statement credit for the eligible charge.

Both programs can help you save time at the airport, but Global Entry also includes TSA PreCheck benefits, so I recommend it for international travelers.

Another perk for international travelers is that the Venture Rewards charges no foreign transaction fees. This means you can use your card abroad without worrying about the additional fees some credit cards charge on international purchases.

The card also offers several travel protections, including an auto rental collision damage waiver and travel accident insurance, which can provide some added peace of mind when you're away from home.

You can also enroll in complimentary Hertz Five Star status, which comes with benefits like a wider selection of rental vehicles and the ability to skip the rental counter (at certain locations).

For a card with a $95 annual fee, these perks can offer strong ongoing value, especially if you travel a few times a year.

Related: 7 of the best starter travel credit cards

If you aren't ready to transfer your miles to travel partners but still want to redeem your rewards for travel, another option is to use your miles to cover eligible travel purchases.

Rather than searching for award availability or navigating airline loyalty programs, you can book an eligible travel purchase with your card and redeem miles to offset the charge within 90 days of the purchase.

When you redeem miles this way, each mile is worth 1 cent. That's less than TPG's valuation of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents per mile, but it offers a straightforward way to use your rewards.

For example, if you book a $300 flight with your Venture Rewards, you can redeem 30,000 miles to cover the purchase. You can also use this feature for other eligible travel expenses, including hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars.

TPG director of site strategy Carly Helfand has relied on this method before, redeeming 100,000 Capital One miles to cover a last-minute Airbnb purchase.

While transferring miles to travel partners can yield higher redemption values, covering travel purchases is a useful alternative when you want to book directly or can't find award availability that works for your dates.

For potentially higher-value redemptions, consider transferring your Capital One miles to the issuer's airline and hotel partners.

If you're new to the world of travel rewards, transferring miles simply means moving your Capital One miles into another travel loyalty program, where you can then redeem them for flights or hotel stays.

Capital One has more than 15 travel partners, including Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club and Wyndham Rewards.

Most of Capital One's airline partners offer a 1:1 transfer ratio, meaning 1,000 Capital One miles become 1,000 miles in the partner program. However, some partners have different ratios, so be sure to check before transferring.

Personally, I love transferring my Capital One miles to airline partners to book flights to and around Europe.

For example, I recently transferred about 6,000 Capital One miles to Air France-KLM Flying Blue to book a Scandinavian Airlines flight from Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) to Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN). I paid just $11 in taxes and fees for a flight that would have otherwise cost about $450 in cash, giving me 7.3 cents per mile in value — well above TPG's valuation of 1.85 cents per mile.

If you're just getting started, don't feel like you need to master transfer partners right away. You can begin by redeeming miles for travel purchases and explore transfers as you become more comfortable.

Related: How to transfer Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners

The Capital One Venture Rewards stands out as a beginner-friendly travel rewards card thanks to its simple earning structure, valuable travel perks and flexible redemption options.

If you're new to the world of points and miles, start by using the card for everyday spending and exploring simple travel redemptions. As you become more comfortable, you can transfer miles to travel partners to unlock even greater value.

And even as you become more experienced with points and miles, the Venture Rewards' simplicity and flexibility make it a card worth keeping in your wallet long term.

For more details, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Rewards.

Chinese arrivals to Thailand fell to 49,494 in the week of October 18–24, down about 24% from the week before, The Nation reported, with Thai officials attributing the decline partly to post-Golden Week seasonality and partly to weaker confidence after a Chinese embassy safety advisory. The October 16 advisory cited cases of Chinese nationals who went missing, were unlawfully detained, or were lured toward the Thailand–Myanmar border, and urged travelers to tighten safety precautions. Thai Hotels Association president Thienprasit Chaiyapatranun told Skift daily Chinese arrivals dropped from about 15,000 during Golden Week to about 9,000, while the Association of Thai Travel Agents said cancellations have pushed Chinese group-tour business more than 30% below last year, with a warning it could halve over Lunar New Year 2027 without government action. The reversal lands after a period of rebuilding: Minor Hotels had told Skift Chinese room nights across its Thailand portfolio were 78% ahead of last year heading into Golden Week, and China had retaken the top source market spot with about 4.2 million arrivals through October 31. Thailand has since cut its 2026 China target to 5.1 million and its full-year visitor forecast to 33 million from 36.7 million, after total foreign arrivals fell 4.1% to 24.4 million from January 1 to October 17.

The campaign features some of the countryâs most architecturally impressive toilets, many situated along scenic routes overlooking fjords, mountains and waterfalls. Some have even won international design awards.

âNorway has become a shithouse country, actually,â Trump told supporters. He also suggested he no longer wanted Norwegian immigrants coming to the United States because he had not received the prize.

Rather than engage in a diplomatic spat, Visit Norway embraced the presidentâs characterization, promoting restrooms that include the award-winning Stegastein viewpoint toilet overlooking Aurlandsfjord and the triangular Golden Toilet on Senja Island.

#6096. Marriott’s Fees Jump 14% as Hotel Owners Seek a Bigger Cut

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Aerial view of The Ritz Carlton Oahu Turtle Bay. Marriott

Marriott said that its talks with hotel owners who want a bigger cut of the pie have been "constructive." It's easier for everyone to stay polite about the fee math when profit growth has revived significantly.

Marriott’s fees are climbing just as some of its hotel owners push for a bigger share of them.

Gross fees rose 14% to $1.52 billion in the third quarter, helped by a larger hotel network and by co-branded credit card fees, which Chief Financial Officer Jen Mason said on a Monday earnings call were “expected to rise in the high 30% range” for the full year. A group of owners wrote to Marriott’s management earlier this year asking for a bigger share of loyalty income, citing the card fees in particular. Net income rose 17% to $790 million.

Strong results may also give Marriott more leverage in those talks. Worldwide revenue per available room (RevPAR) rose 6.5% year over year, far above the 3.5% to 4% the company had projected in August, and Mason cited “a solid improvement in hotel margins.”

The gains reached the hotels that had been struggling most. Limited-service hotels posted a third consecutive quarter of RevPAR gains, up more than 6%.

Marriott beat expectations in the third quarter, with worldwide RevPAR up 6.5% year over year against August guidance of 3.5% to 4%, gross fees up 14% to $1.52 billion, and net income up 17% to $790 million. The company raised its full-year RevPAR outlook to 4.5% to 5%, up from the 1.5% to 2.5% it forecast in February, and offered an early view that 2027 worldwide RevPAR could grow 3.5% to 4.5%. The results land in the middle of a negotiation with a group of owners who wrote to management earlier this year asking for a bigger share of loyalty income, citing co-branded credit card fees, which CFO Jen Mason said are expected to rise in the high 30% range for the full year. CEO Anthony Capuano described Marriott's approach to owners as incremental, pointing to concessions already announced — a lower owner contribution rate on loyalty spending, better reimbursement for redemption stays on high-demand nights, relaxed operating and renovation rules, and a rebate for some well-reviewed hotels — and did not rule out more. Incentive management fees rose 22% to $181 million, which Marriott cites as evidence that owner and brand economics move together. Meanwhile, net room growth held at 4.6%, Capuano called key money the "weapon of choice" in winning development deals, and conversions made up more than a third of signings. The strong quarter arrived a week after Capuano told staff Marriott would eliminate some corporate roles while creating others; neither executives nor analysts raised the restructuring on the call.

#6093. Are Mount Everest climbers dreamers, or just cultists?

In the title of his 1997 bestselling adventure tale, âInto Thin Air,â mountaineer and writer Jon Krakauer employs a double entendre so clever that its effect is extraordinary. Throughout the book, Krakauer recounts his attempt to summit Mount Everest the year earlier in what would become, at the time, the mountainâs deadliest season. Iâve been momentarily halted by that title each time Iâve picked up my tattered $5 thrift-store copy over the last few weeks. Itâs witty, but not grim; accurate but also imaginative. In three words, âInto Thin Airâ conveys not only the literal effect of Everestâs high altitude and how quickly the mountain can take a life, but also the ardent, almost fatuous confidence of those who choose to climb it.

The dissonance between reason and ambition is what makes âInto Thin Airâ such a compelling read. For someone like myself, who knows next to nothing about climbing, Krakauer powerfully elucidates the pull of a mountain like Everest and the trance-like state in which it ensnares its adversaries. Unlike some climbers, Krakauer can wax poetic while staying honest about the stakes. He writes about mountaineering as a spiritual practice, good for the mind and body alike, while questioning why some find that clarity only by staring death in the face. In that respect, extreme climbing is an incredibly selfish endeavor. Before he begins his push for the summit, Krakauer remembers his wife, Linda, telling him before he left for Nepal: âIf you get killed, itâs not just you who will pay the price. Iâll have to pay, too. For the rest of my life.â

That sentiment echoed in my mind throughout âEverest: The Other Side,â the remarkable new documentary from National Geographic, helmed by âFree Soloâ and âNyadâ co-directors Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin. The film is brutally honest in its depictions of cold human narcissism and the relentless pursuit of glory in the name of nebulous spiritual fulfillment. Yet itâs just as candid about humanityâs collective desire for all those things in one form or another.

Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, âEverest: The Other Sideâ forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.â

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

As âEverest: The Other Sideâ asserts, nothing in this already mystifying life is ever so simple. The filmâs subjects, mountaineer Jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson, found love at the edge of the world and made a life together, with Morrison becoming co-parent to Nelsonâs two young sons. But their shared lust for adventure created a prickly tension within their family unit, a strain between their passion and parentage that sits at the documentaryâs emotional center.

Like those pulled by devout religion or extreme acts of faith, Morrison and Nelson are powerless before their distinct higher calling â especially with the literal highest calling of all, Everest, in their sights. They donât just want to summit the mountain from its treacherous north face; they want to be the first people ever to ski down it. In their quest, personal glory and public vanity are forever at odds. Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, âEverest: The Other Sideâ forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.

Because this is National Geographic, the film is only partially concerned with relaying that price. This documentary is made for IMAX-loving, secondhand adventure seekers. Those who want sweeping shots of impossible sights wonât be disappointed.Â

But while âEverest: The Other Sideâ includes countless breathtaking sequences of Earthâs tallest mountain and plenty of nail-biting anxiety in the eventual summit push and ski attempt, those moments are merely the filmâs selling points. The crux of this story is on Nelson and Morrisonâs shoulders, and their sincerity flies in the face of good judgment and self-editing, giving viewers a palpable sense of their egos. This isnât to say that either of them is a raging narcissist who cares only about themselves, but thereâs no doubt that their sportâs seismic, life-altering dangers are on full display, warts and all.

Early in the film, Nelson tries to communicate the draw of climbing, and how fundamentally at odds it is with her role as a mother. âPeople ask me, âHow do you find balance?ââ she says. âThere isnât. Itâs just chaos. Youâre just hanging on. You want to be with your family, but you have a passion, and you want to work, and you need to make money. Youâre all over the map.â

It would be easy to dismiss Nelson as selfish, or, at the worst and most damning, a bad parent. How can someone have young children and decide to part with them for two months for a climb that is about, at face value, little more than bragging rights? How can a parent let their children spend two months wondering if their mother is dead or alive?

These are easy questions to ask from the comfort of a living room or the cushion of a theater seat, but much harder to answer when youâre living the life. Itâs important to remember that, in life, most of us have desires that would yank us in severe directions. It reminds me that cult experts will tell you that any of us could fall into the clutches of a cult, and those of us who argue otherwise are likely among the most vulnerable. Anyone who insists they are too self-aware to be pulled into something that goes against their own interests is admitting that they donât know themselves or humanity very well. Thatâs one of lifeâs great mysteries: Why do we do things that we know are wrong, or bad for us? Death and taxes might be certain, but so are mistakes and regret, no matter how much weâd like to believe that weâre big enough to let go.

Conflict is ever-present in Morrison, who chooses to climb Everest despite its perils. For him, the adventure is about more than pride or titles; itâs about honor and love. The journey is intended both to strengthen his bond with Nelson and honor the memory of his late wife and their two children, who died in a horrific commuter plane crash in 2011, a decade before he and Nelson decide to attempt Everest. Recalling the aftermath, Morrison tells how climbing brought him clarity. Unable to move from the edge of his driveway, consumed by grief, he eventually found the strength to simply walk up the slight incline and into his home â a microscopic example of the human spiritâs extraordinary tenacity he hopes to commemorate in the Everest climb.Â

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

But more tests lie ahead. The route to Everest proves demanding in heart and health. And while training together for the big summit push by climbing a lower peak in Nepal in 2022, Nelson loses her footing in an avalanche the size of a small snow drift. On a ski slope, the drift would be minor. But on a mountain, every movement is measured. Nelson is swept away and under the snow, toward a cliff. We see it happen in real time, captured on a helmet GoPro. The moment is almost unassuming in its speed, but it permanently shapes everything that follows. Nelson is lost amid a series of avalanches, and the clock starts ticking.

Counting the seconds seems futile. But climbing is futile, too. For Morrison, left to search for his partner amid the snow, hazardous ridges and cliffs, it all seems like a waste. More pain, more trauma, more memories that are left for only one person to hold onto. I was immediately reminded of what Krakauerâs wife told him by satellite phone before he began his push from Everestâs base camp. âSaying goodbye to you was one of the saddest things Iâve ever done,â he remembers her saying. âI guess I knew on some level that you might not be coming back, and it seemed like such a waste. It seemed so f**king stupid and pointless.â

Itâs hard not to dwell on that sentiment, already knowing what and who Nelson would leave behind if disaster struck. On some level, and to some people, it is all stupid and pointless. But that split second fortifies Morrison, confirming that his quest to Everest is for everyone that heâs lost, and every heartstopping moment along the way. Itâs a spiritual pursuit, the kind that we make when we travel to a family member or friendâs favorite place to scatter their ashes; the kind that we make when we give eulogies, or just sit in the grass, staring into space, thinking about everything and nothing, everyone and no one.Â

Some may be driven to climb Everest just to say that they did it, while others are looking for something else, something with no name. They want to pierce the heavens and reach through the atmosphere to grasp the indescribable truth that unites us all. And if they donât make it back down to share that peace with the rest of us, it might be enough to experience it just once.

#6092. The power of Latinas’ Trump regret could swing this election

This story was originally published by The 19th.

This story was originally reported by Mel Leonor Barclay of The 19th. Meet Mel and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.

RIO GRANDE CITY, Texas â When Cynthia Villareal voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, she did so trusting his campaign promises of lower gas prices, border security and âassistance for the people â for the middle class.â

The 43-year-old mother of four turned out for Trump alongside a sizable majority of voters in heavily Latino Starr County, which hugs the border with Mexico and had reliably turned out for Democratic candidates for five generations.

Less than two years later, Villareal said the promise of her vote never materialized. âHe said gas prices were gonna go down. They havenât â they havenât at all,â said Villareal, who drives around the Rio Grande Valley for her job supervising home health aides and feels every little surge. Villareal manages workers in a shortstaffed, tough profession where wages have simply not kept up with the cost of living. Many of her best workers, she said, are immigrants without permanent legal status experiencing the brunt of Trumpâs immigration agenda.Â

âI mean, he didnât mention that these ICE agents were just going to be picking up all of these hardworking employees, you know, that have no backgrounds,â Villareal said, referring to immigrants without a criminal record. âTheyâre leaving people without their family, basically, and then some of the people are even dying in there,â she said of immigration detention. âLike, who knows what theyâre doing to these poor people?â

For Villareal, life is more expensive, and her job harder. âItâs just too much.âÂ

Latina votersâ rightward shift was a crucial part of Trumpâs reelection in 2024, and while more Latino men backed the president, Latinas actually made larger strides to the right in the last four presidential cycles.Â

Ahead of the midterms, Latinas are also registering higher levels of regret when thinking about their support for Trump, a dynamic that may decide the outcome of competitive races from Texas to Florida and beyond.Â

Voters like Villareal shed light on how Trump regret among this swingy and powerful group of voters âÂ Latinas vote at higher rates than Latino men â may be the swell that breaks into a blue wave for Democrats this November.Â

âI do think the narrative of this election could be that Latina women, in particular, help decide who is in control of the House of Representatives and the balance of government. And I say that because of the shifts weâve seen over time and the shifts back that we are seeing now among Latina women in particular,â said Stephanie Valencia, who studies Latino voters at Equis Research.

Latinosâ political power this cycle is spread across the midterms map. Latinos make up at least 15 percent of the population in six of the 17 most competitive congressional districts, as well as in 29 other districts considered broadly competitive, mostly in the Southwest, California and Florida. Latino voters could be the deciders in competitive races for the U.S. Senate in Texas and Florida. Also in Texas, Latinos could swing the most competitive governorâs race the state has seen in years and, in doing so, elect the first Latina to the stateâs top job.Â

âTrump appealed to their pocketbooks and people were suffering here. I also think people were tired. Weâve been Democratic for over 100 years â why donât we try something different?â said Cecilia HernÃ¡ndez, who founded the local political group Somos STARR this year in response to the big swings to the right sheâs seen in her community.Â

In an interview at the office of her familyâs trash collection business, HernÃ¡ndez said votersâ views are shifting this cycle.Â

âI think along with everything thatâs happening with immigration and with the cost of living today, what Iâve been receiving a lot is, âIâm in the middle,ââ HernÃ¡ndez said. âThey donât want to be seen as far right, and they donât want to be seen as far left, either.â

Latinas stand out in just how much they are feeling the burn of rising costs. They report higher levels of financial stress and are less optimistic about the national economy, according to multiple surveys of Latino voters conducted over the past year.Â

An expansive survey of Latinos conducted in the spring and sponsored by UnidosUS, a Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization, found that Latinas are more likely than Latino men to say that they have trouble meeting expenses â 23 percent of women vs. 17 percent of men. Men are much more likely to say they can meet their expenses and even have a little left over.

Thirty-eight percent of Latinas voted for Trump in 2024, versus half of Latino men, according to one high-quality analysis, driven by high costs and lack of confidence in the party in power on the economy. The UnidosUS survey of 3,000 Latino voters found that almost a third of Latinas who voted for Trump had regrets about their vote âÂ  seven points more than Latino men.Â

Regret is most striking among young Latinas: 42 percent said they would not vote for him again, a 12-point gap with young Latino men. Latina voters are more likely to register and turn out to vote, and with Latino voters skewing younger, young Latinas wield outsize political power.Â

âLatina women have a large gender pay gap. We also have higher unemployment. We also generally have the responsibility of going to the supermarket and paying the grocery bills and understanding that eggs and and everything else is more expensive,â said Katharine Pichardo, the president and CEO of the Latino Victory Project, which backs progressive Democrats. Latinas are more likely to be closely involved in their kidsâ education and doctorsâ appointments, a frontline view on rising costs that Pichardo said shaped how they voted in 2024 and their views on that vote now.Â

Melissa Morales, the president of Somos Votantes, which does political outreach to Latinos on behalf of Democratic candidates, said Latinas started peeling away from Trump almost immediately in his second term, while Latino men started shifting in the latter part of 2025.Â

While Latinos, like voters overall, broadly rank the cost of living as their top issue, the disparate impact of the administrationâs immigration policies on Latino communities is also registering among Latino voters.Â

A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid October found that only a third of Hispanic voters approve of the administrationâs handling of immigration. UnidosUSâ survey found significant gender gaps between Latino men and women. While both groups rank the importance of the issue about the same, Latinas were more likely to oppose policies like ending birthright citizenship and more funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Latinas were also more likely to support banning ICE from sensitive locations like schools and hospitals and to support requiring warrants for enforcement at home or in a workplace.Â

Some of the most dramatic shifts toward Trump and Republicans in 2024 were logged in Texasâ Rio Grande Valley, where Villareal lives. A string of counties in this part of Texas saw double-digit shifts in Trumpâs favor compared with the 2020 election, after significant shifts to the right from 2016 to 2020.Â

Latina voters in the Rio Grande Valley and around Texas will have a big impact on the Texas governorâs race, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa is locked in a dead heat with three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. Hinojosa describes herself as a populist who will tackle corruption and undue influence in government, which she ties to rising costs, weakened public schools and more.Â

Hinojosa rarely acknowledges the history-making potential of her campaign as a Latina in a state that has never elected a Latino to the governorâs mansion. She instead nods to it by saying that sheâd be the first governor from the Rio Grande Valley, which for Texans may as well mean the same thing.Â

Hinojosa, who is bilingual, flexes her Spanglish easily on the stump, telling voters that the most important lesson she ever got came from her mother was the scolding, âNo te dejes.â It doesnât have a direct translation in English.Â

âThe best thing I can come up with is, âKnow your worth and defend it,ââ Hinojosa said in an interview. Asked if the Spanish phrase was connecting with voters, Hinojosa said, âfor sure with Latinos, and 1,000 percent with Latinas.âÂ

âIâve learned on the campaign trail that this is a saying that is mostly passed down through the women in the family,â she added. âAnd I think itâs because of this knowledge that women have for their daughters, grandmothers have for their granddaughters, that the world is tough, and we have to be strong.âÂ

At campaign events in the Rio Grande Valley in September, several voters cited Hinojosaâs identity and approach to politics as a motivating factor.Â

Juanita Vallejo, 40, of Edinburg, Texas, said she sees Hinojosa as an âempowered woman,â and likes her firm stances in support of public schools and curtailing data centers.Â

âI donât want to say it this way, but Iâm going to say it â she wouldnât kiss ass to Trump. I think she would stand up to what is right,â said Rosie Hernandez, 56 of McAllen.Â

Hinojosa is one of the breakout candidates of the cycle, but she has had to plead for funding from national Democrats hesitant to spend in Texas. Earlier this month, a group of influential Latinos in Democratic political circles put pressure on Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who chairs the Democratic Governors Association (DGA), to invest $10 million in the Texas governorâs race. The DGA decided to send $1 million.

Valencia, who signed onto the letter, said Democratsâ investment in Hinojosaâs race has larger implications for the party and sends a message to Latinos. âSheâs a once-in-a-generation candidate from a state that is disproportionately Latino that has been the unicorn that Democrats have chased for decades,â Valencia said.Â

âTo have such a young, dynamic, charismatic Latina candidate in this environment and to not back her is a statement in and of itself, and it says a lot about how certain national Democrats feel about Texas and how they feel about certain candidates.âÂ

Hinojosaâs ability to build enthusiasm for her campaign after starting out with a low profile as a state legislator from Austin could bode well for one the biggest challenges when it comes to Latino voters: turning them out.Â

Latinos had the lowest turnout rates among the major racial and ethnic groups at 51 percent, compared with 71 percent among White voters and 60 percent among Black voters. Nearly 6 million eligible Latinas did not vote in 2024.

During a town hall in Houston with a local Latino influencer this month, Hinojosa mused about the event likely being the first time a candidate for governor hosts an event in Spanish. Before Hinojosa arrived on stage, the host ushered to the microphone a woman who identified herself as a 46-year-old Houston native who had never voted before. Holding a white and orange slip, she said she had registered to vote earlier that day. âQuiero cambio,â she said to cheers. âNo more Trump.âÂ

As both parties look ahead to the 2028 presidential election, theyâll have to contend with the fact that the Latino vote is a swing vote. Whatever gains Democrats make this cycle, they have a lot of ground to make up â especially with Latinas.

Nine days out from Election Day, Villareal said she is planning to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot. She described her vote this time as against Republicans â a register of regret â rather than about enthusiasm for the Democrats on the ticket.Â

âWe have to trust somebody. We have to vote for somebody no matter what,â Villareal said.Â

âAnd obviously, the way things went in 2024 with Republicans, there wasnât a change at all. Itâs just been worse. So weâre gonna try and see.â

CEO Dom Dragisich can claim a win in budget hotels, with Choice recently outperforming the industry average. But upscale brands grew at a much lower pace than the industry averages.

Choice Hotels' budget brands outpaced their U.S. industrywide benchmark in the summer, offering an early sign of progress for CEO Dominic Dragisich. But the company's higher-priced brands continued to lag.

U.S. revenue per available room (RevPAR) grew 3.8%, roughly a 1.5 percentage points above Wall Street's forecast. Dragisich said on a Monday earnings call that October's RevPAR was about 7%.

Dragisich's core problem in August was that Choice trailed in every price tier where it competes, from economy to upscale, according to CoStar data. The third quarter improved the picture without erasing it.

"We did narrow the gap," Dragisich said, referring to Choice's performance relative to industry averages.

Choice Hotels' third-quarter results gave CEO Dominic Dragisich an early sign of progress at the low end of the portfolio and little else. U.S. RevPAR rose 3.8%, about 1.5 percentage points ahead of Wall Street's forecast, and Dragisich said October RevPAR came in around 7%. But the gains were uneven: Choice's economy brands grew RevPAR 3.5% against an industry figure of about 2.5%, while its upscale and above brands grew just 1.1% against a roughly 4% industry average, and midscale and upper-midscale grew 3.6% against about 4.5%, according to Truist Securities citing CoStar data. Truist analysts C. Patrick Scholes and Gregory Miller wrote that the result implies Choice continues to lose market share, estimating fair share would have been closer to 5% to 6% growth. The U.S. hotel sector overall grew RevPAR 7% in the quarter, according to CBRE. Choice's room count is roughly flat year over year, and Dragisich said he wants net room growth of 2% to 4%. The company took a $24 million charge to terminate an option to acquire an unnamed European hospitality business after the option "eventually migrated to an obligation" and the target's growth became more lease-based. Choice said it is prioritizing organic growth, bought RV membership club Harvest Hosts for about $130 million on October 1, and sold two owned hotels for about $34 million in net proceeds while keeping the franchise agreements, leaving 17 owned hotels.

On its own, this category earned me about 900 points, a solid haul considering I'd earn only 180 points during quarters when live entertainment isn't offered. Still, while planning my purchase, I knew I could do better.

I've been a big fan of Rove over the past several months, using it for a variety of events and travel bookings. Rove offers members the opportunity to earn Rove miles, which are transferable to over 20 airline and hotel partners. This includes partners that aren't offered by any credit card loyalty programs, such as Frontier Miles and Lufthansa Miles & More.

It's free to join. Rove has its own travel booking portal, but for this particular purchase, I focused solely on its shopping portal. At the time, Rove offered 6.5 miles per dollar spent on StubHub purchases.

By booking my tickets through StubHub, I earned over 1,100 Rove miles. An unfortunate downside to shopping through Rove is that your miles often take an extended amount of time to post, which isn't uncommon with shopping portals. I'm still waiting for my miles to land in my account, which Rove indicates could take until early December.

Don't forget to start your purchase in the Rove app, on Rove's website or via its browser extension. If you're using the browser extension or accessing Rove via desktop, make sure all other shopping portal browser extensions are disabled.

With my decision to book through StubHub, there was one more way I could make my purchase work for me: Paze.

Currently, eligible Chase cardholders can earn 10 additional Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent when checking out with Paze at select merchants (through Dec. 31). StubHub is among those eligible for this promotion, meaning I could triple-dip on my purchase.

Checking out with Paze instead of the standard StubHub checkout process earned me roughly 1,800 additional points.

Using Paze at checkout is easy. You should be able to select it as a payment method on your eligible merchant's checkout screen, just as you would with a digital wallet or credit card.

One technical snag to note: I wasn't able to get Paze to work on mobile, but it worked on the first try on desktop. My transaction didn't say anything about Paze, so don't fret if the same is true for you. My points posted with no problem after a few days, but I recommend screen recording your purchase as proof if you're worried.

To summarize, here's how my earnings and their value broke down in the end:

*Valuations are according to TPG's November 2026 valuations and are not provided by credit card or program issuers.

My Freedom Flex is one of my oldest cards, but I still pull it out regularly, thanks in large part to strategies like this. While Chase's Paze promotion isn't limited to this card, the Freedom Flex is the only Chase card currently open to applicants that offers rotating 5% quarterly bonus categories.

Live entertainment reliably appears as a quarterly category every year, so I expect I'll be able to replicate this strategy (or a similar one) in 2027.

The more credit cards you open, the harder it becomes to find new welcome bonuses to earn. With welcome offers being the main way to earn heaps of rewards at once, it's important to have other ways to earn points and miles when that well starts to dry up.

Knowing how to maximize your purchases, especially larger ones or those you're splitting with friends or family, will help you maintain a large rewards balance even when you're not actively applying for new credit cards.

If you're currently not a Freedom Flex cardholder, you can apply and, upon approval, have the chance to earn $250 cash back (or 25,000 bonus points) after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. That's one of the easiest welcome bonuses to earn right now, but this offer ends soon.

If you hold an eligible Ultimate Rewards card, such as the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), you can transfer the points you earn with your Freedom Flex to Chase's 14 transfer partners.

The Timbers weren't able to walk away with the win, but the more than 3,800 points and miles I earned from the tickets I purchased helped ease the sting of that loss.

You can create a strategy like this with virtually any card in your wallet. Consider the offers, limited-time earning rates and promotions that are available for your specific card; take a look at shopping portals like Rakuten and Rove to see what they offer; and use sites like Cashback Monitor to make sure you're getting the best deal.

Effectively maximizing your card's earning potential means thoroughly understanding which offers and deals are available to you and knowing how to combine them. It requires a little extra work on your part, but that effort will be worth it when those extra rewards help take you on your next dream trip.

#6086. Right-wing media and the mystery of Texas’ transgender mailers

On Thursday night, the smear at the heart of the mysterious transgender mailers that have rocked the final weeks of the midterm elections in Texas completed its journey. What began as baseless social media whispers quickly ascended the ladder of conservative influence, jumped into mailboxes across the Lone Star State and ultimately into the comforting prime-time embrace of Fox News.

At a town hall in Fort Worth, a Texas mother of six named Rebekah Smith told Vice President JD Vance that her 11-year-old daughter had received a letter explaining how to transition without her parents ever knowing, and asked how Republicans would keep the government out of her family. “I don’t know who sent that letter to your child,” the vice president said, “but I think the person who sends a letter to an 11-year-old about gender transition, what I call that in my family is a pervert, and that person ought to go to prison.” Host Jesse Watters, never one to let a grievance go to waste, promised that Fox would investigate “this perverted letter.” Vance asked Smith to talk to his staff because he would “like the Department of Justice to investigate that” as well.

Watters rushed to promote the spectacle. “WHOA! Texas MOM tells JD Vance her DAUGHTER received a letter telling her TO TRANSITION TO A BOY,” he posted on X, followed by Vance’s promise. Missing from that framing was the question that should have governed the segment: Who actually sent the material?

Nobody on that stage mentioned that the pamphlet was a fake. Nobody mentioned that the real transgender advocacy group named inside it had disavowed the mailer. Nobody mentioned that sworn testimony filed that same week had tied the text messages that accompanied it to a national Republican organization. The vice president was asking federal prosecutors to chase a forgery that may well have originated in his own party’s orbit — and he was doing it on a network whose viewers had been marinating in that forgery for weeks.

The race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico has become a crucible for dark-money maneuvers. As polls show the Republican grip on the Lone Star State slipping, conservative campaigns and their surrogates have resorted to increasingly desperate tactics. In early October, for example, Talarico took a brief hiatus from the campaign trail to recover from a severe case of the flu. Rather than accepting a routine human illness, the right-wing echo chamber treated a temporary absence as evidence of mental illness. Within days, the fabricated scandal has collapsed — yet the machinery of right-wing media simply pivoted to amplifying a more insidious operation designed to trigger visceral outrage.

This second October surprise involved millions of unsolicited text messages and a wave of physical mailers sent to Texas households with materials that directed readers to the website of the Transgender Education Network of

It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward.

Texas while inserting provocative advice on child emancipation that the real organization says it never authored or authorized. By flooding the electorate with extreme material disguised as progressive advocacy, right-wing operatives appear to have sought to create a fake controversy that could be weaponized in attack ads and campaign speeches. Vance, for instance, told the Fox News audience that Talarico has “a weird fascination with trans kids,” and that “he’ll probably defend the right of the person sending the letter, not the right of the parent who is rightfully creeped out by this.” Vance claimed that Talarico “has actually called it abusive when parents try to prevent their children from transitioning” and that Paxton “has fought hard to prosecute those people, whereas James Talarico has fought hard to protect those people.” Even the distortion had been laundered by then — Talarico called denying a child’s gender identity abusive, a different claim from saying parents must permit medical transition, but at the top of the ladder the difference no longer exists.

That is how a smear works in the closed ecosystem of the American right. It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward. An anonymous account posts it; an influencer adopts it; a donor-funded outlet reports the influencer’s outrage as news; an elected official demands an investigation, and the demand becomes proof the story matters; cable news books the controversy; a vice president promises federal action. Each rung launders the one below it. The correction, when it comes, travels in the opposite direction and arrives nowhere.

The paper trail looks like what you would expect from a covert operation. Texas Transgender Student Union LLC was formed in Wyoming on Sept. 2 through a commercial registered agent that helps owners stay anonymous. After CBS News Texas visited the agent’s address in Sheridan, Wyoming, the agent announced it was resigning. The mailers listed a Houston-area post office box. The Texas Observer reported that the barcode on the envelopes traced to a mail-tracking company that has taken federal campaign money from only one group this year, the National Republican Congressional Committee. The committee said it had nothing to do with the mailers, and the company would not say who paid. CBS News Texas reported that the bulk-mail permit belongs to an Illinois printer owned by the Zerrusen family, who have given heavily to Republican PACs and been photographed with Donald Trump.

When the real Transgender Education Network of Texas filed a petition in Travis County court to unmask the perpetrators behind the impersonation campaign, the partisan safety nets of the Texas judiciary eventually snapped into action. A deposition of Infobip, the messaging company that delivered the texts, which a Travis County judge ordered made public, indicated that the texts were sent on behalf of the Republican Women’s Caucus Fund and a man named John Braun. But on Friday, the Texas Supreme Court, composed entirely of judges appointed by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, issued an administrative stay that blocked its release. Chris Hilton, an attorney who previously served under Paxton, defended him during his impeachment trial and was later pushed out of office amid sexual harassment allegations, argued on behalf of the company that the mailers were not political speech because they named no candidate or party.

Dirty tricks are an old tradition of American politics. This cycle, Republican PACs in Nevada mailed a flyer calling a nonpartisan candidate, Danielle Ford, the “AOC of Nevada,” hoping voters would mistake her for the actual Democratic nominee, Aaron Ford. This week also brought word that the group that funded Cornel West’s 2024 ballot drives raised every dollar through a dark-money network bankrolled by Elon Musk.

The president’s party whines about decoy candidates in Alaska while running them at home. Ratf**king is a long and proud Republican tradition, and the Texas operation fits inside perfectly.

#6084. Skift Commerce Summit 2026: Five Decisions in the Room

AI agents are here. Travel isn’t ready. Decisions made today will determine who controls the booking, the customer relationship, and the economics of travel commerce.

AI agents are already booking travel. One invite-only booking agent reported more than $1 billion a year in transaction volume, half of which was travel. Investors have already placed their bets on who wins and who loses. Most travel companies are still built for a traveler who searches, scrolls, and clicks.

Direct or third-party distribution used to be the primary choice travel suppliers had to make. Now an agent may decide which brands show up, which system can complete the booking, which card pays, and which loyalty program earns. Hotels alone spend more than $105 billion a year on distribution, and AI companies want a share of it.

The agents are here. Travel is not ready. Travel companies have to connect the dots inside the new travel commerce stack, and Skift Commerce Summit brings senior commerce leaders together around five decisions travel companies have to make now.

Operator Ticket $275 · for the people who run commerce at travel companies. Vendor Ticket $1,500 · capped, limited supply. Group rates: events@skift.com

AI has moved quickly into the travel customer journey for inspiration and planning, but not booking… yet. According to Skift Research, direct suppliers lead with a 49% net comfort score, followed by packaged tours at 37%, travel agents at 34%, loyalty portals at 31%, and OTAs at 20%. AI and chatbots score -7%. [1]

However, Skift Research describes the discovery path shifting from “search-scroll-compare” toward “ask-shortlist-decide.” As soon as travelers gain confidence in booking through AI platforms, space for brands “on the shelf” is poised to shrink. [2]

Hotels, airlines, or other travel retailers are racing to optimize for AI discoverability, but the more control they give to AI platforms, the more they risk losing direct customer relationships. They have to decide how to prioritize what they value most, and whether distribution alone is worth it if they become interchangeable within someone else’s interface.

Travelers are comfortable booking across a wide range of channels, but that also means today’s marketplace has a wider swath of competitors.

Travel’s AI discussion is moving downstream. It’s not only a customer relationship question, but also a technological one. Even if they’re discovered, booked, and integrated into the loyalty ecosystem, brands have to ensure the infrastructure works when an AI agent starts to handle trip management.

It’s one thing for an AI assistant to drive traffic to a brand’s site. The open decision is whether travel companies find it worthwhile to give an agent the tools to compare offers, change or cancel an order, and fix problems on the traveler’s behalf.

A better conversational front end can’t compensate for fragmented inventory, legacy servicing systems, or commerce technology designed for humans.

Banks, card issuers, retailers, membership programs, and technology platforms have built businesses around the traveler without having to own (or even sell) an airline seat or hotel room. They can make money from payments, rewards, subscriptions, advertising, financing, and the broader customer relationship surrounding a trip.

That changes the competitive economics for travel companies. A bank can use travel to increase card spend. A membership business can use it to make a subscription more valuable. A technology platform can influence the purchase while monetizing the customer elsewhere. These companies can compete for the same traveler without depending on the booking itself for most of their economics.

The decision is how much of that value suppliers and other travel-native companies can capture themselves as more of the commercial relationship moves into ecosystems built outside the industry.

Non-travel companies are profiting more and more off travel, stepping in to sell ancillaries and earn loyalty. 32% of travelers rank credit-card or bank loyalty programs as the most rewarding, ahead of hotel programs at 26% and airline programs at 20%. [1]

The direct-versus-third-party debate has shaped travel distribution strategy for decades. The economics have never been as simple as choosing one side. A direct booking can carry marketing, loyalty, technology, and acquisition costs of its own. An intermediary can bring incremental demand, reach a customer the brand would not have acquired directly, or fill inventory that otherwise would have gone unsold.

The channel mix is also getting more crowded. OTAs remain important, but banks, credit-card programs, membership platforms, social channels, AI interfaces, and other partners are creating new paths to the customer. Each comes with different costs, different access to customer data, and a different ability to generate demand.

The decision is which channels produce the strongest return for a particular customer, market, and trip. The best distribution strategy may use direct channels to deepen valuable customer relationships while paying intermediaries when they can deliver demand more efficiently than the brand can acquire it on its own.

“The competition to be a travel distributor has never been this intense,” says Skift Research, pointing to credit cards, social platforms, AI-native tools, OTAs, and suppliers all competing for a larger role in the booking journey. [3]

Travel companies can find unique growth opportunities by leveraging an existing customer base, brand, asset, or operating capability to create a new revenue stream. The challenge occurs when they find themselves wading into businesses they were not originally built to run.

The decision is how far that expansion should go. Some adjacencies strengthen the core business because they use capabilities the company already has. Others require new technology, operations, capital, or customer behavior that the company has never had to manage before. Growth can create leverage. It can also create complexity faster than revenue.

A Skift and ZS survey found that 75% of senior travel executives have non-core assets they can monetize, but only 32% described their current approach to doing so as “very” innovative. [4]

Discovery no longer guarantees ownership. Distribution extends beyond an OTA or supplier website and, indeed, beyond travel-native companies themselves. Payments and loyalty can generate value beyond the booking. AI is becoming another intermediary, another channel, and eventually the buyer itself.

Every travel company now faces the same question: which parts of the customer relationship, the transaction and the economics do you need to own before an agent stands between you and the traveler, and which can sit on someone else’s platform?

The Skift Commerce Summit is built to help you answer it, and to show you where your company is least ready.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

#6080. James O’Keefe election sting ends in his own felony voter fraud charges

Conservative activist James O’Keefe set out to expose alleged vulnerabilities in Minnesota’s election system. Now, he faces felony charges stemming from the undercover operation.

O’Keefe, formerly of Project Veritas and current CEO of the O’Keefe Media Group, and conservative influencer Cameron Higby were charged Wednesday with unlawful voting and identity theft after allegedly impersonating registered voters at Minneapolis polling places during the state’s Aug. 11 primary.

According to Hennepin County prosecutors, the men wore disguises, used fake accents and provided election workers with the names of registered voters without their knowledge or permission. They filmed the encounters and later posted videos claiming to expose weaknesses in Minnesota’s voter registration procedures.

The operation targeted the state’s *vouching* system, which allows registered voters to verify the residency of people seeking to register on Election Day. The process requires sworn statements and identifying information from prospective voters.

Neither O’Keefe nor Higby cast a ballot or signed the required vouching oath. Prosecutors contend that misrepresenting their identities while beginning the voting process was itself unlawful.

O’Keefe defended the operation as investigative journalism, calling the prosecution an attack on First Amendment rights. Higby also denied breaking the law, saying the pair intended to expose election vulnerabilities.

But Minnesota officials say the latest operation demonstrated something different from what O’Keefe intended.

Election workers noticed suspicious behavior and reported it, prompting an investigation. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said the state’s system for identifying and responding to potential misconduct functioned as intended. This vouching process itself accounted for fewer than 0.6% of votes cast in Minnesota’s 2024 general election, according to state election officials.

O’Keefe and Higby are scheduled to appear in court Nov. 16. Neither has been convicted.

#6069. Judge tosses DOJ lawsuit seeking to delay Alaska vote certification

A federal judge on Sunday tossed a lawsuit from the Trump administration that sought to delay the certification of the Alaska Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.

Sullivan faces Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola and two other candidates in a contest that could help decide control of the Senate. One of those candidates is also named Dan Sullivan, which prompted the Trump administration to file its lawsuit, alleging that, under the state’s ranked choice system, voters may rank the challenger instead of the incumbent.

The complaint also asked the judge to allow a delay until an “investigation” into whether votes for the challenger, listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., should have gone to the senator, who is listed as Dan S. Sullivan.

But in her ruling Sunday, Judge Sharon L. Gleason of the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska said the relief requested by the administration was “infeasible.”

“[Many] voters have already cast their ballots in the November 2026 general election. Those cast ballots have been commingled and cannot now be segregated or the identity of the person who cast each ballot ascertained,” she wrote.

Should the Trump administration appeal the ruling, it would go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

The case started on Oct. 22, when the Trump administration filed the lawsuit, arguing that the courts should delay the certification of the Alaska Senate race if the incumbent Sullivan were to lose and the margin was less than the number of votes the second Sullivan received.

The Justice Department argued that voters could be confused by the presence of a namesake challenger on the state’s ballot and not cast their intended vote for the incumbent. Initially, the lawsuit was filed against the state, but Peltola and Democrats have intervened to argue that the case should be tossed.

Then last week, The New York Times reported that aides for Peltola were involved in the effort to recruit the second Sullivan to enter the Senate race. The DOJ filed an amended complaint accusing Peltola and Democrats of misleading the courts.

“Apparently emboldened by the success of their reported plot to deceive Alaskan voters, Alaskans For Mary and the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] appear to have turned to misleading this Court,” the DOJ filing said.

Trump himself has accused Peltola of executing a “FRAUD ON THE AMERICAN PUBLIC” and called for both her and the second Sullivan to be removed from the Senate ballot. Under federal law, the state finalized its ballot more than a month ago.

Peltola and Democrats pushed back in their own filing Friday, calling the DOJ’s claims “nonsense.” They also said that they “lack knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief about the truth or falsity of the allegation concerning the purposes of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy and therefore deny any allegation about those purposes.”

And on Saturday, the Republican-led Alaska state government called on Gleason to dismiss the lawsuit, saying that “the relief demanded is inappropriate and not even possible given Alaskan voters’ vital right to ballot secrecy.”

Earlier this year Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired school teacher, successfully sued in state court to be included on the ballot after election officials had previously removed his name. The state Supreme Court ruled that the second Sullivan was a valid candidate and should be included.

Under Alaska rules, voters can rank up to four candidates on the Senate ballot. If no one takes a majority of first-place votes, the candidate in last position is eliminated, with those votes assigned to the voters’ next choice. The process repeats until one candidate has a majority of the remaining votes.

#6066. The strange new math behind the price of your groceries

Walmart recently published a list of things it promises not to do to its customers.

âWe price the product, not the person,â Walmart CEO John Furner announced in a September letter to customers. âYour income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay wonât change the price,â he promised. Nor, he said, would the retailerâs AI shopping assistant, Sparky, use information customers shared to raise prices or conceal cheaper options.

This was nice to hear. I hadnât previously considered that telling a computer I needed toilet paper might result in an emergency toilet-paper rate. There is something faintly unnerving about the specificity of a corporate reassurance, particularly when it introduces several possibilities you hadnât thought to worry about.

It made me preemptively nostalgic for the little paper price tag beneath a box of cereal. Thereâs something reassuringly stupid about it. It tells you what the cereal costs. It doesnât know how much money you make, whether youâre in a hurry or what the temperature is outside. Unless an employee comes along with a new sticker, the person reaching for the same box ten minutes later sees the same number. A modest achievement, perhaps, but one Iâm growing increasingly fond of.

The appeal isnât really the paper. Itâs the transparency of the arrangement. As retailers gather more information about their customers and acquire increasingly sophisticated pricing tools, shoppers risk knowing less about why theyâre paying what theyâre paying. The problem isnât simply higher grocery bills. Itâs the possibility of a transaction in which one side can examine the other in exquisite detail, while the other can barely see the rules.

What prompted the letter from Furner is that Walmart is expanding its use of electronic shelf labels, little screens that let employees update prices digitally from a central computer instead of replacing stickers by hand. The change makes sense. Furner points out that updating paper tags is tedious work, and heâd rather employees spend their afternoons helping customers than tending to a small forest of adhesive rectangles. Digital labels can also help ensure the price on the shelf matches the price at checkout.

And electronic labels arenât, in themselves, surge pricing. Walmart says it doesnât use them to change prices according to who is shopping or the time of day. But efficiency is a different question from trust. Making a price easier to change isnât necessarily a problem. Making it harder to understand how that price was reached might be.

Want more great food writing and recipes? Sign up for Salonâs free food newsletter, The Bite.

Weâve already accepted a surprisingly elaborate set of conditions for saving money on groceries. Download the app. Make an account. Remember the password. Clip the digital coupon before you leave home. After handing over our personal information and completing several minor administrative tasks, weâre permitted to save 75 cents on yogurt. The store, meanwhile, gets a rather detailed account of our preferences. What happens when that bargain runs in reverse?

Last December, Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found that shoppers using Instacart were sometimes shown different prices for identical groceries from the same store at the same time. At one Safeway in Washington, D.C., an 18-ounce box of Signature SELECT Corn Flakes appeared for $2.99, $3.49 and $3.69, depending on whose screen you were looking at.Â

Instacart said the shoppers were assigned to pricing experiments randomly, not sorted by income, demographics or browsing history. It ended the tests after the investigation. That distinction matters, especially because the research didnât establish that anyoneâs personal habits were being used against them. But it demonstrated how quietly prices can diverge when the shopper sees only the number assigned to her. You canât question a difference you have no way of seeing.

I buy a lot of black beans. Enough, presumably, that a supermarketâs software could identify me as a woman with firm opinions about legumes. If that earns me a coupon, wonderful. Iâm considerably less enthusiastic about the possibility of an algorithm deciding that my apparent dependence on black beans means I could stand to pay another 30 cents per can. Itâs one thing to recognize a loyal customer. Itâs another to recognize a captive audience.

Other pricing algorithms raise different questions (McDonaldâs, for instance, faces a lawsuit alleging AI-assisted price coordination among franchises, which the company denies). Prices have always fluctuated; coupons have always rewarded some shoppers more than others. Nor should computers be banished from the business of deciding what things cost. But the supermarket is not an airline, and dinner should not require the same vigilance as booking a flight.

Walmartâs promise is worth taking seriously. The company has drawn a clear line around how it says it will use customer information, and thatâs preferable to leaving shoppers guessing. But itâs a corporate commitment, not a rule every retailer must follow. And the fact that a supermarket now feels obliged to assure us it wonât charge extra because we seem hurried or financially comfortable suggests how strange our expectations have become.

Perhaps itâs naive to want a supermarket not to use what it knows about me against me. Still, I donât need the price tag to know me. I need it to tell me what the cereal costs.

This preserves the illusion that the right doesnât hate female athletes while portraying the players â the white ones at least â as fragile, helping to reassure an insecure male audience.Â

In the past, this kind of tap dance has worked. Now, as Watters implied, itâs floundering, feeling much too tepid when compared Foxâs online competitors and actual politicians flinging unprintable slurs. Watters suggested as much during another segment, when he argued that Republicans need more âfear pornâ if they want to win.

His use of the word âpornâ is telling. Watters was arguing that it doesnât do to be coy any longer â that only the hard-core stuff will move the base. But for Fox News, that would come at the cost of losing advertising dollars and the eyeballs of less radical viewers. This is a true dilemma â and itâs one that couldnât happen to a more deserving network.Â
