#6062. Ali Velshi is on the Big Board now

Six years ago, Donald Trump dropped â11th Hourâ host Ali Velshiâs name at several campaign rallies as an example of the so-called âfake news mediaâ getting what the president thought he deserved: a taste of âlaw and order.â

In May 2020, while covering the Minneapolis protests that arose in response to the murder of George Floyd, MSNBCâs live coverage caught Velshi being struck in the knee by one of the rubber bullets police fired into the crowd.

Months later, Trump referred to the incident multiple times on the campaign trail as âthe most beautiful thing,â earning laughter and applause from supporters. But an emotional Velshi recalled that moment differently in June 2026, as he said goodbye to his old weekend showâs audience.

In that moment and others, he told âVelshiâ viewers that democracy, fairness, transparency and accountability took yet another hit. âThis is how it unfolds. Not always with legislation, not always with imprisonment. Sometimes with a rubber bullet. Sometimes with a police escort. Philosophy repeated until enough people believe it. . . and they believe that the next step becomes possible,â he said. âThe press is not the enemy of the people. The press is the peopleâs guarantee that they will know what is done in their name.â

Then, he reminded everyone watching that the midterm elections were 148 days away.

When I spoke with him last Thursday, the veteran journalist repeated his belief in the pressâ witnessing role, unshaken by the massive changes occurring in the news industry.Â  One of those changes places him at the networkâs famous Big Board as the chief data reporter for MS NOWâformerly MSNBCâcarrying on an election-night tradition made famous by Steve Kornacki.

Velshiâs on-air analysis will be augmented by an additional feed called VelshiCast, a behind-the-scenes look that will stream on MS NOWâs YouTube channel.

Other aspects of MS NOWâs live coverage remain familiar to longtime MSNBC viewers, with Rachel Maddow leading the channelâs supergroup of Nicolle Wallace, Chris Hayes, Jen Psaki, Lawrence OâDonnell, Stephanie Ruhle, Michael Steele, Symone Sanders Townsend, Ari Melber and Peter Alexander.

As for Kornacki, he became NBC Newsâ chief data analyst after NBCUniversalâs owner, Comcast, spun off MS NOW along with USA Network, Syfy, E!, and its other cable channels into a venture known as Versant.

Journalism is in a precarious time, but this administration has placed particular pressure on TV newsrooms. With Paramount Skydanceâs acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, CNNâs and CBSâ teams are facing rounds of buyouts and return-to-office orders to thin their ranks. Meanwhile, Status reported that October 2026 is Fox Newsâ lowest-rated month since December 2023, with the network averaging 1.1 million total-day viewers.

Velshi remains optimistic about his profession, as he said in our wide-ranging conversation about his plans to make the Big Board even more essential on this midterm election night.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Salon: A lot of coverage cited what you said in your farewell message for your last weekend show. One of them, and I think this is important, is that you were reminding people that the show was ending 148 days before the midterm elections.

Well, weâre here now. Youâve started your weekday show, and Iâm curious to hear your impressions of how you think things are going, in terms of that dialogue with viewers and whatâs coming up about Tuesday from a data perspective.

Thanks for actually thinking that through because there is a real through line. I miss my old show a lot, but you know, that moment was so important. What I was trying to do that night, and what Iâve been trying to do since, is convey the idea that this isnât about partisan politics. This is about civic engagement. This is about democracy, and nobodyâs going to do that for you, right? Democracy is not something you pick off a shelf. It is work for all of us all the time, and I donât think weâll ever be free of a moment when democracy is on autopilot.

And so, right now, everybodyâs responsibility is to participate actively. I have a sense that pretty much all of our regular viewers, certainly people in our MS NOW community, are heavily engaged. Theyâre big consumers of news and information. They probably already voted. If not, theyâre planning to, because some people just like voting on election day because itâs exciting. But this moment wants more of us. It needs us not just to vote, but to be engaged in the dialogue, to commit to democracy, to help other people vote, to feel like we are in community with each other, to save democracy.

This doesnât matter whether youâre a Democrat or Republican or an independent, or you donât even think politics matters to you. And I will say that since that day that I left the show, Iâve only felt stronger about this, and Iâve only felt that people are understanding their assignment very, very well. And weâre seeing this from a data perspective.

Every single day, we get new data that shows early voting and advance voting. It is remarkable. At the low end, the states are up 20% compared to the last midterm elections in 2022. Weâre not even bothering to compare it to a presidential election because theyâre different beasts. In some states, early voting is up 40%. Now, what would possibly explain that? Itâs enthusiasm amongst voters. So people are going out and theyâre taking the assignment very, very seriously. Iâm very heartened by that.

So letâs talk about your new role and what you do with the data, and the conversation you have with people about that. Because I think that especially around elections, some of our pessimism and optimism comes from polling, but not necessarily from data.

Youâre 100% right. Thank you for that question too. I led the show on Monday night with three people: Kabir Khanna, whoâs our head of data and analytics; Dave Wasserman from the Cook Political Report; and Larry Sabato from the University of Virginiaâs Crystal Ball. These are the three data nerdiest guys around.

I think itâs important to understand that raw data is of no use to anyone. Even slightly interpreted data is of no use to anyone. You have to be able to look at it holistically. You have to look at polls and also understand their margins of error. You have to understand trends in polling so that even if a poll is good, meaning itâs statistically sound, that doesnât mean itâs correct. Polls have errors, and then the decision about how an election goes depends in part on polling, in part on trends, in part on the weather, in part on the news cycle, in part on whether your decision in an election is because youâre voting in favor of someone youâre excited about or youâre voting against someone youâre mad at.

I think raw data without analysis should be a crime â¦ OK, in this world where people make crimes out of everything, Iâm not sure thatâs the right thing to say. But my point is, itâs really bad. Itâs bad for democracy to throw raw data at people and hope that they interpret it. Itâs also bad for democracy to throw raw data at people and hope they follow it. Like, what am I trying to tell you? If I tell you these races are all ahead, I may not be giving you useful information for you.

So part of it is also managing expectations amongst voters. A âblue waveâ or a âbig blue wave,â I donât use that terminology . . .Â  But Iâll give you a range. Iâll tell you that as of today, the Democrats are likely to win a minimum of eight seats in the House and a maximum of probably in the mid-30s. Thatâs probably the range. Might I be wrong? Absolutely. But thatâs what I want people to understand. And then Iâm going to give you the clues to understand how I got there, so that you can follow along with me. Iâd rather make a data interpreter out of everybody who watches us than be their data interpreter.

â[P]eople are understanding their assignment very, very well.â

In terms of the election night and you being at the BigÂ  â are you guys still calling it the Big Board?

We are. Yes. I tried to call it The Magic Board of Wisdom, but no one took to that.

What you and Kornacki were doing at the Big Board really became a thing over the last decade or so.

People learned to consume election night coverage based around it. I know a lot of folks who may not necessarily watch every single moment of coverage, but keep an eye on developments with the sound off, based on whatâs going on with the Big Board. Itâs kind of like a lot of folks might go into a restaurant or a bar with the TV tuned to a game, but on mute. Iâd like to know how you feel about that mode of consumption.

Well, look: The bottom line is, scientifically, peopleâs visual consumption is their No. 1 source of information consumption. I mean, you can make the argument that smell is actually more important for your survival, but weâre not talking about survival here. The visual component hits before the auditory component does, so thatâs never going to change.

What may change is whether people watch it on their phone or their TV or, you know, through AI glasses, but the visual component is still stronger for everyone than anything else. So we spend a lot of time adjusting the size of the boxes on TV and deciding whether there are too many of them, and whether this is helpful information or confusing information. We want to make it very obvious that this is complicated information, and weâre working hard because itâs our job to present this to you in a way that is consumable and accessible. Which, by the way, has been sort of my stock in trade for my entire career.

So Iâm committed to making this the most visually easy experience. If you donât have audio, and if youâre sitting in a bar or sitting on a plane or wherever, and you canât hear me, youâll still understand everything thatâs going on.

In this election, thereâs emotional sentiment, psychological underpinnings, and consumer sentiment to account for. How much are you able to go into those factors on election night? Because each is also locally dependent. We have a lot of reporting determining the key races, but if you look down the ballot beyond the candidates, you have initiatives and other legislation driven by sentiment.

So we have two ways of measuring sentiment. One is in what we call our voter poll. Thatâs what you would know of as an exit poll, right? We do that in partnership with others. Itâs probably 1000 questions that really allow you to put meat on the bones of the result you just saw.

And I actually think thatâs one of the sad things about fast-moving election coverage, is that you sometimes donât get to sit there and say, âLet me explain to you. We actually know. We asked these voters why they made the decision they made, and they actually told us. So we donât have to extrapolate. We donât have to, you know, twist ourselves into pretzels. We actually have that information.â

âOur capabilities are better today than they were a year ago.â

So I will tell you, a lot of that will happen prior to polls closing. So people think to themselves, âYour coverage always starts before the polls close, or before the polls close in the place that I care aboutâ â thatâs actually where you get the most context. So weâre going to start early in the evening on Tuesday with our exit polls. I think we release them at 5 oâclock, and thatâs great information.

And then subsequently, we are covering every one of those ballot measures. In fact, thatâs part of what Iâm studying today. Iâm studying both the exit polls and the ballot measures today to really understand how theyâre going to correlate with the results.

You know, Iâm an economics reporter, so things like consumer sentiment are really, really clear to me. You know, people keep saying the economy is the most important thing in this election. I remind people the economy is the most important thing in pretty much every single election there is, with the exception of an actual war in which Americans have troops on the ground or an international threat. Thatâs the truth. People care most about how this affects them.

I think thereâs an interesting intersection in this election between people who care about the things that affect them, like the economy, gas, things like that, and people who care about democracy deeply. The second one can be a bit of an extra abstraction for people. The first oneâs absolutely not. So I have to measure how I tell those stories.

So Iâm going to take a little bit of a 30,000-foot view here and look at this in terms of MS NOWâs position in the news industry. On one side, you have Fox, part of a massive media conglomerate, with ratings declining right now, days before the election.

And on the other, CNN. Thereâs a lot of restructuring going on there related to the Skydance merger, a lot of conversation about that. And then thereâs you guys. Iâm wondering if, at this point, things feel different, just in terms of what youâre able to do.Â  I donât necessarily mean just kind of financial resources, but also what kind of backing Versant is giving you this time versus when you were part of the larger NBC Universal structure.Â  I realize this is still a very new situation, but again â Iâm curious about the pros and cons.

At the moment, itâs all pros. So first of all, weâre the scrappy, leaner player in the game now. . . Can we compete with other people? Yes, we can, and weâre doing it very well. As I said, the things that matter â the ability to conduct the analysis, and I donât mean that just for the big board â weâre able to do that. We are going to match everybodyâs expertise and probably exceed it.Â  Our capabilities are better today than they were a year ago.

No. 2, weâre literally the tip of the spear for the conversation that is happening in America right now around what country do we want to be. How is this solvable? Weâre right there.

And Iâm sorry for the folks around us who are dealing with these structural issues and trying to figure out what they are and how to represent themselves in this moment of turmoil, but weâre not struggling with this at all.

But we are not one thing, right? We are covering the story with all the complexity of an electorate that is spread out along the political spectrum. Iâm sure there are some of our viewers who love the idea that the [Democratic Socialists of America] is ascendant, and there are some of our viewers who love the fact that there are ex-conservatives, ex-Republicans like David Jolly running for governor in Florida. Or that there are some Republicans who are running for office because theyâve demonstrated their ability to be independent thinkers. We have the ability at MS NOW to have those discussions across the political spectrum. Weâre very comfortable with it.

In 2024, I interviewed Lawrence OâDonnell right before the election, and we talked a lot about the state of journalism, and specifically how effective the media was in terms of questioning Trump and holding him accountable. I think weâve seen shifts since then, but Iâd love to know whether youâve seen any shift one way or another.

I think so. Once in a while, maybe even daily, Iâll see some headline from a mainstream news organization that makes me cringe. That makes me think: Are these reporters and editors not understanding the moment that weâre in? Are they not understanding that that weirdly neutral headline that you just wrote doesnât actually communicate what just happened? It doesnât capture the fact that your reader and your viewer and your listener are shocked and possibly outraged and really struggling with whatâs going on. But you just wrote a headline that looks like this is just a governmental development, something that the Department of Justice did.

I think most of us are better at this than we were in 2024, and certainly better than we were in 2020 and 2016. Yes, weâve all gotten a lot better. There are still remnants in mainstream media of journalists who treat the activities of this government and this administration as normal, and thatâs not a journalistically difficult thing to unwind, right? Itâs not.

Itâs not difficult to say that journalism exists for two reasons: to bear witness for those of our consumers who cannot bear witness on their own because they canât travel to go see the scene, they canât go to the protest and they canât go to the press conference. We are there to bear witness, and we are there to hold power to account. Thatâs it. If you are not doing those two things every single day, you are not doing your job.

And there are still some members of the mainstream media who are not doing their job. This has nothing to do with what your opinion is or where you are in the political spectrum. Are you bearing witness and are you holding power to account? I think we are generally better at that. Now, what that has done is result in lawsuits. It has resulted in bans for some of us from the White House. Thatâs the consequence of doing your job properly, and thatâs okay. We will meet and face the consequences. Weâll fight back, and we will fight for our right and our viewersâ and our listenersâ and our readersâ rights to get the information that they deserve. Thatâs how you can tell weâre doing a better job at this. When they come for you, it means youâre doing your job.

#6060. The EU and Canada Struggle to Define Their Relationship

World Brief: The EU and Canada Struggle to Define Their Relationship

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how deep Canada-EU ties will go, the resignation of European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, and China’s latest political and military purge.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted senior European Union officials in Montreal on Thursday to discuss bolstering trade and defense ties. Notably downplayed, though, was the EU’s previous offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the 27-nation bloc.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how deep Canada-EU ties will go, the resignation of European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, and China’s latest political and military purge.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted senior European Union officials in Montreal on Thursday to discuss bolstering trade and defense ties. Notably downplayed, though, was the EU’s previous offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the 27-nation bloc.

Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea during her annual State of the European Union address.

“We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said while standing beside Carney. “We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well.” Canadian officials applauded the proposal, with Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador to the EU, saying at the time that Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc.

Yet a statement prepared for this week’s annual Canada-EU summit included a watered-down version of such a future. Rather than explicitly noting the proposed associate member status, the draft text offered “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself,” Politico reported on Wednesday. According to Reuters, a previous draft had included at least two direct mentions of Canada’s associate member status while adding that defining the term would take another year.

“Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography, but we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible,” von der Leyen said on Thursday. She described this type of relationship as open “only to our closest partners outside of Europe who are ready to open a new frontier together,” and she stressed that associate member status is not fully off the table.

Von der Leyen’s decision to back off from her full-throated appeal for associate Canadian membership may have been made due to some member nations’ hesitance. Several EU countries, particularly Germany, had argued that they would not approve such a designation, as it had no legal precedent and had not been fully fleshed out. Others accused von der Leyen of not discussing the idea with European leaders first.

“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem,” one diplomat told the Guardian. “This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying.”

The EU’s move to soften the language is likely to appease at least one foreign leader: U.S. President Donald Trump. Trump had called the EU’s initial proposal “laughable” and warned that such a designation could be considered a “hostile act” that could prompt the White House to cut off trade with Europe in certain areas. Already, U.S. trade relations with Canada and the European Union are greatly strained, with Trump repeatedly returning to his tariff war for economic leverage.

Still, Carney appeared to be unconcerned by Thursday’s language shift. “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”

Who will run the ECB next? European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde announced on Thursday that she will step down from her role in February, officially triggering a race to determine who will take up the mantle of one of the European Union’s top posts. Her eight-year term was set to end in October 2027; her early departure allows the EU to choose her successor before one of its members, France, holds a consequential presidential election that could upset the bloc’s balance.

In April, France will hold a highly anticipated presidential vote that could see far-right National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen take power. Eurozone members had worried that a Le Pen victory could affect who is selected to be the new ECB president, as the populist lawmaker has previously criticized EU financial institutions and expressed disinterest in choosing another mainstream central banker to lead the body. Lagarde resigning early therefore allows outgoing French President Emmanuel Macron to have a say in her replacement instead.

Among the front-runners for Lagarde’s post are former Spanish Central Bank head Pablo Hernández de Cos and former Dutch Central Bank chief Klaas Knot. Whoever is chosen will have to contend with energy price shocks, bond market turmoil, and persistent high inflation.

Meanwhile, it is unclear what’s next for Lagarde, who was the first woman to serve as the ECB president. “I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression, and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters,” Lagarde said on Thursday. Some analysts believe that Lagarde, who is a French citizen, aims to become more vocal in the country’s politics, which have faced weeks of upheaval due to sweeping student-led protests.

Xi’s latest purge. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) confirmed the expulsion of 33 senior political and military officials on Thursday, in one of President Xi Jinping’s most sweeping purges since taking office in 2012. Those removed include Liu Jianchao, the former head of the CCP’s International Department; former Politburo member Ma Xingrui; Zhang Youxia, once the country’s most senior general; and Zhong Shaojun, a top military secretary to Xi.

It is unclear what charges these members faced beyond “serious disciplinary and legal violations.” But the expulsions are part of Xi’s extensive anti-corruption campaign targeting those considered disloyal to the party, and it comes as the longtime leader is preparing to clinch a fourth term in office. “While maintaining a tough stance against corruption, we should also strengthen checks on and oversight over the exercise of power,” read a communiqué released by the CCP’s Central Committee on Thursday.

The announcement concluded this year’s multiday Central Committee meeting in Beijing. Only 279 officials attended the annual conference, compared to 376 members when the current body was formed in 2022. This was the first time during Xi’s term that the plenary’s attendance dropped below 300 people. That suggests that nearly 100 officials were likely purged from the party over the course of just four years, China experts say.

National mourning. Spanish search-and-rescue operations stretched into Thursday following a deadly high-speed train crash the day before. At least 69 deaths have been confirmed thus far, with some 50 individuals still hospitalized, and local authorities fear that the death toll could rise. Madrid declared three days of national mourning starting Thursday.

Early Wednesday, a high-speed passenger train believed to be going around 120 miles per hour slammed into a stopped train near the central Spanish city of Toledo. An initial investigation found that an information technology failure involving railroad switching equipment was to blame. However, critics have accused the Spanish government of failing to provide adequate oversight and maintenance of the world’s second-largest high-speed rail network, particularly after another train crash on the same line killed 46 people in January.

“It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Wednesday. “It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.” With the country holding snap parliamentary elections next month, public transportation reform will likely be a top concern among voters.

The Vatican Museums opened a new exhibition on Thursday that celebrates more than 100 years of papal travel. Dubbed “A Century of the Popemobile,” the showing features eight Mercedes-Benz vehicles that popes have used since 1930 to travel among the faithful. Notable design alterations include Pope John XXIII’s 300 d Landaulet, which included removable rear side windows to allow the pontiff to reach out to those he passed on the road, and Pope John Paul II’s 230 G, which added the car’s transparent dome for greater viewing access.

#6056. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6055. This week: Campaigns make final frantic moves as Election Day arrives

A lot of the midterm vote has already happened in states where early voting and mail-in voting are common, but there’s still time to get supporters to the polls on Election Day.

President Donald Trump will use the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool as the location for his midterm closing argument, though he is expected to hold additional tele-rallies. Trump told reporters Sunday that he wants to show “how beautiful it is.”

Trump held in-person rallies Sunday in Iowa and Kansas. Those states have two of the four Senate Toss-up races, according to Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales.

In Iowa, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is trying to win the seat being vacated by retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Hinson is facing Democratic State Rep. Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist.

In Kansas, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall finds himself in a Toss-up race against Democrat Adam Hamilton.

The other two Senate Toss-ups are in Alaska and Maine, which are both Republican-held seats — and in fact there are no Senate races rated a Toss-up or favoring the GOP where the current senator is a Democrat.

Iowa is also among the keys to the House, with several closely watched contests. Two Iowa GOP incumbents, Reps. Zach Nunn and Marinnette Miller-Meeks, made the 2026 cycle’s final list of CQ Roll Call’s most vulnerable House members.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who has continued to argue that the polling favorable to Democrats should not be believed, was traveling with Trump on Sunday.

“I work almost as hard as this guy. I try to keep up with him, he doesn’t sleep at all,” Johnson said of Trump, before briefly pulling out his impression of the president alongside him at a rally in Iowa.

Johnson is scheduled to join Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., for an Election Eve rally in Virginia Beach before heading to Texas to kick off Election Day.

There, he’ll get things started with an early morning event with Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, along with GOP candidates Eric Flores and Tano Tijerina.

Flores is running in the reconfigured 34th District to unseat Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, while Tijerina is seeking to oust Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar.

The big surprise of the final weekend came out of Michigan, where Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens abruptly announced her support for — and then appeared alongside of — Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP Senate candidate.

Stevens, who had competed in the Democratic primary for Senate and had been expected to appear with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, made a last-minute pivot to embracing Rogers, a decision which left Democrats flummoxed.

“As you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers,” Stevens said Sunday in a video posted to social media.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., was among the national Democrats to criticize Stevens, calling her announcement a “despicable betrayal.”

Separately, Schumer convened a call with Senate Democrats on Sunday as part of the effort to prepare for potential efforts by Trump or his allies to undermine midterm results.

“If Trump and his allies attempt to interfere with the will of the voters, Senate Democrats are prepared to fight back immediately and aggressively, on Election Day and for as long as it takes to ensure the results are respected,” a Senate Democratic aide said in a statement.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

Situation Report: How Big of a Threat Are the Houthis?

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. John is once again flying solo for this edition, but Rishi will be back in action next week!

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Saudi Arabia compares the Houthis to the Islamic State, Riyadh considers UAE reconciliation amid the Yemen war, and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s post-midterms impeachment risk.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. John is once again flying solo for this edition, but Rishi will be back in action next week!

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Saudi Arabia compares the Houthis to the Islamic State, Riyadh considers UAE reconciliation amid the Yemen war, and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s post-midterms impeachment risk.

The Houthis are causing major problems for Saudi Arabia. The Iran-backed militants made significant territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline in September, and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government is struggling to push the Houthis back. Meanwhile, the group has launched deadly strikes in Saudi Arabia that have disrupted air travel and damaged key energy infrastructure.

Riyadh is pushing for more international support as the conflict escalates. In a New York Times op-ed this week, the Saudi ambassador to the United States, Reema Bandar al-Saud, compared the Houthis to the Islamic State, saying that the Yemeni group is “underestimated” in the same way that the Islamic State was before it declared a caliphate.

She urged the international community to “set a clear goal to end the Houthis as an armed terrorist force,” arguing that the Islamic State “was defeated by local forces backed by a coalition of more than 80 nations. The Houthis can be defeated the same way.”

Defining the threat. Unlike the Islamic State, the Houthis do not seek to establish a global Islamic caliphate. Their objectives are less ambitious and are centered on conquering Yemen and removing Saudi influence from the country.

But there’s no doubt that the Houthis pose a significant regional threat. Their asymmetrical tactics, including the use of low-cost drones, have proved to be a serious challenge even for a wealthy country with a sophisticated military like Saudi Arabia. And with Israel having severely degraded the capabilities of Hamas and Hezbollah over the last several years, the Houthis are now one of the most powerful Iranian proxies in the Middle East. In addition to attacking Saudi Arabia, the Houthis have also targeted Israel with strikes, including this year, and in 2022 attacked Abu Dhabi.

The problems the Houthis cause also have global implications—particularly their attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. Their recent territorial gains have given them more control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and have led to a dual-chokepoint crisis as the Iran war has simultaneously impacted traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. There’s also evidence of Houthi collaboration with other terrorist groups in the region, including al-Shabab, an al Qaeda affiliate in Somalia.

“The Houthi threat is not only to Yemenis. We have seen that it’s a threat to Yemen, of course, but also to the region and to the international community,” said Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political advisor to Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba. “This is not a local threat. It’s a threat for everyone.”

International involvement. Though some countries have offered Riyadh increased defensive assistance—such as the United Kingdom, Egypt, Pakistan, and Turkey—there’s been a general reluctance to get directly involved on the ground. Most critically, the United States, which has conducted strikes on the Houthis in the past (including last year), has so far avoided directly intervening this time around.

The internationally recognized Yemeni government is also calling for increased international involvement, but not necessarily intervention in Yemen itself.

“We’re not asking for any boots on the ground,” Noman said. “We’re not asking for people to come to fight on our behalf.” This is “our fight,” and “we have the forces,” Noman said.

What is needed from the international community is humanitarian assistance, Noman said (read more on the humanitarian crisis in Yemen here). Riyadh and the Yemeni government are also pushing more countries to follow Washington’s example and designate the Houthis as a terrorist group to help isolate the group financially. The Yemeni government has also asked the United States for training and intelligence support.

“We’re fighting on behalf of others as well” due to the broader threat posed by the Houthis, Noman added. “That’s why we need the support from our friends and allies.”

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has axed yet another top military official, adding to a long list of firings since he became Pentagon chief. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia has been removed from his role as director of strategy, plans, and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Sylvia was removed for allegedly leaking classified information to the press, a Pentagon official told ABC News.

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

The missing link in Yemen? Riyadh and Abu Dhabi reconciling could be a game-changer in the fight against the Houthis, a top expert on Yemen told John this week. Read more here to find out why the United Arab Emirates could help turn the tide.

Impeaching Hegseth. Hegseth could face impeachment if Democrats win big in next week’s midterm elections. FP’s Rachel Oswald interviewed Democratic Rep. Mike Levin about his support for impeaching the Pentagon chief, and the legal and political considerations. Read it here.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters at the Likud party election night event at the International Convention Center in Jerusalem on Oct. 28.Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images

Friday, Oct. 30: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is poised to host the G-20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia.

Tuesday, Nov. 3: The United States is set to hold midterm elections.

$47.1 billion: The estimated cost of the Iran war to U.S. taxpayers, per a new assessment from U.S. Central Command.

#6052. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6050. Russia’s Next Mobilization Is Already Happening

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: Russia’s Next Mobilization Is Already Happening

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

Nothing in almost five years of Russia’s war on Ukraine did more damage to the Kremlin’s hold on Russian public opinion than when Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree to forcibly mobilize 300,000 men for the war on Sept. 21, 2022. Levada’s monthly mood survey, run continuously since the 1990s, recorded the sharpest one-time collapse in its history: The share of Russians describing their general mood as “great” fell from 15 percent to 7 percent almost overnight, while those reporting fear more than tripled. The share who believed the war was “progressing successfully” dropped from 73 percent in May to 53 percent by the end of September. An estimated 300,000 to half a million men of fighting age left the country within two weeks of the decree, more than had fled during all of the war up to then. Kazakhstan alone recorded some 400,000 arrivals from Russia by late November that year. At the Verkhny Lars border crossing into Georgia, cars were lined up for days.

So acute was the fallout from the 2022 mobilization drive that many concluded it was too risky for Putin to repeat—even in an authoritarian police state where citizens’ opinions matter little. Thus, the biggest question surrounding Russia’s sham parliamentary elections last month was never who would win, but whether another extremely unpopular mobilization would have to wait until after the vote.

Nothing in almost five years of Russia’s war on Ukraine did more damage to the Kremlin’s hold on Russian public opinion than when Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree to forcibly mobilize 300,000 men for the war on Sept. 21, 2022. Levada’s monthly mood survey, run continuously since the 1990s, recorded the sharpest one-time collapse in its history: The share of Russians describing their general mood as “great” fell from 15 percent to 7 percent almost overnight, while those reporting fear more than tripled. The share who believed the war was “progressing successfully” dropped from 73 percent in May to 53 percent by the end of September. An estimated 300,000 to half a million men of fighting age left the country within two weeks of the decree, more than had fled during all of the war up to then. Kazakhstan alone recorded some 400,000 arrivals from Russia by late November that year. At the Verkhny Lars border crossing into Georgia, cars were lined up for days.

So acute was the fallout from the 2022 mobilization drive that many concluded it was too risky for Putin to repeat—even in an authoritarian police state where citizens’ opinions matter little. Thus, the biggest question surrounding Russia’s sham parliamentary elections last month was never who would win, but whether another extremely unpopular mobilization would have to wait until after the vote.

The election itself was depressingly predictable. Putin’s party, United Russia, won roughly 58 percent and 349 of 450 seats, its largest majority ever. The other parties are all Kremlin-approved, with true opposition parties quickly banned. Kremlin insiders told Meduza that participation in this sham was secured “through very dirty means”: state employees ordered to report their own votes, teachers made to track which parents had voted and report every two hours, managers calling out nonvoters in group chats.

More than five weeks later, there is no mobilization decree. The Kremlin, of course, has been denying any such plan all along—18 times in the three months before the vote, according to the Moscow Times’ count. On Sept. 1, Putin called the rumors “chush sobachya” (roughly, “dogshit”) and an “information attack.” Two days later, he said: “There is no scenario today that would require mobilization.”

As Russia observers like to scoff, something isn’t true until the Kremlin denies it. Two days before Putin’s 2022 mobilization decree, then-Duma Defense Committee chair Andrey Kartapolov assured Russians they had no reason to fear that such a thing might happen. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also issued a high-profile denial just before it was announced.

This time around, however, asking whether there will be another mobilization decree may be asking the wrong question. That nothing has been announced does not mean that a new mobilization wave is not happening. Those expecting a grand announcement followed by another stampede to the border will probably be disappointed—because there is no need for another decree.

For one, the old mobilization never quite ended. In May 2023, the Russian Supreme Court ruled that a mobilization period runs from the day it is declared until a decree formally ends it. No such end-of-mobilization decree exists, and the state keeps legislating on that basis. In July, for example, parliament expanded the pool of convicts eligible for military service in a law that explicitly applies “during mobilization, martial law, or wartime.” In August, a Supreme Court ruling mentioned “the period of mobilization” as an aggravating circumstance when it upheld a five-year sentence against a Chita man convicted over a comment on social media. Legally, Russia has been continuously mobilized since 2022. Nothing requires Putin to sign anything new.

Nor is the Kremlin desperate enough for manpower to abandon the methods that have worked so far: financial inducements and ad hoc coercion instead of a dramatic nationwide call-up. Even as Ukraine now imposes around 30,000 to as many as 40,000 casualties on the Russians each month, recruitment is strained but not breaking. According to Janis Kluge, who tracks Russian recruitment numbers by looking at regional budget payments, about 263,000 new contracts were signed in the first nine months of 2026, down from 292,000 during the same period last year, with September running at roughly 1,000 a day. The average sign-up bonus has climbed to almost 2 million rubles (or almost $25,000) per contract, nearly 30 percent more than last year. In the Khanty-Mansi region of Siberia, for example, the one-time sign-up bonus is roughly 30 times the average local monthly wage.

With recruitment struggling to replace battlefield losses, the authorities have increasingly resorted to force. Since June, independent Russian outlets have documented draft raids where plainclothes men in unmarked vans, sometimes with regional government license plates, grab men off the street or out of workplaces and take them to enlistment offices to sign contracts under duress. By late August, three legal-aid groups told Verstka that they had complaints from at least 17 regions. Idite Lesom, a hotline for draft dodgers, took three times as many calls in August as during the same month one year earlier. Its director, Grigory Sverdlin, describes who gets targeted in the recruitment raids: men, largely in poor, remote regions, who are burdened with debt, under police investigation, or facing other exploitable circumstances.

There is a long history of foreigners idealizing Russia and exaggerating its power.

In Nizhny Tagil, authorities reportedly paid private “recruiters” 400,000 rubles per man delivered, and a local prosecutor has complained that violent gangs and corrupt police have joined the trade. Kluge told CNN that coercion of this kind is probably not directed from Moscow, which only sets recruitment quotas for each region to fulfill. Passing responsibility down to governors, employers, and private agents—and not asking questions about how the targets are met—keeps the Kremlin, and in particular Putin, from being associated with the abuses.

The line between regular conscripts—young draftees who normally don’t serve in war—and the contract soldiers who do is also blurring. Since January, Russia has run a perpetual draft, with call-ups year-round and dispatches to units each spring and fall. The General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces said about 120,000 conscripts from the fall cycle began heading to their units on Oct. 10, allegedly none posted to Ukraine. But Putin has repeatedly pledged not to send conscripts or reservists to fight. Only six months after Putin first made that pledge in March 2022, the reservists were called up. Similarly, conscripts barely out of bootcamp were dispatched to repel the Ukrainian incursion into Russia’s Kursk region in August 2024, where many died or were captured.

That teenage or 20-something conscripts aren’t sent to fight and die in Ukraine remains technically true while missing the point, since they are routinely pressured into signing contracts. These contracts are then effectively indefinite due to the 2022 mobilization decree, still active, that makes it all but impossible for them to quit. Their coerced signature on a contract, in other words, removes the distinction that Putin’s pledge to young conscripts and their families relies on. Idite Lesom logged dozens of appeals in August from conscripts (and their relatives) facing persuasion, threats, or worse.

The population targeted by the ongoing mobilization has barely changed since 2022. At that time, the men were disproportionately drawn from non-ethnic-Russian republics such as Buryatia, Dagestan, Tuva, and Yakutia, where poverty, high unemployment, low salaries, few alternatives, and a sign-up bonus made military service a relatively attractive option. The women-led protests against the war that followed were concentrated there as well, as were the harshest crackdowns. The current wave of draft raids has followed a similar pattern so far. It is concentrated in poor, remote, and administratively sidelined places like Penza and Izhevsk, although draft-age men are now also being stopped in the streets of Moscow.

None of this proves that a formal call-up won’t come. If the situation at the front deteriorates sharply or recruitment numbers plummet, Putin could sign a new decree. But that would be a public admission that the quiet system has failed, and any nationwide announcement would bring back the shock—and potential exodus—of September 2022. Until then, Russia will keep feeding its war machine as it does now: With a recruiter intent on meeting his quota and getting his cut, snatching men into an unmarked van with tinted windows in a crumbling post-industrial town thousands of miles from Moscow.

Alexey Kovalev is an independent journalist and former investigations editor at Meduza who left Russia in 2022. X: @Alexey__Kovalev

#6048. Judge dismisses suit alleging FBI officials lied to Congress as ‘rush job’

A federal magistrate judge on Monday threw out a case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress, criticizing it as rushed, flawed and politically motivated.

During an hourlong hearing, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia found that there was no legal justification to continue the case against Nicole Floris and Bradley Benavides.

“What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization” of government against the pair, the magistrate said, describing it as a “rush job” driven by a political push from President Donald Trump.

The government unveiled the charges last month, alleging that Floris and Benavides lied to the House Judiciary Committee during interviews in 2023 about their knowledge of a laptop that used to belong to Hunter Biden but was in possession of the FBI ahead of the 2020 election.

Faruqui, in ruling from the bench, said there was no evidence that Floris and Benavides knowingly said anything false to the committee. He also pointed to mistakes throughout the complaint against Floris and Benavides, as well as the probe that led to the charges.

“The rush to charge here led to critical mistakes,” Faruqui said.

Faruqui said he has signed off on some 400 criminal complaints in the last five years but had never held such a hearing or ruled against the government during one.

The ruling came after an unusual three-day hearing last week, which featured hours of testimony from FBI agent Bryan Witt. Witt testified that the investigation came from a direct assignment by FBI Director Kash Patel the morning after a primetime address by Trump in which he called for the prosecution of individuals involved in the agency’s shuttered Foreign Influence Task Force.

Floris and Benavides both served in supervisory positions at the task force, and Witt testified that the agency investigated the pair for months before focusing on their 2023 testimony to Congress.

Faruqui noted that the transcript showed that many of the supposedly false statements were not false and that officials did not do the work to show that Floris and Benavides knew at the time that some of their statements might have been false, a necessary element of the crime.

Statements by Judiciary Committee majority general counsel Steve Castor about the alleged lies were “inadequate, incorrect and not credible,” Faruqui said, adding that Castor talked about the impact of the supposed lies in the pair’s testimony without having attended the Benavides interview or reviewed the transcript of either interview.

According to Faruqui, the government offered an incomprehensible “word salad” justification as to why the pair might have lied to Congress by arguing they wanted to downplay the task force’s role in handling the laptop ahead of the 2020 election.

“It’s not close, it’s nothing,” Faruqui said.

The government could still appeal Faruqui’s ruling to Chief Judge James Boasberg or seek a grand jury indictment of the pair. However, Faruqui said it was “self-evident” that the government was avoiding presenting the case before a grand jury, noting he had to pause proceedings several times last week for the government to present grand jury indictments, including one failed one.

“It turns out ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days,” Faruqui said, referencing a famous aphorism that a prosecutor “could indict a ham sandwich.”

The government would have had to secure an indictment to proceed with the case regardless of his ruling. Faruqui said the decision to proceed with a complaint, coupled with the timing of the case, made him concerned about the political nature of the investigation.

“There is no other event on the calendar except for the midterm elections tomorrow,” Faruqui said. “I will not bury my head in the sand.”

#6047. Trump Promised Poland More Troops. They’re Still Not There.

Analysis: Trump Promised Poland More Troops. They’re Still Not There.

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

In a surprise decision this May, the U.S. Defense Department canceled a planned deployment of thousands of troops to Poland, a NATO ally that has cultivated strong ties to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Within days, Trump seemingly offered good news for Warsaw: “I am pleased to announce that the United States will be sending an additional 5,000 Troops to Poland,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, framing the decision as inspired by the 2025 election of Polish President Karol Nawrocki, a Trump ally.

In a surprise decision this May, the U.S. Defense Department canceled a planned deployment of thousands of troops to Poland, a NATO ally that has cultivated strong ties to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Within days, Trump seemingly offered good news for Warsaw: “I am pleased to announce that the United States will be sending an additional 5,000 Troops to Poland,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, framing the decision as inspired by the 2025 election of Polish President Karol Nawrocki, a Trump ally.

“I ​thank U.S. President Donald J. Trump for his friendship toward Poland and for the decisions whose practical dimension ​we see very clearly today,” Nawrocki wrote in response.

In July, Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said officials from the U.S. Embassy in Warsaw had told him that U.S. forces would take the place of the canceled rotation “in the coming weeks.” But nearly four months later, those troops still haven’t arrived, and the Pentagon has not made any public statements about when they might be coming.

While it’s unclear what specifically may be preventing a faster deployment, the whiplash hints at the difficulty in executing the administration’s abrupt policy pivots and the reputational cost incurred—as well as the limits of what even a pro-U.S. country such as Poland can expect from its diplomatic efforts.

For Poland, which borders Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad, the presence of U.S. forces serves as a security guarantee against potential Russian attacks. But the specific number of troops is also “symbolic” for Poland, said Philip Bednarczyk, the Warsaw office director for the German Marshall Fund. “If they remove troops from Poland, that’s not what we were shooting for here,” he said.

The Pentagon did not provide a response to questions submitted by Foreign Policy. A Polish official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive negotiations, said that planning for the troop deployment that Trump announced is continuing but that it was “difficult to say” when an announcement might be made.

“There is an ongoing diplomatic Polish offensive in D.C.,” said a former Polish diplomat, also speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive conversations. “I think efforts are necessary also in case of no deployment and no success, because Polish public opinion will then have a clear picture whose fault it was.”

The delay comes despite Poland’s significant investments in defense, its large purchases of expensive U.S. weaponry, and the personal relationship between Trump and Nawrocki. Both U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby have called Poland a “model ally.”

There are likely a number of technical challenges to sending the troops that Trump promised, said John Ferrari, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and a former U.S. Army major general.

For one, the Army only has so many armored units, making it difficult to send an alternate unit on short notice. For another, the Army is likely stretched by the operational costs of deployments associated with the war in Iran. “Part of this may be [that] they just don’t have the money to send them over there,” Ferrari said.

Still, Ferrari noted that the Pentagon had missed an opportunity to clarify that forces would return to Poland: “Even with the sort of deliberative processes, that’s a good amount of time to at least announce it,” he said.

In the meantime, the lack of clarity hurts the reputation of the United States, said the former Polish diplomat. “The credibility of the United States government is decreasing. It’s become frustrating in the context of repeated Pentagon officials’ description of Poland as a ‘model ally.’”

Congress has also not been pleased. “The inaction over the last three months is negligence.” Rep. Don Bacon wrote on Aug. 30, after earlier threatening to hold up billions in military funding over the matter.

Another possible explanation is that the Pentagon is waiting for the conclusion of a review of its force numbers in Europe, which is set to be submitted to Trump in December. That review could significantly cut overall troop numbers, but might shift more forces to Poland, as the review is proceeding concurrently with negotiations over expanding the U.S. military’s permanent presence in the country. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said in September that the discussion involved the possible construction of permanent facilities for as many as 10,000 U.S. troops.

“It’s probable that this troop rotation will begin after the announcement of the strategic review,” said Jacek Siewiera, who served as the head of Poland’s National Security Bureau between 2022 and 2025. “The rotational U.S. presence has made an important contribution to Poland’s security. Our concern is the lack of permanence—given the changed security environment, this presence should now evolve into permanent basing,” Siewiera said.

The Polish official said that discussions on the permanent presence have involved several visits between the two sides, and they expressed optimism that the deal would move forward. “From what we know, we are on the right path to have this decision made,” the official said. Trump has been publicly supportive of the plans.

The former Polish diplomat was more skeptical, saying that “it might be much more realistic if there are clear decisions or public signaling” from Trump, the national security advisor, and the National Security Council. So far, the diplomat added, “these are lacking, just tweets or loose comments.”

For Warsaw, though, there may be little choice but to hope for the best. While European nations are rapidly rearming, none can provide the military capabilities of the United States. Russia’s escalating campaign of sabotage against Europe over its support for Ukraine, meanwhile, makes U.S. military commitments more important than ever—even if the Trump administration has shown increasing willingness to hand Russia economic wins and pressure Ukraine as the White House seeks to negotiate an end to the war.

Sam Skove is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. X: @samuelskove
