#6043. Venezuela’s Exiled Opposition Leader Comes Home

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Latin America Brief: Venezuela’s Exiled Opposition Leader Comes Home

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returns home, Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after losing the presidential runoff, and Latin American diplomats back their candidates in the race for United Nations secretary-general.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returns home, Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after losing the presidential runoff, and Latin American diplomats back their candidates in the race for United Nations secretary-general.

On Sunday, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado announced that she had returned to the country. Tens of thousands of supporters greeted her in the capital, Caracas. In a social media post, she pledged to work “for each family to be reunited, for freedom for every political prisoner, and for freedom for Venezuela.”

Machado was most recently staying in Panama after leaving Venezuela around a year ago to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. In the last few months, the Trump administration instructed neighboring governments to block her return to Venezuela, according to multiple media outlets.

Machado is an influential opponent of acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez. The United States is working with Rodríguez to revive the oil sector in Venezuela after forcibly removing President Nicolás Maduro in January. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the U.S. plans for Venezuela eventually include free elections, but no date has been set.

Though U.S. maneuvers have prompted some investments in the country’s oil sector, working-class Venezuelans are still grappling with poor economic conditions, including annual inflation exceeding 400 percent and daily, hourslong blackouts in some parts of the country.

The Trump administration says a no-bid deal it reached in August to take a partial stake in production at 17 Venezuelan oil fields will financially benefit Venezuelans. But a copy of the agreement viewed by ProPublica showed “the potential benefits to [Venezuelan] people are largely absent from the text,” whose terms “favor U.S. interests at every turn.”

Machado has called for presidential elections by mid-2027. Her team, as well as many Venezuelan analysts, argues that companies considering investing in the country will feel more secure about its regulatory environment after a vote. Elections would also allow Venezuela’s government more legitimacy to tackle macroeconomic problems.

In recent weeks, the United States acted to ease Machado’s reentry into Venezuela by telling the Rodríguez administration that it should permit the move, Rubio told journalists on Monday. The same day, the U.S. State Department announced its most detailed plans yet for when and how elections might occur.

Nominating committees chosen as part of a U.S.-backed dialogue between the Venezuelan government and opposition figures will select new judges for the top court and a separate electoral court by around the end of this year, an unnamed State Department official told reporters in a briefing.

At that point, Rodríguez is expected to declare the presidency formally vacant, triggering a six-month deadline for elections.

In a separate press briefing, Rubio responded to a question about whether Rodríguez might try to delay that timeline. He said: “I clearly intend to see this thing well in advance of the time I leave this position,” referring to the U.S. presidential transition in January 2029.

To many observers in Venezuela, the timing of Machado’s return and the State Department’s new statements on an electoral timeline was no coincidence. “María Corina’s arrival forced the United States to define a road map” toward a vote, economist Asdrúbal Oliveros said in a Wednesday radio appearance.

The U.S. plan to move toward elections is “the only game in town,” Rubio argued in his comments to the press, saying that Washington stands ready to use tools such as sanctions as leverage on the Rodríguez administration. “We have total control of Venezuela,” Trump said on Sunday.

Friday, Oct. 30, to Wednesday, Nov. 4: The United Kingdom’s King Charles III and Queen Camilla visit Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda.

Wednesday, Nov. 4, to Thursday, Nov. 5: Spain hosts Latin American leaders at the Ibero-American Summit.

Friday, Nov. 6, to Tuesday, Nov. 17: Pope Leo XIV visits Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.

U.N. sec-gen race expands. Top diplomats from Latin American and Caribbean countries gathered at the United Nations this week to make public appeals that the next secretary-general come from the region. A group of former foreign ministers published an open letter defending the same position.

Informal U.N. tradition dictates that it’s Latin America’s turn for the role, but after weeks of candidates from Costa Rica and Guyana leading straw polls, a candidate from the United Arab Emirates entered the race last week—raising the possibility that the region could lose its chance to hold the top job.

In recent days, reports suggested that Turkey was considering nominating a former foreign minister and that the Trump administration was floating the idea of backing former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

Devex’s Colum Lynch wrote on social media last week that many in diplomatic circles thought the Emirati candidate would prevail, though China still appeared to support a candidate from Latin America or the Caribbean. Latin American countries have not announced a consensus about their own top candidate.

Supporters of former Ecuadorian presidential candidate Luisa González hold campaign banners and chant slogans demanding her release outside the Modelo Police Headquarters in Guayaquil, Ecuador, on Oct. 23.Marcos Pin/AFP via Getty Images

Opposition figure detained in Ecuador. Last week, Ecuadorian authorities arrested former presidential candidate Luisa González as she faces an investigation for violating campaign finance rules. González is now in pretrial detention; she denies wrongdoing. The arrest triggered fresh criticism that Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa is targeting political opponents.

This year, Ecuadorian authorities have blocked multiple opposition parties from competing in local elections scheduled for November. They include González’s left-wing Citizen Revolution Movement; the Amigo movement, which Citizen Revolution members hoped to use to run for office following that ban; the left-wing Unión Popular; and the centrist Construye.

In August, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights issued a public statement of concern about the mounting legal challenges for opposition actors in Ecuador, calling on the government to “ensure pluralist political participation” ahead of the November vote.

González’s detention “deepens worries about the state of Ecuadorian democracy,” the editorial board of Ecuadorian newspaper El Mercurio wrote last week.

Tacos at the top. Restaurants that receive coveted Michelin ratings often suffer from pressure to maintain them. It was no different for a Mexico City taco stand. El Califa de León was Mexico City’s first taco stand to earn the distinction in 2024. But growing pains and a dispute over who most deserved the credit led the top grillmaster to leave within months, the Washington Post reported. The taco stand lost its star this year.

The affair triggered debates in Mexico City not only about what makes a good taco stand but also why Michelin took so long to honor one after awarding street food in other parts of the world. Those curious to try the Michelin star tacos can now sample them at El Califa de León as well as at its former chef’s new restaurant, Tacos Versalles.

Which of the following taco ingredients is least historically associated with Mexican tacos?

Hard-shell tacos are more associated with the Tex-Mex taco tradition than Mexican. Cotija cheese is from Michoacán, birria-style cooked meat is from Jalisco, and salsa fresca dates to the time of the Aztecs.

Brazilian Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro and his daughters arrive at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport in Miami on Oct. 28. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Enjoy our recent coverage of Brazil’s election: All FP links below are free to read.

A little over a day after Machado returned to Venezuela, another Latin American politician fled his country: Brazilian Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday’s presidential election to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who also left Brazil after losing to Lula in 2022. He was later convicted of plotting a coup.

Brazil’s Supreme Court is investigating the younger Bolsonaro in multiple probes into alleged financial irregularities and money laundering. A Brazilian Supreme Court judge ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his passport on Monday after being briefed by police that he might try to run.

Though he said in a video posted that day that he would never flee Brazil, Bolsonaro and his family carried out a secret journey through Argentina and Ecuador to the United States between Tuesday and Wednesday. Trump advisor Jason Miller helped with the arrangements, the Wall Street Journal reported.

On Wednesday, Bolsonaro baffled observers with a public letter proclaiming himself the rightful president-elect of Brazil, then quickly editing it to simply call himself Brazil’s “leader.” Multiple Brazilian news organizations reported Thursday that the Trump administration communicated to Bolsonaro that it did not support him declaring himself president-elect.

The letter suggested that Bolsonaro was seeking to rally international backing for his claim of election fraud. But that support would have likely been limited: Leaders around the world—including right-wing Latin American presidents—overwhelmingly recognized Lula’s victory, and Bolsonaro’s campaign coordinator said he saw no evidence of fraud.

The United States had not yet recognized Lula’s win as of Thursday, when Trump said he did not want to comment on the election, calling it a “disgrace.” On Wednesday, he said he wouldn’t “get involved” in the controversy over Bolsonaro.

Meanwhile, one of Bolsonaro’s competitors for leadership of Brazil’s right, São Paulo Gov. Tarcísio de Freitas, posted a video on Tuesday saying the “election is over” and suggesting that Brazil move on. Though Flávio Bolsonaro’s trip to the United States may have allowed him to avoid prosecution, he may have also ceded leadership of the political field.

Catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn

#6040. Supreme Court denies DOJ request to intervene in California ballot case

The Supreme Court on Monday denied a request from the Justice Department to intervene in its effort to have California set aside the ballots of 20,000 voters who the Trump administration argues could be noncitizens who illegally cast votes.

The unanimous, unexplained order came hours after the DOJ made the request and just before the votes are counted in the midterm elections. It was the latest maneuver in the fast-moving, high-profile effort by the administration to insert itself in state voting procedures. The application asked the justices for an emergency order for the state to set aside those ballots until the voters’ citizenship could be determined.

“In this case, this Office is informed that the Executive Branch has identified over 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California based on publicly accessible information and who, based on the Executive Branch’s review, are likely not U.S. citizens,” the application said.

The request followed a ruling by a federal judge in California that the lawsuit likely violated several civil rights laws and improperly inserted the federal government in state election procedures.

A separate panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit turned aside an appeal of that ruling Friday.

The Justice Department filed the lawsuit last month, days after state officials had refused to take a flash drive the administration said included the names of the purported noncitizens. The DOJ argued that it had compiled the 20,000 names of alleged noncitizens and that state officials should impose additional requirements before allowing their votes to be counted.

State officials have argued that there is no federal role in the state election and that there was no evidence the voters had actually returned ballots or weren’t citizens.

The application came amid multiple last-minute efforts from the Trump administration to weigh in on state election processes, including a similar letter to Washington state officials and a lawsuit seeking to delay the certification of the Alaska Senate contest due to the presence of two similarly named candidates on the ballot.

The Trump administration has more broadly sought to assert a greater federal role in state authority over elections, dovetailing with President Donald Trump’s evidence-free claims of widespread voter fraud. The push started shortly after Trump began his second term, with an executive order seeking to require proof of citizenship to vote nationwide. That order was largely stopped by the courts.

Separately, the Justice Department sought private records of voters across dozens of states, another effort that was rejected by the courts.

Additionally, earlier this year Trump issued an executive order seeking to curb mail voting nationwide and force states to provide mail officials with lists of eligible voters. That was also stopped by the Supreme Court.

#6039. What Life Is Like by the Strait of Hormuz Right Now

Dispatch: What Life Is Like by the Strait of Hormuz Right Now

BANDAR ABBAS, Iran—Along Iran’s main highway south, debris lies scattered across the road, while bridges and tunnels are damaged or destroyed. Half-buried in the dirt, a broken road sign points toward Bandar Abbas, Iran’s main port city and the gateway to the Strait of Hormuz.

“The war has never stopped here,” said Khaleh Zeynab, 51, a food vendor working alongside Bandar Abbas’s corniche. She gestures toward the beach and the strait. “My son Reza is out there fighting. He’s been working on a ship since the beginning of the war. I know he could be killed at any moment, and that scares me, but he’s a soldier. If he doesn’t do his job, somebody else has to. We have to defend our country.”

BANDAR ABBAS, Iran—Along Iran’s main highway south, debris lies scattered across the road, while bridges and tunnels are damaged or destroyed. Half-buried in the dirt, a broken road sign points toward Bandar Abbas, Iran’s main port city and the gateway to the Strait of Hormuz.

“The war has never stopped here,” said Khaleh Zeynab, 51, a food vendor working alongside Bandar Abbas’s corniche. She gestures toward the beach and the strait. “My son Reza is out there fighting. He’s been working on a ship since the beginning of the war. I know he could be killed at any moment, and that scares me, but he’s a soldier. If he doesn’t do his job, somebody else has to. We have to defend our country.”

When the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran began on Feb. 28, residents in Bandar Abbas watched ships burn, missiles streak across the sky, and fighter jets fly overhead. Months later, explosions from the strait can still be heard almost daily, though it is not always clear whether they are air defense interceptions or fresh attacks.

What is clear, however, is that the war has made life increasingly difficult for communities whose livelihoods depend on the Strait of Hormuz.

Khaleh Zeynab sells bread in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19.

“It’s been tough to make ends meet,” Zeynab said. Before the war, Bandar Abbas drew tourists from across Iran as well as abroad. Since the fighting began, visitors have largely disappeared, while many residents—seeking safety after repeated attacks on the city—left for smaller villages elsewhere in Hormozgan province. At the same time, prices have surged across Iran, especially in urban centers. Food costs have risen sharply, often even doubling, adding to the pressure on families already struggling to get by.

Pouring dough onto a makeshift stove propped up on the sidewalk to make tomoshi, a thin flatbread popular in southern Iran, Zeynab said she is now helping her daughter-in-law care for her three children while Reza is away. He has returned home only once since the war began and has yet to meet his youngest daughter, born just two months ago.

“That’s what this war is doing to us,” Zeynab said with a shrug.

A road sign pointing toward Bandar Abbas, damaged in the U.S. attack on the Shur River bridge, on Sept. 19.

The war has left its mark on Bandar Abbas, too, home to roughly 700,000 people and the economic powerhouse of southern Iran. A critical gateway for imports and exports, the city handles up to 90 percent of Iran’s container shipping, and more than half of the country’s maritime trade passes through its ports.

Several ports, including the city’s fishing port, have been targeted in attacks. So has the Shur River bridge outside the city, which connects Hormozgan to neighboring Kerman province, as well as the provincial center of Iran’s state broadcaster, IRIB. The latter was “completely destroyed by 24 missiles,” said Ahmad Hosseini, a 64-year-old construction worker who witnessed the attack. “So what?” he added. “We will just rebuild it.”

Workers rebuild the Shur River bridge outside Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19.

The Shur River bridge, which was destroyed in a U.S. attack, on Sept. 19.

Ahmad Hosseini, a construction worker, shows us missile fragments he collected from around a damaged building, where they had been scattered by the impact, in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 20.

In recent weeks, attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz have intensified, pushing oil prices once again above $100 a barrel. U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened further strikes against Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. Tehran, meanwhile, has signaled that it is preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities and issued threats against Washington and its allies. At the same time, Iran continues to seek a diplomatic solution. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said recently that Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days remained on the table—an offer that Iran submitted in mid-September, following the collapse of an interim cease-fire. Negotiations have stalled, however, with Iran’s security chief saying the United States had failed to address all seven conditions Tehran had set for reopening the waterway.

For coastal Iranians, however, the strait is more than a geopolitical chokepoint or negotiation tool; it is their lifeline. Fishermen, shipbuilders, tour guides, port workers, and smugglers all depend on the sea—which has now become the war’s front line—for their livelihoods.

Fishermen work by the roadside after a day’s catch in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 22.

Amir, 24, has spent the past five years smuggling alcohol across the strait from Oman and the United Arab Emirates. He declined to give his full name or be photographed, knowing that doing so could get him into trouble with the authorities. He grinned sheepishly as he explained how the operation worked.

Smugglers on either side of the strait use small speedboats to meet at sea, coordinating their movements over radios. Sometimes, Amir and his small crew travel deep into the strait, and on other trips, they cross all the way to the opposite shore.

It is dangerous work, even for someone who knows these waters as well as Amir does. The war has made the business even more precarious, but the income is good, he explained, especially amid soaring inflation and a battered economy.

Amir was still smuggling booze when the war broke out but was caught by the Omani coast guard and spent two months in prison in Khasab, Oman, he said. “After my release, I was deported to Afghanistan. The Taliban then sent me back to Iran,” he said, adding that he didn’t know why he was first sent to Iran’s eastern neighbor.

Twelve-year-old Mohammad works for Amir, who asked not to be photographed, selling shisha along the water in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19.

Since returning, Amir has been serving shisha at a seaside park in the city. He still regularly hears explosions from the strait, which is why he has taken a break from smuggling. But despite the risks, he wants to return.

“My father is a smuggler, too,” he said. “This is where the money is.”

For Ahmad Mokhtari, a shopkeeper in a small village just outside Bandar Abbas, the conflict has brought an unexpected opportunity to make money.

Recent war games highlight how Washington can improve its air defenses so the next round of fighting isn’t worse.

Some dramatic long-term consequences are just beginning to come into view.

But the continued shortfall of refined products means little relief at the pump.

“Many people have moved out of the city to be safer, and this has given many villages a strange boost. I used to come to the city once a month to shop. Now I’m traveling here every single day. Demand in the village has grown so much.”

Bandar Abbas, meanwhile, has yet to return to full capacity. Fishermen cannot venture as far into the strait as they used to, and some ports are operating at reduced capacity. Still, a kind of normalcy has returned.

The beach in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19, where crowds gather for picnics after sunset as the weather cools down.

Twenty-three-year-old Kiana (foreground) poses for a portrait at the seaside on Sept. 19. She traveled to Bandar Abbas from Kerman with her family for a holiday.

In the evenings, when the heat and humidity become more bearable, people venture out along the corniche to meet friends, catch the sea breeze, grab a snack, or pose for photographs. It’s a laid-back atmosphere as the streets fill up. There’s music in the air, and occasionally, some people even dance.

But farther out, tankers remain stranded in the strait, some of them visible from the shoreline. The occasional sounds of explosions are carried across the water.

A beached boat near the shore of Bandar Abbas on Sept. 20. Locals offer conflicting accounts of its provenance; some say it was not there before the war and others that something happened to it during the conflict with the United States and Israel.

“We’ve gotten used to it,” Zeynab said. “The explosions and fighter jets are normal to us now.”

A woman wades offshore in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 23.

Stefanie Glinski is a journalist who covers conflicts and crises with a focus on the wider Middle East. X: @stephglinski

Mohammad Mohsenifar is a journalist based in Tehran.

#6034. How Israel’s Coalition Wrangling Could Play Out

Q&A: How Israel’s Coalition Wrangling Could Play Out

Israel’s elections on Tuesday have delivered a parliament with no clear path to a new government. Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won 27 out of 120 available seats in the Knesset, leaving his right-wing coalition short of the seats needed for a majority, and opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has won 21 seats, also leaving it unable to form a government unless it joins forces with the surging Arab parties that his allies have previously refused to join forces with.

What happens next, and what will coalition bargaining reveal about where Israeli society stands, three years on from the devastating Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the deadly regional wars that followed? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political scientist who is a columnist for Haaretz. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Israel’s elections on Tuesday have delivered a parliament with no clear path to a new government. Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won 27 out of 120 available seats in the Knesset, leaving his right-wing coalition short of the seats needed for a majority, and opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has won 21 seats, also leaving it unable to form a government unless it joins forces with the surging Arab parties that his allies have previously refused to join forces with.

What happens next, and what will coalition bargaining reveal about where Israeli society stands, three years on from the devastating Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the deadly regional wars that followed? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political scientist who is a columnist for Haaretz. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Ravi Agrawal: Dahlia, you’ve covered so many elections in Israel. Why was this particular election seen as so important for the country’s future?

Dahlia Scheindlin: We definitely had record turnout, which means that the vast majority of the voters saw it that way.

I don’t think I’ve ever seen two major blocs of voters as polarized. The opposition parties won a clear majority of 67 out of 120 parliamentary seats. This is getting a bit lost in international coverage. The opposition parties have a majority, and they share the sense that the country is heading for a disaster. They believe that Netanyahu was deeply committed to his alliance with his ultranationalist, extremist, religious fundamentalist political partners, and that they had sacrificed the best interests of the country for an attack on the Israeli judiciary that was unpopular among the majority from the start of 2023.

It sparked such a social backlash that it left Israel open to attack—the worst attack in Israel’s history, obviously—and then the government refused to take responsibility for it. And the issue of the government refusing to establish an independent commission of inquiry into what happened on Oct. 7, 2023, was among the most animating issues for the opposition voters.

Those who support Netanyahu see Israel as having been attacked on numerous fronts. They believe that only Netanyahu has the kind of political savvy and international clout to be able to resist pressure to end the wars that they believe are a matter of survival. When they think about Oct. 7, they think of how close Israel was to existential destruction. In their minds, Netanyahu is the prime minister who managed to marshal Israel’s closest ally, the United States, to join Israel in its war against Iran. They believe that Israel must continue on that path. They also believe Israel must never give up any control over the West Bank or Gaza, or leave its positions in Lebanon and Syria, and that these are a matter of survival.

RA: You suggested the international media is missing the headline here. But isn’t it true that Netanyahu is better placed than we expected?

DS: First of all, I’m looking at the data. Mr. Netanyahu and the parties that are loyal to him did not achieve a majority of the votes. Netanyahu’s loyalist parties won 44 percent of the vote; 56 percent wanted Netanyahu out.

The problem is that the opposition is composed of many fragmented political parties. If the opposition can’t form an alternative, then it doesn’t really matter. The biggest elephant in the room here is that the Zionist parties of the opposition—parties representing mostly Jewish citizens of Israel—have stated time and again that they do not want to build a coalition with parties representing mostly Arab or Palestinian Israeli citizens. But ultimately, it is a completely self-imposed constraint—and, frankly, it’s racist.

RA: So Israel has a parliamentary system with many parties, and we’re now going to enter a period of coalition wrangling. But it’s also interesting to me that this election had at least some element of the personality contest that comes with a presidential system. So you’ve mentioned Netanyahu; the other figure everyone was talking about was Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party.

DS: The fact that he’s a former IDF (Israel Defense Forces) chief of staff puts him in the highest level of esteem among most Jewish Israelis. There is a constituency of people who are in the center but lean right, who prioritize security issues and believe that Israel needs to be militarily strong and a Jewish state. But beyond that, they’re not extremists; they want a liberal society that separates religion from the state and ensures the separation of powers. They’re not happy with Netanyahu’s leadership, which has tried to consolidate power in the executive. And that group has supported somebody like Eisenkot time and again.

RA: Give us some insight into how the coalition wrangling works out. Now that we know a couple of the main characters, could Eisenkot cobble together some of these other opposition parties, plus the Arab parties, and maybe try to form a government, or is Netanyahu the one who has the best shot at trying to do so? How does this all work?

DS: The various scenarios for how to reach a government are manifold, and they are all uncertain. One scenario is that nobody can build a government, and Israel goes into another election, which is the precedent we had from 2019 through 2022, when we held five election cycles for this very reason.

Another scenario is that there is a minority government, which is legal as long as it’s sworn in with more votes than those against it. It is inherently unstable, because there is a majority of parliamentary seats who could vote to disband the Knesset and call new elections. There is also a possibility—and not an unlikely one—that, for example, Netanyahu is asked to form the government by the president, and somebody from the Zionist opposition parties defects to his side.

Most Israeli parties are amalgamated factions of smaller parties. There’s a lot of speculation about a unity government between Likud and the mainstream Zionist parties, with bargaining over who would be prime minister when. That is very complex, legally and politically. Netanyahu would want to be first in any rotation; the opposition parties would not want to accept that. If he goes second in a rotation, he’s in trouble because he is legally not supposed to be serving as a regular minister since he is under indictment for three counts of corruption and has been standing trial for the last six years. But you can see how many options are on the table. None of them are great ones.

Main opposition parties fail to muster majority.

Early results indicate deadlock in parliamentary elections.

RA: It does seem like Israel is generally becoming more right-wing, more focused on its security at the cost of soft power. Netanyahu has frequently said he’s happy to turn Israel into Sparta. And it seems like what is so striking from everything you’ve said so far is that Netanyahu won a fair number of seats, and despite the opposition’s performance, he is still somewhat popular. Clearly, the differences between him and the potential opposition are not that great on some key issues on security. So what does this mean for Israel’s overall trajectory, no matter who actually forms a government after this?

DS: It’s a good observation about hard power versus soft power. Israel is a militarist society and has placed so much emphasis on the image of the omnipotent army, but of course, it was no less invested in its global image over the decades and prided itself on being part of the family of democratic nations in the West.

But in recent years, the country has unapologetically moved away from its liberal trajectory. Across the board, Israelis increasingly think that the entire world is against them, that the whole world is inherently anti-Israel and antisemitic no matter what Israel does. That goes beyond the right wing. The backlash against Israel in the immediate days after Oct. 7 was proof of concept to those who already felt that way and also really scared a lot of Israelis who didn’t necessarily think that way.

RA: But Dahlia, since you speak to so many voters and have your pulse on how Israelis think, can you play out that school of thought of feeling like everyone’s against you, of feeling that much of the region and the world is antisemitic? Where does that lead? What is the logical conclusion of that feeling?

DS: Netanyahu told us where that will lead just a day or two before the election. He said that in light of the possibility that Israel will be facing more sweeping sanctions—even more than it already is—it would have to build a separate economy that is free of the global system, and that Israel can just do that based on cryptocurrency. Nobody took it very well. But again, he maximized his vote. Netanyahu’s supporters are not deterred; they think that Israel has always been a resilient country, so they’re not as worried, whereas the Israelis who didn’t vote for the government are terrified at the idea of being shut out of the world that they want to be part of. They see themselves with a more globalist orientation.

RA: How much do regular Israelis reckon with the change in attitude toward Israel in the United States, as more and more Americans seem to be openly discussing a changing U.S.-Israeli relationship, in part because of Israel’s politics over the last few years, and in particular over Gaza and U.S. military support for Israel in that war. It doesn’t seem like this has been a change election on that front.

DS: The majority of Israelis believed it was a change election, just not in the ways the international community was looking for. I’ve never seen a bigger gap between how outsiders view Israel and how Israelis are talking about their country since Oct. 7. It’s natural that from the outside, people don’t always see the inside of any country, but I do think the gap has gotten so much bigger.

For Israelis, American attitudes are a background issue. It occasionally makes a headline when a new Pew or Gallup survey comes out showing the erosion of Israel’s position. But again, that’s when the majority of Israeli Jews return to the idea that people were probably always against Israel, and that certainly in America, they have that “woke disease” that has poisoned the public mind toward Israel and has nothing to do with Israel’s policies—even those who are critical of Israel’s policy at home. When they hear that kind of criticism from abroad, they get defensive.

People who are already opposed to the government will say that this is another thing they think is problematic or that they’re worried about. But it’s not the number one most urgent issue for them. There is an awareness of the possibility of a change in America following the midterms and an awareness of where the Democratic Party is going. But I think the presidential election and the possibility of a change of administration is too abstract for Israelis right now.

It was always a profound and frankly incomprehensible mistake to think that you could just hold people under a hostile and violent military occupation. The day-to-day reality of Palestinians is so bad that there would always be some sort of escalation. I know of no national movement seeking self-determination that has ever given up on their self-determination, no matter how good their quality of life. Palestinians have neither.

That’s the delusion in every unresolved ethno-nationalist territorial conflict, especially when the gap is so huge and one side enjoys full sovereignty—complete international integration and great economic indicators—while the other side has none of those things, nor national self-determination. There’s no reality in which that would ever go away or fail to escalate. The longer it goes on, the more extreme the escalations become.

So it’s not just bad for Israel’s foreign relations or image. Primarily, it’s bad for the Palestinians who continue living under this hostile and very violent regime, and of course for Gaza, the vast destruction of which is incomprehensible at this point. But it’s bad for Israel, too. Israel’s democracy cannot really ever be fulfilled. These are the same state institutions who are ultimately implicated in that regime, and this is what ultimately fed into the chaos that we saw in 2023.

It is also the source of the deepest divisions within Israel over the very nature of its regime, which is what was at stake in 2023 and what so many Israelis thought was at stake in this election, even if they didn’t make the connection that it’s fundamentally connected with occupation and Palestinians.

Ravi Agrawal is the editor in chief of Foreign Policy. X: @RaviReports

#6032. In DC on election night? Here’s where to watch results roll in

Some races may be too close to call, but one thing will be certain Tuesday no matter what — bar specials.

Residents of D.C. observe election night like some other cities observe major sporting events. And after the Nationals failed to advance to the postseason this year and with the first playoff game for the Washington Spirit still a few days away, the midterms will be the main ticket in town.

“It’s usually standing room only every time. I don’t think it matters whether it’s presidential or midterms,” said Matt Weiss, who owns Capitol Hill’s Union Pub.

The Halloween vibes aren’t over yet at Union Pub, thanks to a special “Midterm Massacre” menu. Inspired by competitive Senate races, it features $9 cocktails and shooters like the Haunted Horsefeather (Kansas), Maineiac Martini (Maine) and the Devil’s Duck Fart (Alaska).

While the pub will also be showing the Washington Capitals play the Dallas Stars at 7 p.m., Weiss said the sound will be on for election results rather than hockey. He expects around 50 percent more business than a regular Tuesday, which is already a busy night with weekly trivia.

Weiss said he can’t remember a time when his bar, which originally opened as Red River Grill in 1995, wasn’t showing election returns coming in.

“It’s just like being open for the Super Bowl or being open for the Washington Spirit being in the finals; we do benefit from having these types of events,” said Jesse Rauch, a partner at metrobar.

Rauch’s bar in Northeast D.C., known for its decommissioned railcar, isn’t usually open on Tuesdays, but election night is different.

With some races taking longer to call than others, Rauch said he’ll stay open as long as he can.

“We’re gonna play it by ear,” he said. “I do need to send my team home at some point to make sure that they’re well rested and all that. But we’ll stay open for as long as the energy is good.”

Given the District’s political leanings, most of the election night fans will be cheering on Democrats up and down the ballot. Kamala Harris carried more than 90 percent of the vote in D.C. in 2024, while President Donald Trump had 6 percent.

Rauch did point to one thing that might affect his sales, but he said he doesn’t mind.

“A lot of people in D.C. are in Maryland and in Virginia and in Pennsylvania door knocking, and they’ll be door knocking until the very end. Because of that, some people just aren’t in town, which I’m really proud of my neighbors who are able to do that,” he said.

If you’re looking for a place to be on election night, here are a few airing the results:

Teddy and the Bully Bar 1200 19th St. NW“We’ve got $8 oyster shooters, $8 NYC Mules, $4 New York style hot dogs, a $9.99 Angus beef smashburger, $5 soft pretzels with house-made beer cheese, $8 funnel cake with raspberry coulis and powdered sugar, and much, much more.”

Union Pub201 Massachusetts Ave. NE“Midterm Massacre Menu featuring $9 cocktails and shooters inspired by some of the country’s most competitive Senate races.”

Shaw’s Tavern520 Florida Ave. NW“Grab your crew, order a round of margaritas, and settle in as the results roll in … Taco and margarita specials all night.”

Barrel613 Pennsylvania Ave. SE“We’ll have the midterm election results on C-SPAN all night long, and we’re letting the cocktails have their own race: Blue Passion Fruit Margarita, Red Strawberry Daiquiri. Every drink counts as a vote.”

metrobar640 Rhode Island Ave. NE“Slices & Sips Happy Hour till 7pm … $10 pies from El Jefe and our rotating happy hour menu of craft cocktails, local beer, and wine.”

Boundary Stone116 Rhode Island Ave. NW“All parties, independents, political junkies, and the politically exhausted are welcome … All night happy hour. Burgers, wings, fish & chips & pub favorites.”

Red Derby3718 14th St. NW“Live Streaming RESULTS Watch Party: 1/2 price BURGERS, $4 Natty Boh’s, Blue Wave Shooters.”

Roofers Union2446 18th St. NW“Red or Blue? We’re voting for tacos! … Live election coverage, Taco Tuesday specials & margaritas.”

Highlands Tavern3421 Connecticut Ave. NW“To keep the energy going through the early morning hours, we are pouring $5 pints of local Senate Beer all night long.”

Pitchers 2317 18th St. NW“Join us at Pitchers for an election watch party and bingo as we watch the results unfold together.”

Busboys and PoetsAll locations“Enjoy live election coverage on TVs throughout the restaurant, games and activities, great food, community conversation, and all-night happy hour beginning at 3 p.m.”

With just days to go until the U.S. midterm elections, many Europeans and Canadians are watching closely to see if Democrats will retake Congress and perhaps begin to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump for his final two years in office.

Canadians, who have been on the receiving end of some of Trump’s harshest trade actions, are so hungry for news about the U.S. midterms that they are searching for information at a higher rate than even Americans, according to Google search trends.

With just days to go until the U.S. midterm elections, many Europeans and Canadians are watching closely to see if Democrats will retake Congress and perhaps begin to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump for his final two years in office.

Canadians, who have been on the receiving end of some of Trump’s harshest trade actions, are so hungry for news about the U.S. midterms that they are searching for information at a higher rate than even Americans, according to Google search trends.

“Normal, average Canadians know so much more about the United States and care so much more about the United States,” said retired Royal Canadian Air Force Maj. Gen. Scott Clancy, a former director of operations for the North American Aerospace Defense Command. “Whereas Canada doesn’t even come into the daily [consideration] for the vast, vast majority of Americans in any given day.”

Europeans are also gripped by midterm fever. After Canada and the United States, midterm election information searches were the highest in Denmark, Qatar, and Norway—three countries that have also been rocked by Trump’s foreign-policy actions, from his aggressive claims on Greenland to the war against Iran.

Damian Murphy, the senior vice president for national security and international policy at the liberal Center for American Progress think tank, said that European officials he’s met with lately are “laser-focused on the midterms.” Murphy said he has been struck by the granular level of knowledge his European interlocutors have shown for the state of play of individual House races.

“What I’ve been telling them is that you shouldn’t have super high expectations for what any Congress can affirmatively do,” Murphy said. “In our system, the executive has a lot of power when it comes to the conduct of foreign policy. But what is important is the political message that it will send to the rest of the world: that the American people repudiate all of this—ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement], the Iran war, the treatment of allies.”

Other foreign observers have cautioned against high expectations of a U.S. reversion to pre-Trump foreign policies even if Democrats win control of Congress.

“Let us not overestimate the consequences of a defeat for the Trump administration in the midterm elections,” said former French Ambassador to the United States Gérard Araud in a recent post on X. “An American president holds considerable powers, particularly in foreign policy, and Trump can rely on the Supreme Court to bypass Congress.”

The experiences of Trump’s surprise 2016 and 2024 presidential election wins also continue to act as ballast against runaway hopes of a blue tidal wave.

“My philosophy of life is to have low expectations, and I apply that to the midterms as well. My mission is to stamp out any glimmer of hope of a return to normalcy after the midterms,” said one European diplomat, who requested anonymity to give an unvarnished take on the U.S. political situation.

One outcome with a strong chance of occurring in November, though, is a vote on impeaching U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over allegations of violating war powers and war crimes laws. A vote on the defense chief’s impeachment is likely to happen the week after the midterms.

Even if Republicans find the votes to protect Hegseth in the impeachment vote, a new impeachment inquiry may be launched in January if Democrats win control of the House, as is predicted.

Like the midterms, Canadians are likely to closely follow any impeachment process against Hegseth.

The former Fox News host “deeply offended” many Canadians this fall, Clancy said, when he separately appeared to disparage Canadian troop cadets and denigrated the contributions of NATO allied troops who joined the U.S.-led mission in Afghanistan.

“Personal friends of mine perished during that conflict,” Clancy said.

#6026. The Gulf Isn’t Ready for a Renewed Iran War

Analysis: The Gulf Isn’t Ready for a Renewed Iran War

By the narrow measure of barrels shipped, the Persian Gulf has weathered eight months of war better than most energy analysts expected. Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week ending Oct. 18, above the prewar level of 23.3 million, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. JPMorgan analysts wrote last week that energy markets are “converging on a forever conflict” and that view has encouraged a belief in the Trump administration that the region can absorb another round of fighting.

That view confuses how much oil and gas are still flowing from the Gulf with the state of the plants and terminals that move it. Since the war began on Feb. 28, Iranian missiles and drones have damaged refineries, liquefied natural gas (LNG) trains, and export terminals across the Gulf, and the Houthis have opened a second front in the Red Sea. Much of what has been lost will take years to rebuild. The cost will fall mostly on importers in Asia, Europe, and the developing world that built their energy systems around reliable Gulf supply.

By the narrow measure of barrels shipped, the Persian Gulf has weathered eight months of war better than most energy analysts expected. Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week ending Oct. 18, above the prewar level of 23.3 million, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. JPMorgan analysts wrote last week that energy markets are “converging on a forever conflict” and that view has encouraged a belief in the Trump administration that the region can absorb another round of fighting.

That view confuses how much oil and gas are still flowing from the Gulf with the state of the plants and terminals that move it. Since the war began on Feb. 28, Iranian missiles and drones have damaged refineries, liquefied natural gas (LNG) trains, and export terminals across the Gulf, and the Houthis have opened a second front in the Red Sea. Much of what has been lost will take years to rebuild. The cost will fall mostly on importers in Asia, Europe, and the developing world that built their energy systems around reliable Gulf supply.

U.S. and Israeli planners have drawn up options for a short, intensive campaign against Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile and drone arsenals, and energy infrastructure after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, the New York Times reported last week. President Trump has not approved it. This week, the Wall Street Journal reported that Washington has told Gulf governments to prepare for such an offensive. Iranian officials have responded by naming Saudi oil facilities, Gulf data centers, and undersea cables as targets. The next round would likely concentrate on the assets and importers that Gulf states can least afford to lose.

The Gulf’s reputation as a dependable supplier rests on decades of investment as much as on geology. After the 1973 oil embargo, consumer nations created the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the 1980 Carter Doctrine committed the United States to keeping the Gulf open by force. After the 1991 Gulf War and the 2003 invasion of Iraq, Gulf states invested in redundancy. Saudi Arabia expanded the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the United Arab Emirates built a pipeline to Fujairah to bypass Hormuz, and Riyadh kept spare production capacity in reserve. All of this assumed that U.S. power would protect the region’s infrastructure or at least deter attacks on it. This year’s fighting has overturned that assumption.

A recent Reuters investigation documented at least 135 Iranian drone and missile attacks on at least 84 infrastructure sites across seven Gulf states since the war’s start. Iranian-linked strikes damaged five of Saudi Arabia’s nine largest refineries and both export manifolds at Fujairah, the UAE’s main terminal outside Hormuz. At Qatar’s Ras Laffan, the world’s largest LNG complex, strikes on the cold boxes that house liquefaction equipment took out two LNG trains representing about 17 percent of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy expects repairs to take three to five years and to cost an estimated $20 billion in annual revenue. Since much of this equipment is custom-built, the losses will outlast any cease-fire or peace agreement with Iran.

Proponents of a renewed campaign point to U.S. and Gulf air defenses, which by most measures have performed well. The UAE reported intercepting 132 of the 137 ballistic missiles fired at it on the first day of the war. The Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) estimated in March that more than 90 percent of Iranian projectiles had been intercepted across the theater. Interception rates, however, are the wrong measure for energy infrastructure. A refinery or LNG complex does not need to be hit repeatedly to be taken offline; it needs to lose only one critical component. On March 18, Qatar’s Defense Ministry said its forces intercepted four of the five ballistic missiles Iran fired at Ras Laffan. That attack took out the two trains cited above. An 80 percent interception rate still produced a loss of LNG supply that will last for years. The Financial Times reported that the missiles were maneuverable enough to evade Patriot batteries.

A second round would also begin from a weaker defensive position. JINSA estimated that by late March, Bahrain had used up to 87 percent of its Patriot interceptors and the UAE and Kuwait roughly 75 percent. Even if defenses performed better next time, a handful of missiles reaching a gas train, a pumping station, or a terminal manifold could remove capacity the market cannot replace for years. For planners, the share of Iranian missiles stopped should matter less than what the few that get through will hit.

Neither appealing to Washington nor diversifying security partners nor back-channeling with Tehran is insulating the region from the consequences of war.

Meanwhile, since declaring a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia on July 20, the Houthis have struck Saudi Aramco’s 400,000-barrel-a-day Jizan refinery three times, forcing it offline for repairs in August. Drone strikes on East-West pipeline infrastructure in September led Riyadh to shut the line for 11 days, halting loadings at Yanbu. The group claimed new attacks on the pipeline’s pumping stations on Oct. 24 and Oct. 26, which Saudi Arabia has not confirmed. The pipeline built to cope with a Hormuz closure has become one of the most exposed parts of the Saudi export system.

Asia, which received nearly nine-tenths of the crude shipped through Hormuz before the war, has borne the brunt. In March, Bangladesh closed its universities early, rationed fuel at the pump, and diverted gas from four of its five state fertilizer plants to keep the grid running. Pakistan imposed a four-day workweek and closed schools. India limited households to one subsidized cooking-gas cylinder every 25 days as crowds besieged dealers. The Philippines declared a national energy emergency, and in May rotating blackouts left nearly 2 million people on Luzon without power. By September, Bangladeshi garment exporters reported canceled orders and idled production lines, hospitals in Sylhet were losing power almost hourly, and some families in Dhaka waited until midnight for enough gas pressure to cook dinner. Europe’s exposure runs mainly through refined products; European diesel premiums hit records in September.

Iranian strikes on Saudi oil facilities, combined with the Houthi campaign, would place both Saudi export routes under simultaneous attack while the region’s other bypasses are already degraded. Recovery timelines would lengthen toward a decade, and the Saudi spare capacity that has absorbed supply shocks since the 1990s would erode. Buyers and sellers are already adjusting in ways a second round would make permanent. On Oct. 22, QatarEnergy signed a deal to buy up to 4 million metric tons a year of U.S. LNG from Cheniere through 2054, supply that does not pass through Hormuz. If fighting resumes, Gulf producers may find that the market share they cede to the United States, to coal, and to other suppliers does not return.

The alternative to another round is a negotiated settlement in which both sides give ground, and the outlines of one are already visible. Qatari mediators delivered a draft agreement to Tehran on Oct. 25 that reportedly sets out a seven-day sequence of reciprocal confidence-building steps, backed by several guarantor states. A senior Iranian official dismissed it as “not an offer,” but Tehran is expected to respond this week. Washington has moved from demanding an end to Iranian enrichment to seeking a “meaningful” reduction, while Tehran’s priorities are relief from the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions. A deal that trades verifiable limits on enrichment and an unconditional reopening of Hormuz for phased relief on the blockade and sanctions would require each side to accept terms it has so far resisted.

Those concessions carry political costs, but they are cheaper than the alternative. The U.S. military’s costs had reached $47.1 billion by mid-October, according to U.S. Central Command, $29 billion of it for replacing expended munitions. A short campaign would not repair Ras Laffan or restore Saudi spare capacity, and it would invite exactly the retaliation that air defenses cannot fully stop.

Gulf producers spent five decades persuading the world that their supply could withstand regional wars. Eight months of fighting on two fronts have badly weakened that case. A negotiated end to the war would give the region time to rebuild it. Another round, on top of the Saudi-Houthi war, would leave damage to infrastructure and to importers’ confidence that markets are likely to carry for a generation.

Amir Handjani is a board member at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft and a partner at KARV, a strategic advisory firm based in New York. X: @ahandjani

#6023. The Security Challenges Facing the Next Israeli Leader

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: The Security Challenges Facing the Next Israeli Leader

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Israel’s election results remain unclear, but whether current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu again emerges triumphant or a new government, perhaps led by Gadi Eisenkot, takes power, the country is at a crossroads. Although Israel has demonstrated its military power throughout the Middle East, it is trapped in endless conflict on multiple fronts, overstretched at home, and damaging its long-term relationship with the United States.

In the three years since Oct. 7, 2023, when a Hamas terrorist attack killed almost 1,200 Israelis, Israel’s regional military power has reached new heights. Not only did Israel smash Hamas after the attack, but it also took on the far more formidable Hezbollah, severely weakening its leadership, arsenal, and fighting forces in a continuing campaign. In 2025 and then again in 2026, Israel (along with the United States) attacked Iran, killing much of its senior leadership and setting back its nuclear program and military. In addition to striking its enemies, Israel now occupies around 70 percent of the Gaza Strip, large parts of Lebanon, and several miles along its border with Syria, using these buffer zones to guard against another Oct. 7-like attack and make it more difficult for terrorist groups to use drones, rockets, and other short-distance systems to strike Israel.

Israel’s election results remain unclear, but whether current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu again emerges triumphant or a new government, perhaps led by Gadi Eisenkot, takes power, the country is at a crossroads. Although Israel has demonstrated its military power throughout the Middle East, it is trapped in endless conflict on multiple fronts, overstretched at home, and damaging its long-term relationship with the United States.

In the three years since Oct. 7, 2023, when a Hamas terrorist attack killed almost 1,200 Israelis, Israel’s regional military power has reached new heights. Not only did Israel smash Hamas after the attack, but it also took on the far more formidable Hezbollah, severely weakening its leadership, arsenal, and fighting forces in a continuing campaign. In 2025 and then again in 2026, Israel (along with the United States) attacked Iran, killing much of its senior leadership and setting back its nuclear program and military. In addition to striking its enemies, Israel now occupies around 70 percent of the Gaza Strip, large parts of Lebanon, and several miles along its border with Syria, using these buffer zones to guard against another Oct. 7-like attack and make it more difficult for terrorist groups to use drones, rockets, and other short-distance systems to strike Israel.

These conflicts, however, have brought with them additional problems for Israel that its new government must address. In particular, Israel has failed to translate military success into lasting strategic gains.

The Iran war is the most pressing security challenge. What was intended as a short war is now in its ninth month, with no end in sight—and indeed escalation seems possible. Although the United States is focused on the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz and the security of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and other Gulf allies, Israel is more concerned about Iran’s long-range missile arsenal and provision of drones and money to anti-Israel proxies, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, allowing the group to rearm.

More broadly, Israel must break the cycle of endless conflict. In the last three years, Israel has used military force in eight countries and territories: Gaza, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Qatar, Syria, the West Bank, and Yemen. Israel’s enemies, however, show no sign of folding, even as the populations they claim to represent suffer tremendously. Israel can degrade its enemies’ military capabilities, but it is far harder to stop them from rebuilding or get them to abandon their hostility. Iran may emerge from the war wounded but vengeful, and it may commit at least some of the resources it gains under any cease-fire agreement, such as the one the United States proposed in June, to countering Israel. Hamas and Hezbollah are far weaker, but Hamas is still the most important Palestinian actor in Gaza, and Hezbollah, too, remains formidable.

This lack of progress makes Israel’s wars unsustainable even as their human cost is staggering. In Lebanon, Iran, and the West Bank, Israeli operations have killed thousands of civilians as well as many enemy fighters, while the civilian figure for Gaza is in the tens of thousands. Israel has devastated infrastructure in Gaza and parts of Lebanon, with mass displacement in both areas. Even if the new Israeli government places little weight on this suffering, other countries do, and support for Israel is low in most of the world.

Israeli leaders may dismiss this general collapse in support as a necessary price to pay for its security, but it also shapes how key allies treat the country. Israel has long hoped to secure an alliance with Saudi Arabia, but this is politically impossible for Riyadh when the deaths of Palestinian children are a regular feature in the news.

Pollster Dahlia Scheindlin on whether Benjamin Netanyahu can stay in power.

Main opposition parties fail to muster majority.

Early results indicate deadlock in parliamentary elections.

Far more consequential are the effects on Israel’s relationship with the United States. Polling by the Pew Research Center indicates that only 16 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans have favorable views of the Israeli government. Among young adults, those figures are 12 percent for Democrats and only 28 percent for Republicans.

The United States supports Israel militarily, economically, and diplomatically, as well as being a partner in the Iran war. Even if most forms of support continue, the coming years could see increased congressional scrutiny of military assistance to Israel, less diplomatic support in the United Nations and elsewhere, and a possible decline in financial support.

Because the endless wars draw on Israeli reservists, they are also increasing strains in Israeli society. In addition to the risk of casualties, the reservists are away from their jobs and families for long stretches, with no end in sight. There is an Israeli joke that one-third of Israelis pay taxes, one-third work, and one-third serve in the military. The joke is that it is the same third, as Israel’s large Arab population and most of its ultra-Orthodox community do not serve. Reflecting this disproportionate burden, one contentious issue in the latest election was the question of whether Israel’s large and growing Haredi population should be forced to serve in the military.

Historically, Israel has excelled at operations and tactics while having a short-term, narrow mindset about how to achieve security in general. As one Israeli security official joked to me on a recent trip, “The Hebrew word for ‘strategy’ is ‘tactics.’” This mentality has helped Israel score impressive military victories over Hezbollah and Hamas, but it has also left Israel trapped in multiple endless wars with little hope of lasting security. The new Israeli government, whether led by Netanyahu, Eisenkot, or another figure, must translate military dominance into sustainable political arrangements. Otherwise, Israeli society risks exhaustion while the country loses vital international support.

Daniel Byman is a professor in the School of Foreign Service at Georgetown University and the director of the Warfare and Irregular Threats Program of the Center for Strategic and International Studies. His latest book is Spreading Hate: The Global Rise of White Supremacist Terrorism. X: @dbyman
