#6020. The Fog of Tech

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

Why the Future of War Can’t Escape the Past

At a time when debates about national security tend to be polarized along partisan and ideological lines, there is one thing analysts and policymakers across the political spectrum seem to agree on: the future of warfare will be determined by technology. Hypersonic missiles, quantum computing, drone swarms, and artificial intelligence have all been hailed as transformative technologies that will shape battlefields, remake strategies, and upend established military doctrines.

Without question, these technologies are already having a tremendous impact. In Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Ukraine, and elsewhere, every party with the capacity to employ artificial intelligence and autonomous systems has done so—in the air, on land, and at sea, and at times in massive numbers. And there is also no question that in order to maintain its status as the world’s preeminent fighting force, the U.S. military must ensure that it has the most sophisticated and cutting-edge capabilities available. To continue developing and operationalizing these technologies, defense planners should prioritize scaling and integrating them and developing innovative operational concepts to employ them. The risk of being overtaken by rivals such as China is real.

But an equally significant risk exists: call it “the technology trap,” in which policymakers develop a misplaced sense of certainty about how innovations will change war and what warfare will look like in the future, while not paying enough attention to the unchanging fundamentals of war. An excessive focus on the role of technology would be shortsighted and lead militaries in dangerous directions, especially if planners are highly confident about how new capabilities will develop and make decisions in line with that confidence—which will almost certainly be misplaced.

For war planners, faith in technological answers can obscure the most fundamental questions: Who kills, who dies, and who decides? In the post–Cold War era, this myopia has contributed to dreadful outcomes in Afghanistan, Iraq, Ukraine, and Gaza. In the decade to come, as U.S.-Chinese tensions persist, the fog of tech could help pave the way for a disastrous great-power war. Policymakers should worry less about getting the right technology at the right time and more about how fixating on technology might make them lose sight of the essential elements of war and find comfort in false certainty.

More than 50 years ago, the military historian Michael Howard famously cautioned that future wars are unknowable. “I am tempted indeed to declare dogmatically that whatever doctrine the Armed Forces are working on now, they have got it wrong,” he wrote. “I am also tempted to declare that it does not matter that they have got it wrong. What does matter is their capacity to get it right quickly when the moment arrives.”

But Howard may have been a bit too sanguine about the costs of getting it wrong. For Americans, the paradigmatic example from recent history is how the U.S. military’s technological prowess in the 1990–91 Gulf War seemed to herald a new, high-tech American way of war that would guarantee victory in the post–Cold War era. Instead, Washington slowly and painfully learned that the technological advantages that beat Saddam Hussein’s regime could not defeat insurgencies in Afghanistan and Iraq during the post-9/11 wars.

Predicting the role of technology in future wars has become even harder today thanks to the speed, scale, and complexity of contemporary technological progress. In the past, transformative innovations tended to be expensive at their outset—in resources or personnel—or required specialized knowledge and skills accessible to only a few. Think of the combined power of the rifle, the railroad, and the telegraph in the nineteenth century, or fighter jets and nuclear weapons in the twentieth century. By contrast, many of today’s technologies have low barriers to entry: they are cheap to produce, and access to the knowledge necessary to make them has been democratized and globalized. Enemies today often face each other on more equal battlefields, making it trickier for war planners to understand when and for how long new tools will confer an outsize advantage.

Focusing too much on procuring the shiniest equipment also obscures the ways that high-end technology works in tandem with more basic tools. In the 2010s, defense planners failed to account for this dynamic when predicting future battlefields, which they believed would be dominated by sophisticated platforms. In 2017, a senior Pentagon official declared that the F-35 stealth fighter would be “a war winner.” The 2018 National Defense Strategy, drafted under the direction of Elbridge Colby, who now serves as undersecretary of defense, anticipated that a few primarily high-end capabilities—including advanced computing, artificial intelligence, robotics, hypersonics, and biotechnology—would “ensure we will be able to fight and win the wars of the future.”

Instead, what emerged were conflicts such as the war in Ukraine, which can be described as World War I meets World War III. Sophisticated Russian ballistic missiles wreak havoc on Ukrainian cities, as do precision-guided glide bombs delivered by fighter aircraft out of the range of air defenses. At the same time, however, highly lethal bombs are dropped by drones carried aloft by simple balloons, and one of the most effective antidrone defenses consists of fishermen’s nets (or similar netting) draped over security checkpoints, critical infrastructure, and, in the case of Izium, an entire small Ukrainian city. A sense of certainty that sophisticated tech would dominate battlefields represented a failure of imagination that has produced real-world consequences: a dozen years ago, few would have predicted that during a U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, cheap Iranian drones would assault soft targets in Gulf Arab states, as they have since February.

An obsession with technology can obscure the precept that war remains a human endeavor. As the military theorist Carl von Clausewitz said almost two centuries ago, “War is not the action of a living force upon a lifeless mass . . . but always the collision of two living forces.” Technology can inadvertently make war appear mechanical and sterile. But the nature of war has not changed. Its language is violence, and technology simply offers new and different ways to communicate. Therefore, the fundamental questions of war remain salient regardless of technological change: What are the ends (particularly with respect to politics), the ways, and the means?

Perhaps the most perilous time for leaders to be distracted by the allure of technology is when considering whether to go to war in the first place. They often mistakenly believe that technology will make doing so less costly in political terms, particularly if they assume innovations will help reduce casualties. A fixation on the tangible and quantifiable advantages technology confers can detract from vital debate and discussion of the broader consequences of resorting to violence. This dynamic likely influenced Russia’s decision to invade Ukraine. Putin and his advisers believed that the Russian military was sufficiently capable thanks to a massive technological reform effort that began in 2009. In the run-up to the 2022 full-scale invasion, Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu proudly claimed that more than 70 percent of Russia’s military had advanced weapons. Within weeks of the invasion, it had become clear this had conferred little advantage on Moscow. The same goes for the U.S.-Israeli attempt to topple the Iranian regime in 2026, a decision shaped in part by the belief that the sophistication of the American military, particularly when compared with its opponent, made success almost inevitable. In the wake of U.S. strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in 2025, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared that the attack showed Tehran that Washington’s military capabilities are “nearly unlimited.” In fact, the limits of those capabilities became glaringly obvious when the Iranian regime withstood the 2026 onslaught and even managed to close the Strait of Hormuz.

There are ways to avoid the technology trap. The first is to determine a clear goal before going to war. Planners must develop a theory of victory before a single shot is fired and then steadily put that theory into practice. These critical processes cannot be negated by or outsourced to technology. Before launching the 2026 war on Iran, the Trump administration failed to clearly articulate the operation’s goal, instead offering a shifting set of justifications and rationales and various descriptions of the desired end state. The hope seems to have been that technological wizardry would make it possible to achieve everything on a long wish list without having to prioritize or navigate tradeoffs.

To clarify goals, planners must identify what Clausewitz termed “the center of gravity” of a military operation: “the hub of all power and movement, on which everything depends.” This is where an opponent’s power originates, so it needs to be the focus of a military’s attention and resources. During the 1990–91 Gulf War, the commander of U.S. forces in the Middle East, General Norman Schwarzkopf, identified the center of gravity as Saddam Hussein’s command and control of his military. Accordingly, U.S. strategy focused on impeding Saddam’s ability to communicate with his troops and weakening the Iraqi military’s ability to execute orders—a state of affairs that helped convince Saddam to accept a cease-fire. Without this clarity about where to direct efforts and how to measure their impact, a military will struggle to achieve its ends. Early in the 2003 Iraq war, the U.S. military’s inability to identify the Iraqi population as the center of gravity—that is, failing to understand that the political and military leadership no longer wielded control—resulted in years of devastating losses by encouraging tactics that fomented anti-American sentiment, fueled an insurgency, and made it more difficult to establish a credible and functioning government.

Another way to avoid the technology trap is to conduct deliberate, impartial, and regular reviews of lessons learned during and between wars. Iran closely studied the attacks that Israel and the United States carried out on its nuclear sites in 2025. Recognizing that another war would likely pose an existential risk to the Islamic Republic regime, Iranian security officials engaged in a serious and intense effort to prepare. By devolving command and control at both the political and the military levels during the 2026 war, the regime has survived a lengthy onslaught. U.S. allies are, of course, equally capable of such adaptation. In recent years, NATO’s Joint Analysis and Lessons Learned Centre has maintained a team of researchers dedicated to studying the war in Ukraine, a smart way to institutionalize this task and a potential model to apply to other theaters.

The combination of a focus on strategic aims, preparation, and learning remains crucial for effective decision-making in war and cannot be replaced by technology. Similarly, the ways and means of warfare are influenced by technology but have not been fundamentally changed by it. Consider, first, the importance of coalitions and the difficulties of managing them. Going to war exposes the distinct and sometimes even opposing interests, objectives, and perspectives of allies. Planners can devise workarounds when they face disagreements in the heat of conflict, but those may be short-term fixes that mask strategic cleavages.

In early 2026, the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran relying solely on each other. Although the U.S. and Israeli militaries have never operated more closely together in the history of their relationship, their limited success calls into question the partnership’s strategic acumen, despite its remarkable technological capabilities. The two countries notably failed to bring in other partners in the region or in Europe. Early on, several U.S. allies and partners denied the American military access to their territory, bases, and airspace. Although U.S. defense planners have always understood that they might not receive such permissions—Turkey, for example, was unwilling to let the U.S. military invade Iraq from Turkish territory in 2003—the resistance this time was of a different quality and scale. Although most countries ultimately acquiesced, the ones that initially declined threw a wrench into U.S. defense planning, since the American way of war is predicated on an unparalleled global basing network. According to several media reports, Israel found ways around this challenge by setting up a military staging area in Iran during the 2025 war and one in Iraq in 2026. But the ad hoc nature of such creative approaches causes problems for military planning.

As the war has dragged on, the Arab Gulf states have not formally joined the U.S.-Israeli coalition, although at various times during the conflict, Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have used military force against Iran. Their willingness to use force was significant in and of itself, but it did not influence the battlefield, despite some of the sophisticated capabilities those countries possess. On the other side, Iran masterfully managed its proxy, the Lebanese militia Hezbollah, pulling it into the conflict and enabling Tehran to project power through relatively unsophisticated technologies such as rockets, mortars, and most notably, cheap drones that Hezbollah repeatedly deployed against Israeli soldiers in Lebanon and Israeli civilians inside Israel. Meanwhile, Russia also helped Iran target U.S. military facilities in the Gulf, resulting in devastating (though not determinative) consequences.

The complexities of coalition maintenance are on display in Europe, as well, where defense planners are wrestling with a security trilemma. First, they must figure out how to incorporate a highly capable and modernized Ukrainian military into continental defense planning. As Germany turbocharges investments in its military, Europe must also contend with a shift in its internal balance of military power—one with uneasy historical echoes. And, incredibly, during the past year, Europeans have had to consider the risk of aggression on the part of the United States, as President Donald Trump mused about securing U.S. control of Greenland. These three realities introduce a host of tradeoffs into European strategy, since prioritizing any one of them would likely make it harder to deal with the other two—and no technology offers a way out.

Technological determinism can also lead to faulty assumptions about casualties—both civilian and military. Today, target selection is increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, and strikes are increasingly carried out by autonomous systems. Many have argued that these technological advances will improve targeting and better protect civilians. To date, however, it is unclear whether autonomous systems have delivered on this promise. During the war in Gaza, for example, Israeli military personnel have been able to rapidly approve targets generated by an artificial intelligence system called Lavender. But such systems reflect the rules of engagement set by decision-makers, and after Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel in 2023, the Israeli military raised the level of civilian casualties it would accept when striking Hamas militants. Perhaps for that reason, researchers who conducted an experiment testing the decision-making of around 2,000 Israeli military personnel found that in hypothetical scenarios involving high levels of collateral damage, they demonstrated “algorithmic aversion” and a desire to rely more on human decision-making.

Ironically, civilians may become more vulnerable, not less, as new technologies make it harder to attack military personnel and targets, increasing the risk of collateral damage and even providing some parties with an incentive to deliberately attack civilians and soft targets. Many militaries, including the American one, increasingly employ technology to minimize the risks borne by their own forces. This desire for immaculate war is not new. Nearly 700,000 U.S. service members participated in the Gulf War in 1990–91, and contrary to expectations of a bloodbath, only 143 of them died, an outcome that bolstered arguments that technology had made it possible to carry out major military operations with minimal risk to American troops. Two years later, the Battle of Mogadishu undercut that view, as the U.S. military withdrew from Somalia after 18 service members died in a protracted fight with Somali militants armed with cheap and relatively low-tech weapons such as rifles, machine guns, and rocket-propelled grenades. Early in the present century, the rapid American overthrow of the Taliban in Afghanistan rekindled the dream of relatively bloodless warfare made possible by innovations. But the grinding fights that followed there and in Iraq once again poured cold water on the idea.

Technological hopes spring eternal, however, and the U.S. military once again seems to be planning operations that use high-tech tools to reduce risks to its personnel. In an operation carried out in Venezuela this past January, that meant employing special operations forces complemented by space-based and cyber platforms and more than 150 aircraft and drones—all to capture a single person, Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. In Iran, it has meant waging a war to transform conditions on the ground, but with attacks carried out primarily from the air and by sea.

To be sure, this approach is linked to the fact that the United States is not engaged in existential wars. And when the U.S. military has fought an adversary that perceives the conflict as existential, as in the Iranian case, American officials are often surprised that their adversaries refuse to back down and are willing to absorb staggering losses. Even if technology allows for fewer American casualties, that does not mean it should short-circuit robust political debate about whether to go to war. Casualties, after all, are hardly the only cost that contemporary warfare can impose. Even wars that produce relatively low casualties can destroy economies, bring down governments, and rip apart societies.

Countries that haven’t waged war in many decades, such as China, may be even more susceptible than the United States to the technology trap. Such countries might focus on acquiring innovative tools rather than preparing for adversaries that know how to integrate new technologies at scale. This may present some opportunities for Washington given its substantial recent experience in formulating concepts of operation tied to technological advancements. But countries such as China might be no less confident about their capabilities, even though they are significantly less experienced, which means the risks of miscalculation and escalation could easily increase.

Deep faith in new technologies could result in much smaller militaries, as machines replace human personnel. In the United States, this shift could widen the gap that already exists between ordinary Americans and those who serve, as even fewer Americans will have connections to—and therefore care about—how, when, where, and why Washington resorts to military force. This detachment of the military from the society it serves is corrosive to the institution itself and to democracy more broadly since it undermines the principle that war-making should reflect the will of the people. Countries that rely on conscription won’t face quite the same problem, but technological determinism will affect their relationships with their publics, as well: even if such countries need fewer citizens to serve, the technology trap could still reduce social cohesion by further marginalizing the sectors of society from which conscripts tend to be drawn.

Perhaps the most pernicious effect of the technology trap might be the way it could hollow out deterrence, as policymakers are tempted to adopt a myopic approach to the use of force shaped by deterministic views of technology’s impact on the battlefield. Deterrence requires an adversary to cogently read signals regarding capability and will. If both parties in a conflict have confidence in their own capabilities and in those of the other side, they may face increasing pressure to outdo each other in demonstrating a greater will to fight. Such a dynamic could result in a dangerous escalation spiral, particularly if it is paired with assumptions that technology will minimize the role and responsibilities of humans.

It is possible to escape the fog of tech. The most important thing for strategists and officials to grasp is that even though the means of warfighting will keep changing, the fundamental nature of war will not. There is not, and will never be, a shortcut—technological or otherwise—to answering the hard questions one must confront before sending troops to fight, kill, and die.

MARA KARLIN is Professor of Practice at the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University and a Visiting Fellow at the Brookings Institution. She served as U.S. Assistant Secretary of Defense for Strategy, Plans, and Capabilities during the Biden administration and in policy roles at the Pentagon during the Obama and George W. Bush administrations.

#6019. Why Trump’s Hail Mary on Fuel Prices Fell Short

Analysis: Why Trump’s Hail Mary on Fuel Prices Fell Short

Understanding the conflict four years on.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s eleventh-hour pivot back toward Moscow in a desperate bid to lower fuel prices ahead of next week’s midterm elections is not going great. But neither is his war on Iran, with oil prices climbing toward $120 a barrel and one U.S. lawmaker describing the administration’s plans for a renewed war on Iran as “insane.”

Three weeks ago, in a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump made a deal to purchase Russian diesel, which is forbidden under U.S. law. While the measure would have involved risible amounts of additional barrels into a strained global market, it has descended into farce. The three Russian tankers loaded with fuel may not be allowed to dock in U.S. ports. U.S. energy traders are unwilling to chance running afoul of long-standing sanctions against buying Russian energy. And Democratic lawmakers have said that any buyers will face congressional and legal scrutiny.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s eleventh-hour pivot back toward Moscow in a desperate bid to lower fuel prices ahead of next week’s midterm elections is not going great. But neither is his war on Iran, with oil prices climbing toward $120 a barrel and one U.S. lawmaker describing the administration’s plans for a renewed war on Iran as “insane.”

Three weeks ago, in a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump made a deal to purchase Russian diesel, which is forbidden under U.S. law. While the measure would have involved risible amounts of additional barrels into a strained global market, it has descended into farce. The three Russian tankers loaded with fuel may not be allowed to dock in U.S. ports. U.S. energy traders are unwilling to chance running afoul of long-standing sanctions against buying Russian energy. And Democratic lawmakers have said that any buyers will face congressional and legal scrutiny.

The global benchmark price of oil, which was about $70 a barrel before Trump started the Iran war in February, rose to over $117 a barrel on Friday. U.S. nationwide average gasoline prices are $4.20 a gallon, more than a dollar higher than the year before; no president ever has kept gasoline above $4 more than Trump. Diesel, which powers the entire economy, is worse: At $6.32 a gallon, it is about 70 percent higher than one year ago.

Another of Trump’s pro-Russia moves to keep energy prices in check was a pressure campaign on Kyiv to refrain from targeting Russian oil refineries with drones and missiles. U.S. negotiators including Steve Witkoff said that Kyiv should show “gratitude” toward Washington by curtailing strikes.

Ukraine complied for a spell in October, before remembering that what Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calls “long-range sanctions” are the country’s best way of severing the sinews of Russia’s war machine. Overnight Thursday, Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil targets, with a devastating attack on a large Rosneft refinery that makes jet fuel for the military.

U.S. leverage over Ukraine is less than it used to be, since the Trump administration has not delivered any new military or financial assistance since Trump took office for a second time, and on several occasions, including this past month, has suspended what assistance there is, including some access to Starlink’s military-grade satellite internet service and intelligence sharing about inbound missile strikes. (While Ukraine has pleaded in vain for additional missile interceptors, the United States has pleaded poverty. This week, the United States sent a Patriot air defense system from Texas to Israel ahead of an anticipated restart to the fighting in the region.)

The U.S. pivot to Russia isn’t limited to diesel deals and strong-arming Ukraine, though. In addition to stopping future aid, U.S. officials have reportedly been cautioning countries on the front line of Russia’s shadow war to tone down their warnings about Moscow’s hostile intentions. And on Friday, the U.S. welcomed Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov to the G-20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, to the irritation of European allies. The abandonment of Ukraine has lately raised bristles in the European Parliament, where some politicians are redoubling their support for Ukraine even as Trump retreats.

“This is not one of those instances of many different shades of gray. There’s clearly an aggressor who is in the wrong, and that’s Russia, and so I think, for me, that stands clearly,” said Reinier van Lanschot, a Dutch member of the European Parliament from the Volt Europa party and a vocal critic of Russia’s invasion.

Kyiv’s energy war on Russia may hurt on the margins, but the real culprit is Trump’s war on Iran.

It won’t help consumers, won’t help Kyiv, and won’t mean riches for Moscow.

But Trump’s travails aren’t limited to his limited leverage over Ukraine. The war in Iran, which is now in its eighth month and likely to escalate in coming weeks, has kept oil prices high as shippers struggle to navigate a strait strewn with high costs, Iranian drones and missiles, and, for the first time, limpet mines.

It may get uglier after the midterms. The Trump administration is reportedly considering a sharp military attack to try to once and for all break the back of a regime that has withstood war and sanctions for nearly half a century. Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy, who was briefed on defense planning, described the war plan as “insane.”

None of Trump’s moves to placate Putin will help him in the midterms, but they could haunt him in the two years remaining in his presidential term. Winter is coming for Ukrainians who endure daily and undefended assaults from Russian missiles, but it may be coming as well for an administration that has aided and abetted.

#6017. Trump’s closing midterm argument, Reflecting Pool edition

President Donald Trump on Monday delivered an unconventional midterms closing argument after spending weeks dropping comments at rallies aimed at sowing doubts about the election — and what he might do to contest races Republicans lose.

After barnstorming states with competitive Senate races the last few weeks, Trump delivered his final message in Washington, D.C. He even chose the Reflecting Pool by the Lincoln Memorial — the site of a refurbishment he oversaw that was plagued by questionable work that continues to reverberate politically and legally.

There had been rumblings online last week that he would be in Michigan to close out his rally blitz alongside former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, who is in a Toss-up race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. That race was rocked Sunday when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost a primary to El-Sayed, endorsed the Republican nominee. Alas, Trump chose the nation’s capital and mused about pool liner colors, an issue that has not overtaken voter concerns about the cost of living, corruption, the Iran war and other issues, according to public polling.

“We resurfaced the bottom in a beautiful dark blue, very dark blue. They call it ‘American flag blue,’ but it’s very dark,” he said, wearing a suit, tie and white baseball cap. “And if you had a regular blue, like I personally love the lighter color blue, but then you wouldn’t have any reflectors.”

He also plugged his proposed arch, made questionable statements about crime rates and boasted about his other Washington, D.C., fountain and park projects. He did not mention Tuesday’s election —which he deemed “the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime” — until after the 22-minute mark. Once he moved on from boasting about his D.C. projects, Trump touted his second administration’s policy record. And himself.

“As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime. The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history,” he said. “These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

He noted he had held 29 rallies in recent weeks. He contended Iran’s military platforms and stockpiles were “way down.” He touted statistics about the economy.

“Personal incomes are the highest in history. The poverty rate is at an all-time record low,” he said, adding. “American exports are at an all-time high, and more people are working today than at any point in the history of our country. And the United States is now by far the largest supplier of oil and natural gas anywhere in the world.”

The Reflecting Pool event came after he spent weeks on the campaign trail making warnings about elections — specifically, ones Democrats have won and might win this week.

For instance, during an Oct. 20 campaign rally in North Carolina for former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, who is running against former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper, Trump returned to casting doubt on his 2020 loss.

“What a lot of people don’t know is that we got screwed in 2020,” Trump said that evening, referring to the presidential race he lost to Joe Biden. “We did great. But you know who … didn’t allow it to happen was Michael Whatley. We were winning everything. You went to bed [at] 10:00. The race was over.

“Then all of a sudden, Georgia happened and some other things happened. Pennsylvania happened,” he said, continuing to cast doubt on his losses that year in both states despite no evidence of fraud.

“But we can’t forget,” he told loyalists in eastern North Carolina. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales lists the race as leaning toward Cooper.

Trump also offered the same crowd a preview of what his administration and political organizations have signaled for Tuesday at strategically selected polling stations with competitive House and Senate races.

“You know what didn’t happen? North Carolina didn’t happen,” he said to cheers about the 2020 election. “Because he had 619 lawyers at every station watching, watching, watching.”

Democratic lawmakers and pro-voter groups have warned for months that they fear pro-Trump election monitors — or even federal agents — could try to intimidate anti-Trump voters from casting ballots. Some sources have even raised concerns the administration might try seizing ballots in places that could swing a close outcome toward Republican candidates.

Trump’s rally rhetoric also suggests he will raise doubts not just about the outcomes the votes produce, but how they were cast.

“The whole thing is corrupt,” he told rallygoers Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa. “Go to paper ballots, everybody. Nice, beautiful paper ballots. You know, the paper ballots cost 9 percent of what these crooked machines cost, so you’d save a lot,” he said, without offering evidence that electronically cast ballots are problematic.

He even set the stage for casting doubt over or challenging Democratic-won races in states with GOP chiefs executive.

“And even Republican governors, many of them, they, they just do it,” he said of using voting machines over watermarked paper ballots. “I don’t know, it’s hard to believe. But you go to paper and you have the ballot there, and it’s so simple, and they put it in stacks.”

Still, Trump and his team have questioned the counting of paper ballots before — in 2020 in places like Arizona, Georgia and Pennsylvania, but to no avail. That didn’t stop him on Sunday, like at previous campaign stops, from alleging Democrats would still try shenanigans.

“It’s, look, they’ll try figuring something [out], but it’s much harder, because they have to cheat,” he said without providing evidence. “Because without, look, their policies are so bad.”

One GOP strategist, granted anonymity to be candid, said it was “normal” for any party to contest “some” election results.

Former Pennsylvania GOP Rep. Charlie Dent on Friday said Trump’s rally rhetoric appears mostly aimed at influencing public opinion and could be lacking a legitimate legal strategy.

“I’m not sure how he would intend to make a challenge to the certification of some members who may win by comfortable margins,” Dent said. “There might be circumstances where you have some contested outcomes shortly after the election that are very close. But then you’ll have a legal process and a recount process to go through to ultimately determine who the winner is.

“But once those winners are determined and the states certify those elections, then everything that’s done or said in Washington is merely ministerial at that point,” he added. “If there are objections to a particular outcome, there are legal remedies candidates can seek out.”

Mark Zaid, an attorney who has sued the Trump administration multiple times, said Monday that “the danger with his rhetoric is that he expects people to react to what he says and implement his words into action.

“He did that on Jan. 6 and he continues to do it now,” Zaid added, referring to the January 2021 Capitol riot by a pro-Trump mob following his fiery Ellipse speech that morning raising doubts about his loss to Biden.

“My own view is that post-Nov. 3 he will act far more like a cornered animal, more dangerous than when an avenue of escape is available — and implement a scorched-earth response to anything that is thrown at him,” he added. “I find it amazing that his rhetoric seemingly goes unchallenged by his base.”

Trump appeared in a relaxed mood on Monday, joking that he intended to rename the Reflecting Pool to include his name.

“I’m only kidding,” he said, looking toward assembled media members. “Please, don’t report it.” Later, about the midterms, he said the party of sitting presidents typically loses, adding matter-of-factly: “We gave this a very strong shot.”

1. How did right-wing presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro react to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s runoff election victory on Sunday?

He called for his followers to protest his loss in Brasília.

He said he would request an annulment of the election.

Lula became the first Brazilian presidential candidate in history to come from behind to win the election’s second round, FP’s Catherine Osborn reports. Bolsonaro, the subject of several criminal probes, subsequently fled to Miami, where he called himself “the leader of Brazil.”

2. Student-led protests in Serbia that began in November 2024 culminated in the defeat of longtime right-wing leader Aleksandar Vucic in elections on Sunday. What incident sparked the original demonstrations?

Vucic’s decision to send military equipment to Russia

The collapse of a concrete railway station canopy

A factory spill that polluted the Danube through Belgrade

The revelation of a mass domestic surveillance network

The student protesters’ improbable victory against the Vucic regime could be instructive for their counterparts in the United States and European Union, Edward P. Joseph writes.

3. The Chinese Communist Party’s fifth plenum began on Monday. Traditionally focused on economic policy, what is the priority for this year’s gathering?

The shift in focus is a sign that Chinese President Xi Jinping is worried that his anti-corruption campaigns aren’t paying off, FP’s James Palmer writes in China Brief.

4. Early results show no clear winner from Israel’s parliamentary elections on Tuesday. But what is clear is that voter turnout was at its highest this century. About what percent of Israel’s registered voters turned out to cast a ballot on Tuesday?

Even if the opposition bloc succeeds in forming a governing coalition, there is little indication that Israel’s policies toward Palestinians will dramatically change, FP columnist Steven A. Cook writes.

5. At a Texas rally on Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump floated adding a 51st state. What territory or country did he suggest?

Trump’s “America First” foreign-policy agenda has been wildly unpopular with voters, as recent polling indicates, Jonathan Monten, Jordan Tama, and Josh Busby write.

6. The third Russia-Africa Summit began on Wednesday in Moscow. Russian President Vladimir Putin asserted that Moscow would champion greater African involvement where?

In the continent’s own critical minerals industry

At the World Bank and International Monetary Fund

African leaders’ attendance has dipped since its high point in 2019, partially driven by Moscow’s unfulfilled promises on the continent and the forced recruitment of Africans into Russia’s military ranks to fight in Ukraine, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.

7. Why were three French nationals sentenced to life in prison in Iraq on Thursday?

For spray-painting protest graffiti on Iraq’s parliament building

For smuggling weapons to the Popular Mobilization Forces

The arrests highlight how conflicts and divisions that may feel distant to Washington remain alive and pressing in the Middle East. Earlier this month, Hekmat Aboukhater wrote about how the Trump administration is inflaming sectarian divisions in Iraq.

8. Ireland said on Friday that it will set up a government body that, for the first time, would research and prepare for the possibility of what?

Sending troops to defend Palestinians in the West Bank

Unifying with the U.K.-run Northern Ireland

The announcement comes as Scotland and Wales also push for greater autonomy from London, which has reeled from years of dysfunction, Jamie Maxwell wrote in May.

9. Contestants gathered in Belgium on Monday to participate in a competition to see who could craft the most impressive sculpture made from what material?

Among the chocolate creations were birds, an elf, and a praying mantis, as photographed by The Associated Press.

10. An Australian court ruled on Monday against an inmate’s claim that his inability to have this product violated his right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.” What product did the inmate sue to access?

The court found the ban on Vegemite, a yeast-based spread, was justified because of the product’s potential to impair drug-sniffing dogs’ ability to detect narcotics as well as its possible use in brewing alcohol, The Associated Press reports.

#6014. The Limits of American Power

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

The war in Iran is far from the first time that U.S. policymakers have failed to appreciate the limits of American power. But the Trump administration’s use of military force against the Islamic Republic since February 28 offers a particularly glaring example of a mistake that has often characterized American strategy in recent decades. The war was launched without a clear rationale and with a constantly shifting set of objectives—from changing Tehran’s regime and squelching its nuclear ambitions to, more recently, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which wasn’t closed until the war started. The results, not surprisingly, have been bad both for U.S. interests and for the Middle East.

Still, to focus only on the blunders in Iran is to miss a deeper problem in U.S. foreign policy—one that preceded and will outlast Donald Trump’s presidency. Although the particular missteps in Iran may stem from the shortcomings of this president and the team around him, the overestimation of the potential of military force has been a growing feature of American strategy since at least the end of World War II. A tendency to wish away the limits of power accounted for some of the greatest mistakes of U.S. statecraft during the Cold War, with Vietnam the clearest and most consequential example. Yet despite an apparent commitment to internalizing the lessons of that overreach, this American delusion—our excessive faith in the capacity of military power to achieve victory and thereby fundamentally political ends—has gotten worse rather than better, especially in the past quarter century.

And unfortunately, there is good reason to worry that the delusion will deepen in the years ahead. Presidential power is becoming increasingly personalized as the constraints on it continue to erode. The politicization of the military (along with the diplomatic corps and intelligence communities) is making it less likely that policymakers will receive the best advice, including frank warnings about risks and costs. And the rise of artificial intelligence and new weapons technologies reinforces a sense of complete battlefield awareness and mastery, feeding superpower hubris. The risk of overreach has never been higher, at a time when the damage from overreach is becoming more difficult to repair.

In April 1975, Colonel Harry Summers, a member of the U.S. delegation dealing with postwar issues in Vietnam, was meeting in Hanoi with a North Vietnamese counterpart, Colonel Tu. “You know, you never defeated us on the battlefield,” Summers observed. To which Tu replied, “That may be so, but it is also irrelevant.”

Summers went on to write a seminal book about the war, On Strategy: A Critical Analysis of the Vietnam War. His key takeaway was simple: there are limits to American power that are neglected at immense cost. War is, and always has been, a contest of human will, shaped by heroism and cowardice, fear and elation, chance and uncertainty; no matter how superior a military force, it is not guaranteed strategic victory.

The book became required reading for many military officers, including me. I had joined the Naval ROTC unit at the University of Texas two years before the encounter between Summers and Tu. The draft had just ended, and the fall of Saigon was still to come, but discussion of Vietnam consumed our ranks. As I studied the American failure, I came to see that a great strength had become a fatal liability: our fundamental faith that we, the United States of America, had to win and thus would. We had won World War I, we had won World War II, and we had at least fought to a draw, holding off the North Koreans and Chinese, in Korea. And somehow, at all costs, we would win in Vietnam.

To believe you can win is important. It inspires troops and keeps the public engaged. But when the commitment to winning is not coupled with sound policy judgment, when the principles of war are disregarded in the false belief that technology or firepower can overcome the inherent frictions of combat, when tactical successes are viewed as a guaranteed path to a strategic win, when the cost in blood and treasure rises inexorably while any claim to righteousness collapses, it is essential to reassess. In Vietnam, the answer to mounting losses was simply “more”—more troops, more bombs, more money. To lose the fight was seen as anathema to all we stood for; we would keep fighting in spite of the increasingly evident limits to our power. When the end finally came with the rushed U.S. withdrawal from Saigon in 1975, many military and political leaders could still not understand how the United States had won nearly every skirmish, battle, and fight but lost the war.

The military I entered in 1977 was struggling in the aftermath of Vietnam. The “peace dividend” meant a dramatic drawdown in manpower and money. Readiness was at an all-time low across the services—army enlistment had fallen by 60,000 and the number of navy ships from around 650 to barely more than 500. Meanwhile, the transition to an all-volunteer military had proved challenging: drug abuse and racial tensions were high, morale among senior leaders and young troops alike was low, and new recruits lacked basic skills.

When President Ronald Reagan took office in 1981, he began the largest peacetime expansion of the U.S. military since the Korean War. Over the course of eight years, he increased defense spending by 35 percent. There was a slew of major procurements: the M-1 Abrams tank, the Bradley Fighting Vehicle, the Apache and Black Hawk helicopters, the F-15 and F-16 fighters, the B-1 bomber, the E-3 Sentry. The navy built back toward 600 ships, including 15 aircraft carriers, 100 attack submarines, and cruisers and destroyers equipped with the revolutionary Aegis Combat System. For troops, pay rose, recruiting goals were met, and standards were restored. Just as important, Congress passed the Goldwater-Nichols Act in 1986. It fundamentally changed the military by strengthening the role of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, establishing the regional combatant commanders as the warfighters, ensuring joint force integration, improving joint planning and procurement, and leading to the establishment of the U.S. Special Operations Command. By 1990, the military I entered in the 1970s had been transformed. Our troops were well trained, well equipped, highly motivated, and, most important, well led.

In July 1990, I left San Diego on a routine six-month deployment to the western Pacific. I was a SEAL task unit commander assigned to Amphibious Squadron Five and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit. Little did I know that this reinvigorated military and our civilian leaders were about to be tested, raising the question of whether the United States had learned anything from Vietnam and the other failed missions of the recent past.

On August 2, 1990, Iraqi President Saddam Hussein ordered the Iraqi army into Kuwait. Within hours of the invasion, the National Security Council convened and options for U.S. action were presented to the president. “This is the first test of the postwar system—as the bipolar world is relaxed, it permits this,” Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger emphasized. “If [Saddam] succeeds, others may try the same.”

Fortunately, American leadership had never been stronger or more experienced—and in wartime especially, leadership matters. President George H. W. Bush was a young navy pilot when he was shot down near Iwo Jima and eventually rescued by an American submarine. Bush understood war. Later in life, he had served as U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, de facto ambassador to China, director of the Central Intelligence Agency, and vice president. No president in American history had come into office with more national security experience. Nevertheless, Bush surrounded himself with some of the most remarkable diplomats, military officers, intelligence professionals, and strategic thinkers of their time: Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser; Secretary of State James Baker; Secretary of Defense Dick Cheney; Colin Powell, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; and many more.

U.S. Central Command, which would spearhead the military effort against Saddam, was led by General Norman Schwarzkopf. Schwarzkopf was a Vietnam veteran who had been awarded three Silver Stars for heroism and two Purple Hearts for combat injuries. Upon his return from Vietnam, Schwarzkopf had reflected: “Nobody is more antiwar than an intelligent person who’s been to war. . . . And when they get ready to send me again, I’m going to have to stop and ask myself, ‘Is it worth it?’ That’s a very dangerous place for the nation to be when your own army is going to stop and question.”

Grappling honestly with that question—Is it worth it?—is the imperative of good leadership. Bush carefully weighed the costs and risks associated with confronting Saddam and decided the war was worth it. Together, the United States’ political and military leaders developed a strategy with clear goals and objectives and built both popular and international support for the operations to come. It would prove to be the finest application of political and military power in recent American history—and its success is thus worth lingering on.

The success of the Gulf War rested on several fundamental principles that were at the heart of American strategy. First, that the United States should begin by taking the moral high ground. The high ground implies that you hold a dominant position when facing an enemy. The moral high ground shows that the fight is worth it. With it, leaders can inspire troops, galvanize publics, and rally allies.

Immediately after Saddam’s invasion, Bush ordered the deployment of military forces into the region and worked with Saudi Arabia to establish a footprint in the kingdom in the event military action was necessary. Bush was still hoping to avoid a conflict, but he saw a similarity “between the Persian Gulf and the situation in the Rhineland in the 1930s, when Hitler simply defied the Treaty of Versailles and marched in.” Yet he knew that he had to convince the international community and the American people that any actions he might take would be moral, legitimate, and in the interests of the United States and its allies.

Bush and his team engaged in a full-court diplomatic effort to build support from Arab states in the region, from European allies, and from Moscow and Beijing. Although skeptical of the United Nations, Bush nonetheless sought a variety of UN resolutions that condemned Iraq’s invasion, imposed sweeping economic sanctions, and authorized the use of force if necessary. Simultaneously, he built the case with the American people, a large majority of whom ultimately approved of his handling of the crisis. And although Bush believed he had the authority as commander in chief to commit military forces without congressional approval, he sought and received Capitol Hill’s support.

Second, Bush and his administration recognized the value of building an international coalition, even if the United States had the firepower to go it alone in strictly military terms. This was partly about legitimacy, partly about the chance to send a message. Saddam’s invasion presented an opportunity to shape what some in the administration thought of as a “new world order,” one in which aggression would be met with collective action; major powers would come together despite their ideological differences; and the United Nations and international law would play a critical role rather than be ignored. Bush leveraged the strong personal relationships he had developed over his long career in public service, gaining the support of everyone from Germany’s Chancellor Helmut Kohl and France’s President François Mitterrand, to Saudi Arabia’s King Fahd and Egypt’s President Hosni Mubarak, to Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. As secretary of state, Baker also embarked on a campaign of shuttle diplomacy that took him across the globe, adding to the coalition.

In the end, the United States did not simply get the support of the international community. Much of the costs of the conflict were borne by others. The allied force ultimately assembled—750,000 troops from 36 countries, including 540,000 Americans—was the largest since World War II. It included, critically, an Arab coalition with forces from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Egypt, Syria, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, and Bahrain. The coalition was challenging to manage; British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once quipped that “there is only one thing worse than fighting with allies, and that is fighting without them.” But Bush understood that international support brought operational legitimacy and regional stability. It sent a message to Saddam and to the world.

Third, Bush and his advisers were intent on establishing clear goals and objectives, with political and military dimensions aligned. Politically, the purpose was to uphold international law and restore peace in the region. The military objectives supported those political objectives. The coalition would drive Iraqi forces out of Kuwait. But in doing so, it would attempt to minimize friendly casualties, maintain the alliance, and limit the duration of the war. U.S. leaders were clear from the beginning: there would be no push to Baghdad or protracted engagement with the Iraqi army.

Yet even with these limited objectives, neither civilian nor military leaders were under the illusion that success would be easy or cost-free. Driving out a determined enemy that owns the terrain requires overwhelming firepower and a willingness to commit to ground operations. As Carl von Clausewitz stressed in On War, the defense is stronger than the offense, since the defense has only to preserve and protect, while the offense must impose its will on the enemy. He argues that the only way to overcome the inherent strength of the defense is through overwhelming firepower. The Iraqis were prepared to defend the ground they had taken in Kuwait; they owned the terrain, the geography was in their favor, and they had an experienced fighting force after eight years in combat against the Iranians. But Cheney, Powell, and Schwarzkopf understood the principles of war. They had a clearly defined objective. They massed U.S. firepower in the most important areas, accepted risk in less important ones, and were prepared to maneuver against the enemy. And they were committed to leaving when the objectives were reached, not allowing the war to go on too long.

To accomplish these goals meant putting troops on the ground—a lot of troops. U.S. military and civilian leaders understood that defeating the Iraqis would take more than just airpower. Early on, Cheney observed, “The history of air campaigns suggests they are not terribly successful.” Powell agreed: “To further deter Iraqi action with Saudi Arabia would require U.S. forces on the ground. . . . It would mean a major confrontation. Most U.S. forces would be committed to sustain not just for one or two days.”

If I have learned one important lesson in over four decades of military service, it’s that to defeat the enemy, you must stand on the ground he holds dear and own it. It is why Alexander invaded Persia, William the Conqueror crossed the channel to England, Genghis Khan rode into China, Sherman marched to Atlanta, the Allies landed at Normandy, and the United States rolled into Kuwait. (It is why today the Israelis are in Gaza and Lebanon and why the Russians will never be victorious until they hold Kyiv.) But as Cheney cautioned, “We should start this only if we are prepared to see it through. . . . The problem is the American people might have a short tolerance for war.”

Operation Desert Storm began with air attacks at 2:38 AM Baghdad time on January 17, 1991. After 43 days of air operations and 100 hours of ground operations, Washington’s political and military objectives had been achieved. The Iraqi army was ousted from Kuwait, and most American forces were soon on their way home.

“We’re doing something decent and we’re doing something good,” Bush wrote in his diary. “Vietnam will soon be behind us.”

Desert Storm was a reset, but not in the way it should have been. It presented an opportunity to internalize lessons about how to use force effectively and about what military power could and could not achieve. Instead, it spurred a wave of triumphalism. When I returned from Desert Storm, where I’d led a special operations task force, the euphoria was palpable: we were winners again. The victory proved intoxicating, drawing us back into the false belief that our power could do almost anything to shape the world to our liking.

Adding to this euphoria was the technology that had been on display against Iraq. Precision-guided munitions could put a 500-pound bomb on a moving target from 20,000 feet in the air. Tomahawk cruise missiles could be launched from ships and submarines hundreds of miles away. A GPS satellite could guide an infantry battalion across a flat desert at night and get it to exactly the right destination, and the joint surveillance target attack radar system could see the Iraqi army as it maneuvered. Digital command and control systems could provide computerized air-tasking orders, secure satellite communications, and digital planning tools. No military in history had ever commanded the battlespace as precisely as we did during Desert Storm. It made sense to build on this success to spur a revolution in military affairs that would improve the way the United States fought. But the experience also fueled a widespread belief that technology could overcome the inherent frictions, costs, and risk of war.

In the 1990s, U.S. military missions, in line with the confidence that followed Desert Storm and the hopes of the post–Cold War world, were focused on supporting norms and containing humanitarian harms—some successful (Bosnia and Kosovo), some less so (Somalia). But it was after 9/11 that the failure to learn the right lessons from the Gulf War became especially clear, with a persistent misunderstanding of the limits of American power and what the military could and couldn’t achieve. The war in Afghanistan began with the right intentions but devolved into a protracted fight with shifting goals, misaligned military and political objectives, and a determined Taliban force fighting on its home ground. Even after the special operations mission that killed the al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, the goals and objectives in Afghanistan kept shifting. As always, the strength of the military was our troops: they were courageous, disciplined, technologically savvy. We made mistakes, but there was no lack of fighting spirit or tactical successes. Even public support remained strong throughout most of the war. But we faltered by assuming that the quick victory could extend to the complex task of fighting an insurgency, conducting counterterrorism operations, and building a nation. Lest I appear too righteous in my critique of American strategy, make no mistake: as a combat leader in Afghanistan, I fell into the same trap of believing that more troops, more weapons, and more money could solve some of the most intractable problems. They could not.

The Iraq war, based on a far shakier case at the outset, also degenerated into a counterinsurgency and counterterrorism mission with insufficient forces, a small coalition, and an evolving timeline. Once again, our troops were everything the American people could have hoped for, but our leaders repeatedly disregarded the fundamental principles of war. Our claim to the moral high ground was based on flawed intelligence, our international support was limited, and our goals shifted from removing Saddam to trying to build a Western-style democracy. We may have entered Iraq and Afghanistan with noble intentions, and perhaps in the long term the seeds of freedom we tried to plant will take root. But so far, minimal gains have come at immense cost to our military and our troops, our home front, and our international legitimacy.

Yet even these recent experiences—which several key members of the Trump administration witnessed firsthand in their own military service—did little to instill caution when it came to Iran earlier this year. To be clear, the Iranian regime is despicable. It is responsible for the death of hundreds of American troops. It threatens its neighbors, uses proxies to attack our allies, and has killed tens of thousands of its own people.

Given the fall of the Assad government in Syria, the destruction of Hamas’s power in Gaza, the crippling of Hezbollah in Lebanon, and a weakened supreme leader in Iran itself, it is easy to appreciate the allure of trying to change the Iranian regime. What’s more, coming off the dramatic capture of President Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, where the U.S. military exercised remarkable speed, lethality, and courage to overcome a very sophisticated defense, it was all too easy for U.S. policymakers to assume once again that the power of our technology and the courage and experience of our soldiers made us virtually invincible. But there is a reason no U.S. president has attempted to change the regime in Iran since 1979, and it has little to do with determination or political will. The challenges of legitimacy, coalition building, and geography; the will of the enemy; and the reality that it would be necessary to put American boots on the ground to achieve such an ambitious end all argued against it.

From the start of the Iran war, there was no attempt to build international legitimacy. It began on February 28 with a U.S.-Israeli strike. To make matters worse, an early airstrike went awry and hit an Iranian elementary school, resulting in the deaths of 120 students. Mistakes happen in war, but not acknowledging our error added to the sense of illegitimacy and vindictiveness, losing whatever moral high ground we might have had. The Trump administration failed to notify any U.S. allies of the impending strike, most notably neighboring Arab states, which resulted in a lack of regional trust from the outset. Later, when the president sought allied support to open the Strait of Hormuz, he was met with an international cold shoulder. This refusal came as no surprise: Trump had been notoriously caustic with European leaders.

There was never a clear understanding of the goals. The administration at first said it wanted regime change. But later Trump told reporters that he never cared about regime change. The administration claimed the urgency of preempting an imminent Iranian nuclear weapon. But when pressed, Trump later dismissed such concerns as inconsequential, since there was little left in Iran but “nuclear dust.” After Iran closed the strait, and reopening it to shipping became the primary focus of both military strategy and diplomacy, Trump told the world that it mattered little since the United States didn’t need the oil. The objectives seemed to change by the day. I have no doubt that American military planners understood the limits of airpower when it came to achieving U.S. aims in Iran; this should have been a signal to the White House that unless the military planned to invade Iran, victory was unlikely.

Geography was always going to be a limiting factor. In my almost 40 years of military service, much of that time in the Middle East, no general or admiral I ever met talked about Iran without talking about the Strait of Hormuz. It was the Iranians’ weapon of mass destruction, their bulwark against invasion, their ace in the hole no matter the game. Additionally, the Iranian leadership was in the position of the defenders: they only had to preserve and protect themselves to win. And protect they have. At this point, it is highly unlikely the U.S. military will ever stand on the ground they hold dear and call it our own.

The U.S. war was also limited by the will of the enemy. From 1980 to 1988, Iran and Iraq fought a vicious war claiming the lives of hundreds of thousands of Iranians. It should have been clear from the beginning of this war that the Iranians would fight and fight hard. The zealots in Iran control the narrative, and they are battling for their survival.

Such a grave failure to recognize and appreciate the limits of power is not a new phenomenon in American history, or in military history more broadly. With every revolution in military technology, from mounted cavalry to motorized units, from the single-shot musket to the Gatling gun, from propeller-driven aircraft to jets, leaders desperately want to believe that they can wish away the basic nature of war. As our ability to project power around the globe becomes more formidable, we desperately want to believe that geography is no longer important. As new media allows us to see national outrage among an adversary’s population, we desperately want to believe that we can spur change with little risk or commitment. And as AI speeds up tactical decision-making, we desperately want to believe that the lessons of military experience can be disregarded. These beliefs are illusions.

More concerning, however, is that there are several structural trends in the United States that suggest the problem will get worse rather than better, no matter how vivid the lessons of the Iran war may seem at the moment. The first is the trend toward more personalistic presidential leadership, in which loyalty to the leader becomes more important than loyalty to institutions. When institutions designed to provide a president with the best military, diplomatic, economic, or intelligence advice are led by loyalists, there is a risk that advice will be shaded, inadvertently or intentionally, to reflect the president’s desires. This is a recipe for disaster. A leader needs the unvarnished truth, the best advice possible, regardless of his or her personal position on the issue. The growing concentration of power in the executive branch has unfolded over several administrations, and despite occasional noise from Congress, there is little sign this will change. Here, too, Trump may be a particularly flagrant example, but he’s unlikely to be the last president susceptible to such temptations and operating with few constraints.

The dangers of personalistic presidential leadership are severely exacerbated by more politicized leadership in the military. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ongoing purge of military leadership will undermine the civil-military dynamic for years to come. Trump and Hegseth have forced out senior officers across nearly every service, including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the chief of naval operations, and the army chief of staff. Hegseth has intervened to block career advancement in unprecedented ways, personally removing dozens of officers from promotion lists, often with no explanation (although a disproportionate number seem to have worked for leaders who were viewed as obstacles to Trump’s domestic political goals). While remaining military leaders will largely stay committed to serving honorably and providing their best advice to civilian leaders in the Pentagon and the White House, this purge is bound to have a chilling effect on the willingness and ability of senior officers to give frank counsel, especially when it comes to the costs and limits of what force can achieve.

And finally, the rapid introduction of new technologies, from AI and unmanned vehicles to robotics, cyber- and space-based systems, will once again make it all too easy to wish away the fundamentals of war. Technology will always be an important factor in how wars are fought, and every military must seek greater lethality, survivability, and situational awareness. But although these capabilities are necessary, they are not sufficient to overcome the basic principles of war. Leaders must understand technology for what it is—an enabler. It can improve the application of military power, but it cannot compensate for misguided policies that draw us into conflict in the first place.

Today’s U.S. military is the finest, most professional armed force in the history of the world—yes, the history of the world. But that doesn’t mean we can disregard the limits of our power.

We will be limited by moral uncertainty. If the reasons for a conflict are dubious or worse, it will prove challenging to build a coalition, motivate troops, maintain civilian support, and undermine the will of the enemy. Such failures explain why the Greeks defeated the Persians at Salamis, the English defeated the Spanish at Gravelines, George Washington defeated the British, the Russians defeated the Germans at Stalingrad, the Vietnamese defeated the French and the Americans, and the Ukrainians are defeating the Russians today. Although the moral high ground does not guarantee military victory, it is a foundation on which success rests.

We will be limited by geography. No matter the advances in technology, geography will always be a critical factor in determining the outcome of any engagement. Every military leader knows that the terrain dictates how the enemy will fight, where he will position his forces, how he will supply his troops. It is the oceans and the rivers that provide natural barriers to an advancing force, and the terrain and the waterways that will limit the ability of the attacking force to maneuver, hold ground, resupply, and project power. The Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el Mandeb Strait present the same challenges as the English Channel, the Rhine, or the Volga.

We will be limited by the will of the enemy. There is a “sleeping giant” in every population that will rise from its slumber and fight hard, driven by a sense of righteousness, a desire for survival, or both. Invaders, aggressors, and first strikers all elicit a visceral response from the population they seek to mollify. Never underestimate the enemy’s will to fight—a mistake we have made again and again.

We will be limited by our hesitancy to put troops on the ground. No American wants to lose our young men and women on a foreign battlefield, but sometimes it is necessary to achieve the greater good. During World War I, over two million young doughboys deployed to Europe. During World War II, over five million GIs fought the Nazis and island-hopped to Japan. In both cases, mankind was better for their sacrifice. Of course, if there is any doubt about whether we own the moral high ground, leaders will be hesitant to fully commit. In that hesitation comes defeat.

We will be limited by time. This is not a uniquely American limitation, but we seem to suffer from it more than most countries. It has been said that the Russians will eat grass before they capitulate. The United States’ reputation is that sooner rather than later, we will tire of the fight and leave. Much of this reputation stems from the reality that our democracy demands public support to sustain a long engagement. Even with a compelling reason to send our young men and women into battle, the cost in blood and treasure can soon outweigh our collective sense of the necessity of the fight.

Finally, we will be limited by the quality of our leadership, political and military. Without experienced leaders—leaders who understand the need to establish legitimacy, to build coalitions, to have clear and attainable goals, to commit to the task, to limit the duration of the fight to only what is necessary—all the power in the world will be irrelevant.

William H. MCRaven served in the U.S. Navy from 1977 to 2014, including as Commander of United States Special Operations Command from 2011 to 2014. He was Chancellor of the University of Texas from 2015 to 2018.

#6013. ‘I Welcome Their Hatred’

Analysis: ‘I Welcome Their Hatred’

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.
