Get audio access with any FP subscription.

As Election Day approaches, the president of the United States is onstage, lambasting the powerful forces ranged against him—the judges, the media, the ultra-wealthy. Addressing 20,000 of the millions of regular Americans who love him, he defies his enemies, declaring, “They are unanimous in their hate for me—and I welcome their hatred!” The crowd roars.

Oct. 31 marks 90 years since President Franklin Delano Roosevelt delivered that speech at Madison Square Garden, as the 1936 presidential race neared its climax. In a world again beset by angry populists stoking economic distress, the rise of autocrats, and the floundering of moderate politicians, Roosevelt’s barnburner speech has come to seem relevant once more.

As Election Day approaches, the president of the United States is onstage, lambasting the powerful forces ranged against him—the judges, the media, the ultra-wealthy. Addressing 20,000 of the millions of regular Americans who love him, he defies his enemies, declaring, “They are unanimous in their hate for me—and I welcome their hatred!” The crowd roars.

Oct. 31 marks 90 years since President Franklin Delano Roosevelt delivered that speech at Madison Square Garden, as the 1936 presidential race neared its climax. In a world again beset by angry populists stoking economic distress, the rise of autocrats, and the floundering of moderate politicians, Roosevelt’s barnburner speech has come to seem relevant once more.

Roosevelt had entered office ready to work with established power as he launched his reflationary, state-expanding New Deal. Yet the president had grown increasingly frustrated by the obstructiveness of the Supreme Court—which had blocked programs such as the National Recovery Administration, designed to end “cut-throat” competition—and by the hostility of newspapers and tycoons. His enemies insinuated that he was a communist, and a would-be dictator. He also faced the rise of the radical right, which sought to exploit the public’s fear and frustration.

Roosevelt realized that by facing down the “economic royalists,” as he put it in his acceptance speech at the 1936 Democratic National Convention, he could cast himself as the people’s tribune, uniting the disparate groups supporting him. In that speech on Halloween, he warned that “powerful influences” were striving to bring back leaders who were “indifferent” to ordinary Americans’ economic plight. “Government by organized money,” he charged, was “just as dangerous as government by organized mob.” He hoped in his second term to become such forces’ “master.” Three days later, almost 61 percent of voters backed him, in one of the most decisive presidential election victories in U.S. history.

The speech resonates today even in that land of actual royalists, the United Kingdom. In the 2019 general election, the left-wing Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn quoted Roosevelt’s speech. But since then, political commentators, most of whom were never keen on Corbynism, have done the same. Their overarching goal is to ensure, as Roosevelt did, that power does not fall to the radical right.

In 2024, Corbyn’s successor, Keir Starmer, lead Labour to back into office, in an election marked by widespread public frustration with the long-dominant parties. From the left, the Greens and “Gaza independents” made gains, while support for the far-right party Reform UK hit 14 per cent—and has continued to rise. When it became clear that the new prime minister’s response was to remain stolidly managerial while at times adopting the language of Reform’s own arguments, liberal-left fears rose too.

In the two years that followed, a series of voices—in the Guardian, the London Times, and elsewhere—called for Starmer to learn from Roosevelt’s tub-thumping at Madison Square Garden. The prime minister, they argued, should pick battles with entrenched interests, carving out a clear narrative about how overcoming those interests would improve voters’ lives.

Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn speaks at Birmingham City University in Birmingham, England, on Nov. 21, 2019.Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

Writing in Prospect magazine, Ben Ansell, professor of comparative democratic institutions at Oxford, was one of those arguing that the speech offered the center-left a model for beating the radical right by using its own populist means against it. In January, as Starmer’s popular support plumbed terminal new depths, the veteran pollster Peter Kellner called on him to learn from Roosevelt’s speech by “declaring war” on the champions of Brexit. “Would he be taking a risk?” Kellner added. “Absolutely — and that’s the point.”

Starmer didn’t have it in him, but this was never just about his personal skillset. Across the democratic world, the center-left has been under pressure for a decade to find effective ways to respond to right-wing populism, as exacerbated by social media. Now that Starmer has been replaced by the former mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham (a politician much more ready to talk about power), those same voices reiterate their case. They point to the punchier approach taken by the prime ministers of Spain and Australia, and the success of Manuela Schwesig, the Social Democratic premier of the east German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, in holding back the advance of the extreme right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

Political scientist Robert Ford is the author of books on the radical right and Brexit. He plays his students at the University of Manchester footage of Roosevelt’s speech, he told me, because “it shows us how much bolder a center-left politician was 90 years ago.” As the center-right loses ground to its more populist rivals, he argued, the left and the radical right are “coalescing around in-group/out-group politics at a mass level, whatever politicians do.” This is forcing center-left politicians to ask themselves, “How can we best make use of this?” Roosevelt’s us-against-them speech offers a useful example, Ford suggested, because the genial president delivered “a polarizing message in a non-polarizing tone”—a trick he thinks Burnham is well-placed to copy.

Read More In this black-and-white photo, Teddy Roosevelt points to the middle of South America on a map as another man looks at the map from the other side of it. Both men wear suits, ties, and wire-frame glasses. In this black-and-white photo, Teddy Roosevelt points to the middle of South America on a map as another man looks at the map from the other side of it. Both men wear suits, ties, and wire-frame glasses. The ‘Donroe Doctrine’ Is a Roosevelt Redux Then as now, big stick diplomacy will lead to costly cycles of intervention and retrenchment. Argument | Tom Long, Carsten-Andreas Schulz

Then as now, big stick diplomacy will lead to costly cycles of intervention and retrenchment.

Within weeks of Starmer’s election, the Guardian columnist and historian Andy Beckett exhorted him to emulate Roosevelt’s speech. Now, nearly two and a half years later, Beckett told me that the more consensual tone struck so effectively by social democrats in the buoyant 1990s has been “tested to destruction.” In a period of widespread economic insecurity and visibly extreme inequality, “if social democracy has any chance now, as in the 1930s, it’s got to be much more aggressive rhetorically.” Roosevelt’s example, he said, offers a way for center-left leaders to unite with their more left-wing colleagues against a common enemy.

Each of those pointing back to the speech appears to have alighted on it independently, as they combed history for ways out of the British center-left’s constraints. This makes it all the more striking that they all homed in on the same oration, and a U.S. one at that. But then, Britain’s political pantheon lacks a figure like Roosevelt: at once centrist by instinct, radical by necessity, and charismatic by nature. Perhaps the nearest equivalent is Tony Blair, but he was never driven to declare war on entrenched power in the midst of economic crisis.

The question Roosevelt’s example raises for today’s Labour leaders is: which enemy? Ansell said that Burnham tried targeting the bond markets, which “didn’t work quite so brilliantly.” He might focus more fruitfully on exploitative gambling companies, Ansell suggested, or right-wing British tycoons who denounce their home country from tax exile. Or the heads of the United Kingdom’s notoriously inefficient privatized utility companies.

Ford, however, contends that Labour should concentrate its fire on perhaps the most aggressive expression of private power: big tech, and specifically Elon Musk. As populists have demonstrated, putting a face on the enemy can help dramatize political fights, and bolster public support. In the wake of a series of inflammatory interventions over such issues as immigration and free speech, Musk is very unpopular in the U.K. In 2025, he appeared by video link at an extreme right rally in London and told the crowd that “you either fight back or you die.” A few months later there came the scandal over Musk’s AI, Grok, producing images of child sexual abuse. Ford suggests Musk’s public stances make him “a golden opportunity for any center-left populist looking to do a bit of an FDR.”

Roosevelt signs the Glass-Steagall banking reform act at the White House in Washington on June 16, 1933.Universal Images Group/Getty Images

In the United States itself, where the radical right is already in power, Roosevelt’s speech has been pressed into service too—but not by the sort of moderates from whom critics long to hear it. In 2018, Maureen Dowd of the New York Times used it to criticize Barack Obama for failing to take an Roosevelt-style approach to the bankers who caused the 2008 crash. While this was historically unfair—Roosevelt, like Obama, initially bailed the banks out—it highlights the fact that Roosevelt’s controversial address remains the province of those to Obama’s left.

Elizabeth Warren has embraced the speech since at least 2015; Bernie Sanders has repeatedly conjured it too, as in a speech on June 13, 2019, where it triggered a raucous standing ovation. In 2025, Jamie Raskin clipped the speech in a tweet endorsing the “Rooseveltian” now-Mayor of New York City Zohran Mamdani.

In April, Democratic Rep. Greg Casar used it to help launch the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ 10-plank agenda for this year’s mid-term elections, which is focused on stopping “price gouging” by corporations and “[abolishing the unlimited spending power of Super PACs.” Much more contentiously, the far-left streamer Hasan Piker used the line on X to fend off accusations of antisemitism, after saying that “if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action.”

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders delivers a speech in Washington, D.C., on July 17, 2019. Cheriss May/Getty Images

Casar’s approach seems much more effective than Piker’s, explicitly aiming to bring left and moderate Democrats together around economic policies intended to re-channel populist anger away from the targets that President Donald Trump attacks, toward those the left blames for the cost-of-living crisis. For this to work, however, moderate Democrats might need to go beyond their attacks on “billionaires” and “the Epstein class,” and strive to match the bravura of their most successful ancestor.

The real lesson of the speech is not that welcoming the hatred of plutocrats is always effective, no matter who says it. Those lines landed precisely because they were not delivered by an angry leftist, but a cool-tempered centrist, driven finally to declare that the vested interests had gone too far.

In the United States, as in the U.K. and elsewhere, the potential impact of adopting Roosevelt’s strategy lies in that clarifying surprise.

Phil Tinline is a documentarian and journalist and the author of Ghosts of Iron Mountain: The Hoax of the Century, Its Enduring Impact, and What It Reveals About America.

#6011. 15 moments that shaped the 2026 midterm campaign

Republicans began the 2026 election cycle on a high, with a governing trifecta in Washington and heavy optimism that the coalition that swept Donald Trump back into the White House represented a durable new voting bloc. They had a favorable Senate map and insisted there were opportunities to expand their narrow House majority.

But Trump’s policies, economic anxieties, historical trends and an unpopular war have upended  the calculus for the midterm elections. At the close of the campaign, the fight for Congress is taking place mostly on Republican turf, a striking shift in less than two years.

Here are 15 moments that shaped the 2026 midterm campaign:

Less than three months after taking office, Trump made good on a campaign promise: a 10 percent minimum tariff on all imports and higher duties on nations that run trade surpluses with the U.S. Since proclaiming “Liberation Day,” the on-and-off tariffs have injected uncertainty into the economy and hurt key sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing and consumer goods by driving up costs. Polls show the tariffs, which economists estimate have cost the average American household about $1,100, are viewed unfavorably by most voters, likely hurting Republican candidates in several states.

Republicans celebrated a key legislative achievement last summer, with the enactment of the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which they later sought to rebrand as the “Working Families Tax Cut.” The law’s tax provisions became a focal point for the GOP during the campaign, while Democrats slammed the included health care cuts. Before passage, North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis drew scorn from Trump for opposing the measure and soon announced his retirement, opening up a pivotal Senate seat that Democrat Roy Cooper is favored to flip.

Trump kicked the mid-decade redistricting wars into high gear when he directed Texas to redraw its congressional lines, resulting in five seats getting revamped in Republicans’ favor. Other GOP-led states followed suit, though Democrats have remained competitive in several of these redrawn districts. Meanwhile, California voters approved a Democrat-drawn map aimed at helping the party flip five Republican seats, and a court-approved map in Utah gives the party a prime pickup opportunity.

Democrats had a big night in the off-year elections, with a pair of decisive gubernatorial victories: former Rep. Abigail Spanberger flipped the Virginia governor’s mansion and Rep. Mikie Sherrill won in New Jersey. The two moderates focused their campaigns on cost-of-living issues, as did progressive Zohran Mamdani in his winning race for New York mayor, giving Democrats a blueprint for 2026.

The Trump administration began sending federal immigration agents to Minnesota in late 2025, but Operation Metro Surge picked up in January and ultimately led to the fatal shootings of two people by federal agents. That in turn intensified Democratic calls to “abolish ICE” and made immigration enforcement a defining issue in Democratic primaries across the country.

Not long after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran, Trump predicted that the conflict would last a few weeks. It didn’t play out that way, and the ongoing war has become a focal point of the campaign. Higher oil costs have led to higher prices, the blame for which Democrats have pinned on Trump and Republicans in Congress. While Trump’s job approval ratings had fallen before the start of the war, they’ve dropped further since then.

Facing serious sexual misconduct allegations, California Democrat Eric Swalwell, who was running for governor, and Texas Republican Tony Gonzales resigned from the House just as their colleagues were preparing to expel them from the chamber. Swalwell dropped his gubernatorial bid and Gonzales left behind an open seat that has grown increasingly competitive.

In invalidating Louisiana’s congressional map, the Supreme Court pared back the Voting Rights Act and set off a new phase in the redistricting wars, as GOP-led Southern states sought to redraw districts with substantial Black populations. Not all attempts were successful, but Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee ended up with new maps.

A week before the Republican Senate primary runoff in Texas, Trump publicly backed scandal-plagued state Attorney General Ken Paxton’s challenge to Sen. John Cornyn. Paxton went on to win that contest, but has had a tougher general election fight against Democrat James Talarico. Two other incumbents the president targeted for defeat — Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy and Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie — also lost their May primaries to Trump-backed challengers. But Trump’s endorsement power had its limits: Several of his picks, including Iowa gubernatorial hopeful Randy Feenstra, lost primaries this summer.

June 23 was a big night for Mamdani as three House candidates he endorsed, including two fellow democratic socialists, won their primaries. Two of them ousted incumbent Democrats, Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat, and a third defeated the hand-picked successor of retiring Rep. Nydia L. Velázquez.  The New York primaries kicked off a strong summer for progressive candidates in states such as Colorado, Michigan and Minnesota.

Maine Democrat Graham Platner appeared to have weathered an array of controversies when he easily won his June primary to take on Republican Sen. Susan Collins. But about a month later, he ended his campaign following a report that he had sexually assaulted a woman he once dated, which he denied. That set off a weekslong scramble for Democrats to replace him on the ballot, culminating with a party convention at which former state Senate President Troy Jackson became Democrats’ new nominee.

The sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham shocked Washington but also touched off a scramble for South Carolina Republicans to replace him on the November ballot. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed the late senator’s sister, Darline Graham, to fill his seat, and she then won Trump’s support to seek a full term. Boosted by the president, Darline Graham went on to secure the nomination via a primary runoff, but her general election against Democrat Annie Andrews has tightened significantly.

Republicans gathered in Dallas for a first-ever midterm convention.  The two-day event offered them a chance to hone their message, fire up voters and lavish praise upon Trump, the gathering’s brainchild. Speakers, including Trump, stoked fears about democratic socialism, but polls showed the event didn’t provide the GOP with the bounce the party was anticipating. The president followed the convention with a series of rallies in red states, where he implored Americans to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

Alaska’s competitive Senate race features two candidates with the same name: Dan S. Sullivan, the GOP incumbent, and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., listed on the ballot with no party affiliation. Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, has said she was unaware of the effort to recruit the second Sullivan, but The New York Times reported that top aides to her campaign were closely involved in the ballot-stacking plan. The Trump administration is attempting to block certification of the results if the incumbent doesn’t win, but, on Sunday, a district judge dismissed the lawsuit.

Less than 48 hours before polls were set to open on Election Day, Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens served up a November surprise Sunday, endorsing Republican Mike Rogers for Senate over Abdul El-Sayed, who had narrowly bested her in an August Democratic primary. While it was unclear how much influence her late decision could have on the race, a high-profile intraparty fight was surely not how Democrats wanted to close out the campaign. Even so, the El-Sayed campaign said Sunday was its biggest fundraising day, bringing in $2.4 million.

#6010. The Chokepoint Trap

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

How the Search for Economic Security Will End in Geopolitical Calamity

Henry Farrell, Abraham Newman, and Yeling Tan

Policymakers used to ignore chokepoints. Now they have trouble seeing anything else. U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration warns allies against dependence on China while it hunts for ways to exploit those allies’ own dependence on the United States—on its market, technologies, financial system, and security umbrella. Beijing, meanwhile, accuses Washington of economic coercion while leveraging its dominance over critical supply chains to press the United States and Europe. Europe hopes to build the euro into an alternative global currency to evade the dollar’s iron grip. Smaller players, too, have gotten into the act, as Iran tries to leverage its control over the Strait of Hormuz to put a stranglehold on the global oil trade.

This obsession with wielding and countering chokepoint power may seem sudden, but it has evolved over the last quarter century as a byproduct of globalization itself. As economies integrated, chokepoints proliferated: manufacturers extended supply chains across borders, banks routed transactions through the U.S. dollar system to minimize costs and delays, digital services took advantage of economies of scale, leading the market to become dominated by a handful of platforms. After the September 11, 2001, attacks, the United States combined its advocacy for free markets with an increasingly ambitious effort to exploit its dominant position in these networks, surveilling global communications and using its influence over banks worldwide to cut off financial flows to its adversaries. But even as it did so, most politicians and business leaders continued to focus on globalization’s economic efficiencies.

Moves by Trump in his first term, however, caused world leaders to take more notice of chokepoints. The COVID-19 pandemic heightened countries’ fears of external dependence. Then, during Trump’s second administration, China learned that the best way to stop him is to squeeze a chokepoint. The United States’ hubristic erosion of basic norms of constraint led other countries, such as Iran, to explore options they had never previously dared to exploit.

Compared with an excessively rosy vision of globalization that emphasized the efficiencies of interdependence, it may now seem savvy to view the world economy as a system of chokepoints that countries can either turn to their advantage or see turned against them. But the chokepoint view has its own deadly blind spot. It is leading policymakers to focus on capabilities rather than strategy—to fixate on what leverage they have, and what leverage others have over them, rather than considering what happens when many countries build up their chokepoint power all at once.

The result is a familiar but dangerous dynamic: the security dilemma, in which one country’s efforts to secure itself make others feel threatened and respond in kind, leaving everyone less safe. The more that countries strengthen their control over chokepoints or protect themselves from coercion, the more they can make rivals feel that their own economic security has been undermined and provoke retaliation. As economic scholars such as David Bulman and Matt Ferchen have pointed out, each country’s individual actions contribute to the construction of a collective trap. The United States’ efforts to hamstring Chinese technology firms, for instance, led China to accelerate its technological development, which in turn spurred American fears of Chinese domination—a self-perpetuating spiral. Each side’s attempt to become safer makes others feel less secure, driving further escalation.

Escaping the chokepoint trap will be difficult precisely because it is collective. Any government that exercises restraint risks becoming a victim. And although the chokepoint trap may resemble the security dilemma, during the Cold War the measures that ultimately contained a runaway cycle of military provocations were implemented only after the deadly threat of the Cuban missile crisis focused leaders’ attention. An obsessive focus on chokepoints might lead to collective disaster, but it will be remarkably hard for states to jump off the escalator and balance making credible threats with offering credible assurances and seeking collective understandings. The most likely outcome is a fragmented world in which governments and private actors alike face increased volatility and the risk of escalation into something much worse: economic shocks, cascading disruptions, and even war.

In the traditional security dilemma, one country’s defensive move can appear offensive to another. A state may seek peaceful relations with a neighbor but worry that a belligerent leader could someday come to power next door. To hedge against that small but real risk, it might invest in a new weapons system or modestly increase the size of its army. Its neighbor could reasonably become alarmed. What if the buildup is preparation for an invasion? It may respond by ramping up its own defense spending, leading the first country to grow more suspicious and build up its military further, setting off an escalatory spiral.

Sometimes, of course, governments do have genuinely belligerent intentions. But even if all countries genuinely want peace, they can end up violently distrusting each other and seeking to field massive, expensive armies. In such a mistrustful atmosphere, innocent mistakes can easily be misinterpreted. In a classic 1978 essay about the security dilemma, the political scientist Robert Jervis argued that countries can mitigate the risk of misinterpretation by ensuring that the acts they undertake to enhance their security are obviously defensive rather than offensive—for example, by investing in fortifications deep inside their own territories instead of deploying troops to forward bases. But even passive defenses can heighten tensions: if a country feels better protected against retaliation, its rivals may fear that it will find aggression less risky.

In later writing, Jervis suggested that similar ambiguities might undermine economic and technological security, too. But economic warfare is even likelier to generate unintended escalation than the traditional security dilemma. Unlike military investments, economic policies can be difficult to classify as offensive or defensive. When China builds up its semiconductor sector, is it merely protecting its domestic economy or augmenting its capacity to coerce? Industrial policy can be enacted for a purely defensive reason—to establish resilience against geopolitical shocks. But if such a policy succeeds in building economies of scale, other states might reasonably fear that industrial dominance might be converted into coercive tools.

Economic security officials are usually more interested in building capacity than in restraint, whereas traditional economic policymakers are more accustomed to soothing their own markets than to assuaging the concerns of competitors, let alone adversaries. Defense bureaucracies have strong command-and-control structures for a reason: ill-disciplined communications and misaligned decisions can have disastrous consequences. The institutions that make economic policy, by contrast—including central banks and departments of commerce—are usually not set up to speak with one voice. Many are weakly coordinated, and significant authority is delegated to local-level investment and trade agencies. Sometimes, as with central banks, their autonomy is deliberately protected. Whereas military units deployed on discrete missions cannot act without explicit authorization, most economic agencies enjoy wide freedom to act without being accused of going rogue. As this year’s disagreements between the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Federal Reserve over bond yields illustrate, standard bureaucratic infighting can shade into visible conflict.

When governments pursue chokepoint warfare, the problems these institutional ambiguities create get much worse. In September 2025, on the heels of a series of high-level economic negotiations between top U.S. and Chinese officials aimed at stabilizing the bilateral relationship, the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security enacted the so-called affiliates rule, which expanded export controls to cover more subsidiaries owned by entities on two U.S. government watch lists. The bureau publicly described the measure as an attempt to close a loophole and lighten administrative burdens; it has since suspended the rule. But the timing made outsiders unsure how to discern its broader strategic meaning. Was Commerce merely tightening the enforcement of existing export controls as part of an ongoing bureaucratic process, or was the United States, as Chinese officials suggested, deliberately engaging in “maximum pressure” tactics in between rounds of bilateral talks?

It can be even harder to interpret what autocracies intend, since policymakers in such regimes are more insulated from public scrutiny. For example, even after China promised to relax its restrictions on the exports of rare-earth minerals and magnets in July 2025, companies that applied for export licenses experienced unexplained delays. It was unclear whether China was deliberately signaling its ability to control critical supply chains or simply struggling to channel requests efficiently through a newly created export-control bureaucracy.

Governments engaging in economic warfare often intentionally write or enforce regulations ambiguously to prompt private actors to overcomply. This behavior makes others much more likely to interpret even hapless bureaucratic mistakes, delays, and unintentional overreach as malign and deliberate plotting. Such mistakes deepen mistrust among great powers, which are already inherently inclined to overrate the possibility of deliberate threats.

Conversely, leaders are often excessively optimistic about their ability to surgically inflict economic pain on target countries. The flow of commerce cannot be steered as carefully as drones can be guided to bomb weapons factories. Even precision measures, such as putting specific firms on export-control lists, can be ineffective. Controlled goods may end up in the possession of subsidiaries or clandestine intermediaries. Broad attempts to close loopholes can go too far, putting thousands of firms with complex ownership ties in the cross hairs of the economic security state.

In October 2025, China again expanded the reach of its rare-earth export controls to retaliate against the affiliates rule and further efforts by Washington to restrict Chinese firms’ access to U.S. technologies. If these measures had not been suspended the following month, they would have affected production chains throughout Europe and Asia as well as in the United States. Officials who dream of an optimized form of chokepoint warfare in which they can fire an economic sniper rifle at judiciously selected targets regularly discover they are wielding a blunderbuss whose pellets fly in all directions—and the collateral damage only increases the risk of retaliatory spirals.

The more some countries move to control key chokepoints, the more others will worry about how those chokepoints may be weaponized and seek to leverage their own. The result is a world bristling with chokepoints and defenses in which every power still feels completely insecure. Even the most ordinary kinds of mutual dependence can begin to look like existential security risks. Put another way, in a world in which everything is connected, nearly everything could be considered a chokepoint. A piece of legislation introduced in the U.S. Senate in 2025 and the House in 2026, for instance, identifies even smart ovens and clothes dryers as potential security threats.

Historically effective ways of limiting trade disputes may fail in chokepoint warfare. In traditional tariff wars, governments often try to match like with like, responding to a butter tariff with a countertariff on eggs. Maintaining proportionality is much harder when economic security risks are diverse, when different chokepoints confer different kinds of leverage, and when countries that want to retaliate against the weaponization of one network have to turn to different networks to respond.

In April 2025, when the United States threatened China with sweeping tariffs and boosted its export controls on semiconductors, China could not retaliate by imposing an equivalent restriction on American semiconductors because it does not control the same chokepoint. Instead, it used its advantage over a different bottleneck, rare earths. But when countries weaponize entirely different chokepoints that sit at the center of complex and global supply chains, there is no easy way to judge whether a reaction will match the economic magnitude of the original act. Any notion of a simple escalation ladder that adversaries can climb up and down becomes a fantasy.

Rapid and unpredictable technological change makes this dynamic even more dangerous. As Jervis warned, countries persistently worry that technological innovation will create enduring advantages for their adversaries. Such anxieties can worsen the chokepoint trap, inspiring countries to try to impede their rivals’ progress and race to beef up their own autonomy. The Biden administration, anticipating that AI might swiftly accelerate advances in a variety of military and civilian domains, sought to impede Chinese AI development by restricting the country’s access to specialized semiconductors. Administration officials stressed that their goals were limited, describing their approach to China as “small yard, high fence.” Unsurprisingly, Beijing rejected this benign framing and saw the moves as a threat to its long-term future. China accelerated its own semiconductor development and is encouraging its companies to wean themselves from U.S. products, leaving the United States with less influence over Chinese technological development and more reason to worry about future Chinese aggression.

After the attacks of September 11, 2001, the United States began to make much more systematic use of economic and technological chokepoints: snooping on both adversaries and allies, and exploiting the dollar’s dominance to investigate and impose sanctions on foreign banks and companies. American officials came to see the global economy’s interconnectedness as something to manipulate—to deter U.S. opponents or strongarm allies into compliance. The George W. Bush and Obama administrations expanded sanctions to squeeze Iran’s economy, forcing Tehran to the negotiating table. The first Trump administration introduced new technological controls to limit Chinese companies’ access to advanced semiconductors, setting the precedent for the Biden administration’s efforts to impede Chinese AI more broadly.

But during this period, American officials usually paid little attention to the cumulative downside. Financial sanctions, for example, were attractive because most of the costs fell on the foreigners they targeted and foreigners who wanted to do deals with the targets. Exploiting chokepoints became a self-perpetuating enterprise with little purpose beyond sustaining itself. A 2024 Washington Post analysis found that the United States was sanctioning people, properties, or organizations in a third of all countries. Bill Reinsch, a former Commerce Department official, told the newspaper that such sanctions had become “the most important foreign policy tool in the U.S. arsenal,” but “nobody in government is sure this whole strategy is even working.”

Yet the more the United States exploited chokepoints in this way, the more it provoked countermeasures and imitation. And as other powers have begun to develop their own chokepoint capabilities, they are proving no more cautious. China has never hesitated to use economic pressure to get its way. But it used to threaten countries’ access to its domestic market rather than control global bottlenecks. Two key events altered this playbook. In 2013, leaks made by the former U.S. National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden revealed the extraordinary reach the United States had in global information networks. Then, the first Trump administration’s punishing campaigns against the Chinese telecommunications companies ZTE and Huawei demonstrated Washington’s willingness to coerce.

After these shocks, China’s technological debates began to emphasize themes such as “information security” and “decoupling.” Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose speeches once focused on straightforward industrialization, increasingly stressed how economic development could not be separated from national security. His “dual circulation” strategy both sought to reduce dependence on overseas markets and reduce China’s exposure to foreign economic pressure. As Beijing became more conscious of its vulnerability to U.S. technology and finance, it not only accelerated technological self-reliance but created new government structures that mimicked those that Washington used to target other countries, such as an export control regime and security screening for inbound and outbound investment.

China justifies these measures as self-defense. But it has rapidly moved from proportionate responses to dramatic counterescalation. When, in April 2025, Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs, China not only imposed licensing restrictions on rare-earth exports but also suggested, a few months later, that its dominance over rare-earth processing gave it regulatory authority over the entire semiconductor supply chain. China also barred some exports of dual-use goods to U.S. defense contractors and civilian technology companies, sanctioned U.S. firms it claimed were engaging in arms sales or technology cooperation with Taiwan’s military, and launched antitrust investigations into Google, Nvidia, and DuPont. Although some of these measures were subsequently suspended or terminated as a result of negotiations with the United States, China has since repeatedly demonstrated its ability to hit back against what it perceives as foreign economic coercion.

In another counteroffensive, Beijing has begun creating a “blocking” regime to punish companies that comply with other countries’ economic security restrictions. Foreign banks that follow U.S. law and stop doing business with a sanctioned Chinese refinery could well be sued in Chinese courts in the future. Rules promulgated in August of this year make it illegal for Chinese firms to provide information or do business with six organizations that do due diligence and risk assessment on supply chains and promote labor rights, making it harder for them to generate the forensics that help companies worldwide comply with American laws.

By now, China has reshaped its economic policy around a narrow view of its national security concerns. And just like the United States’ chokepoint exploitation did, China’s moves to fence off ever larger parts of its economy will prompt destabilizing counterreactions and imitations. An examination of data from the Global Trade Alert, an independent monitor that tracks government policy changes affecting international trade flows, captures governments’ growing willingness to choke off trade. Since 2020, countries have, on average, enacted seven times as many export restrictions per year as they did between 2010 and 2019. The chokepoint trap is closing on governments as they find themselves entangled in an ever more complicated web of economic and technological conflicts.

In this dynamic, Europe—whose economy is nominally larger than China’s—finds itself perpetually forced to accommodate. Its ability to formulate coherent economic-security strategies and design policy tools is better developed than those of Beijing and Washington. Over the past few years, it has delivered what could be a powerful anti-coercion instrument that would allow it to retaliate extensively against economic pressure, an economic security strategy that identifies the risks of chokepoint warfare, and a Chips Act 2.0 that calls for maintaining Europe’s position as an “indispensable player” in supply chains. But it has struggled to turn words into leverage. It remains deeply dependent on U.S. technology and security guarantees; its dreams of controlling its own chokepoints dissipate in the face of the risk that Washington could tear up its NATO commitments. So far, Europe has not even attempted to deploy its anti-coercion instrument against the United States, despite the Trump administration’s repeated coercion.

Europe is increasingly constrained by dependence on China, too. When the EU imposed countervailing duties on Chinese electric vehicles it found were unfairly subsidized, China was quick to target vital sectors in EU member states, forcing European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to spend precious political capital keeping Berlin and Madrid behind a common EU policy. In September 2025, when the Dutch government attempted to assert its sovereign authority over Nexperia, a Dutch chip manufacturer that was purchased by a Chinese company, Beijing prevented the firm from finishing the chips in China, creating a supply chain crisis across the European car industry. According to a mid-2026 report by Tobias Gehrke, a senior policy analyst at the European Council on Foreign Relations, Chinese threats are preventing European member states from even contemplating the comprehensive actions they would need to reduce their dependence.

Every European wish to assert strategic autonomy is hemmed in by the expectation that the United States or China will split its solidarity. And national security decisions remain the domain of member states, preventing the EU from leveraging potential chokepoints. Europe has made huge strides in acting collectively to impose sanctions against Russia, but enforcement still largely depends on national governments. The result is a bloc that understands the dangers of escalation better than the United States or China but cannot do much to avoid them.

Japan, meanwhile, began to think about the threat posed by Chinese coercion early and has better tailored its approach, balancing strategic autonomy and resilience against potential external coercion with control over vital technological chokepoints. It has created a national stockpile of rare earths to mitigate Chinese efforts to pressure its economy while making itself indispensable to U.S. military supply chains. But even Japan has shown it can succumb to the seduction of chokepoint politics: in 2019, it limited South Korea’s access to key semiconductor chemicals in response to the country’s pursuit of reparations for World War II harms.

And now, even smaller, poorer countries have been caught up in the spiral. Some have benefited from the spread of chokepoint warfare in the short term: the Philippines, for instance, won millions in grants from the United States when Washington attempted to press allies to block Huawei from their telecommunications infrastructures. Others are simply getting squeezed. The Kachin Independence Army in Myanmar is selling dysprosium and terbium, which are used in industrial magnets, to fuel its civil war against the military junta—giving China, the main buyer, greater leverage over the conflict. Greenland, with its vast supply of natural resources, has faced repeated military threats from Trump. As time goes on, the costs are likely to heavily outweigh the benefits, even for countries receiving some side payments. Governments in smaller, poorer countries want the autonomy to chart a path toward greater prosperity for their citizens. The global obsession with economic security makes finding that path harder.

Right now, the United States and China are locked in a short-term stasis. Washington is moderating its use of chokepoints out of fear of ferocious blowback, and China sees little benefit in direct provocation. But this moment of stability is likely to be fleeting. Even after Trump leaves the White House, the United States will certainly keep pressing for global technological dominance, and it is likely to continue its efforts to dominate energy. China will keep pursuing policies aimed at quietly building dependencies and undermining the United States’ coercive power. Stalemates are fragile in a world in which the incentives inexorably point toward escalation.

The powers with the most latitude to shape the world now see chokepoints as capabilities. Their vision rarely stretches to the strategic implications of their actions. As they build their offensive capacities and shore up their defenses, they convince themselves that they are ensuring their own security. Instead, they are miring themselves in a chokepoint arms race that will render them, as well as everyone else, much less secure. The jealousies of the traditional national security dilemma are now spilling over into the global economy. A world in which economic chokepoints become forts, garrisons, and guns all at once will be characterized by perpetual low-level economic conflict and the ever-present risk of larger conflagrations.

To identify broader solutions, some scholars and policy thinkers look to the Cold War for inspiration, emphasizing the value of de-escalation and mutual restraint. During that era, the risk of nuclear war was mitigated with regular meetings to establish a shared understanding of redlines and systems that ensure effective communication in a crisis. Over time, these gave rise to more formal arrangements, such as treaties regulating arms and troop movements, enforced by satellites and other means of monitoring. An assurance-based security logic can, in some cases, insulate economic chokepoints from weaponization. Singapore, for instance, has signed agreements with Australia and New Zealand to keep essential supplies flowing between their countries. In 2022, the World Trade Organization’s members agreed not to place export restrictions on food purchased by the World Food Program for humanitarian purposes.

Yet it will be difficult to turn such commitments into a large-scale system of effective communication and mutual restraint. It took the Cuban missile crisis and the threat of nuclear annihilation to awaken the Cold War’s antagonists to how individually rational acts could lead to collectively awful outcomes. Today, as the cycle of mutual suspicion gathers speed, it becomes increasingly hard to reverse. The more governments create bureaucracies devoted to identifying and controlling economic chokepoints, the more a chokepoint logic becomes the default lens through which they make even routine economic policy. It is no coincidence that Europe, the great power that is the most hesitant to actually weaponize chokepoints, is also the power that is least capable of deploying them.

It is more likely that the chokepoint trap will tighten. Military competition has long driven states to build similar institutions—armed forces, defense bureaucracies, and domestic weapons industries. This kind of mirroring is already beginning to happen in economic security. China is becoming more like the United States, building bureaucratic tools to leverage chokepoints against its adversaries; meanwhile, the United States is imitating China, intervening in its domestic economy to reshape it around security concerns. The European Union will choose between managing its slide to irrelevance or radically reforming its internal balance of power in order to keep up. Smaller powers will do what they can to emulate bigger ones while relying on their protection.

This will be hard for governments, but much worse for international business. Firms will have to navigate a labyrinthine and unpredictable global economy in which payment and information systems are fragmented and clashing powers try alternately to press them into service or squeeze them out of existence. Multinational corporations may become unified entities in name only, as their subsidiaries face countervailing pressures from host governments. Economic efficiencies that seem natural today, such as the seamlessness of international financial transactions, may evaporate as governments equate global infrastructures with national insecurity.

Even this is not the worst-case scenario. The greatest risk posed by the chokepoint trap is not its predictable miseries but its unpredictable disasters. Suspicion, misunderstanding, and intense competition in the realm of economic security can create an ideal recipe for war. Take just one hypothetical. It is not difficult to imagine a scenario in which additional Chinese restrictions on rare-earth magnets degrade, among other things, the United States’ ability to rebuild the missile stockpiles that this year’s Iran war has depleted. Whether or not Beijing intended this effect, U.S. leaders could easily interpret such an act as evidence that China plans to launch a military offensive against Taiwan before the United States can achieve full independence from Chinese supply chains, prompting a sense of urgency in Washington to strike first.

There is plenty of historical precedent for what may seem to be a marginal and worst-case scenario. In The Economic Weapon, the historian Nicholas Mulder documents how, in the 1930s, Axis powers’ fears of League of Nations sanctions and potential economic isolation led them to aggressively seize territory and resources before it was too late. The chokepoint trap is bad enough. What it leads to can be worse.

HENRY FARRELL is Stavros Niarchos Foundation Agora Institute Professor of International Affairs at Johns Hopkins University and an External Professor at the Santa Fe Institute.

ABRAHAM NEWMAN is John Powers Chair in International Business Diplomacy at the School of Foreign Service and a Professor in the Department of Government at Georgetown University.

YELING TAN is Professor of Public Policy in the Blavatnik School of Government at Oxford University and a Nonresident Senior Fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

#6009. 'Squad' rakes in record $2.35M while slamming the door on cop donations

Panelists Meghan Hays and Tiffany Smiley discuss how Democratic socialist candidates receive millions in progressive political contributions on ‘America Reports.'

A joint fundraising committee for four progressive House Democrats has raised a record $2.35 million so far this election cycle, while barring donations from the Fraternal Order of Police, according to federal filings and the committee’s disclosure.

The Squad Victory Fund is authorized by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.; Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.; Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass.; and Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich. The fundraising gives the four lawmakers and their allied political groups a shared vehicle to collect and distribute campaign contributions.

ILHAN OMAR’S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME

"Squad" members of Congress Tlaib, Omar and Ocasio-Cortez. (AP Photo/Amanda Andrade-Rhoades, File; Photo by Scott Heins/Getty Images; AP Photo/Angelina Katsanis)

The fund’s donor rules also make clear which groups it says it will not accept money from, and one is the Fraternal Order of Police, the nation’s largest police organization. It also bars donations from corporations, federal lobbyists and fossil fuel interests. The disclosure does not explain the FOP exclusion.

SOCIALIST PRIMARY SWEEP SPARKS LAUNCH OF NEW RESOURCE LAYING OUT WHAT’S AT STAKE IN 2026

The Squad Victory Fund says it will not accept contributions from the Fraternal Order of Police, the nation’s largest police organization. (Tom Brenner/The Washington Post/Getty Images)

The fund’s other participants include four allied PACs. Contributions are generally divided equally among the eight participants, with each slated to receive 12.5%, though donors may designate their contributions for a specific participant.

The fund has raised $2,351,388.02 in the 2025–2026 election cycle, its highest total to date, according to its FEC summary.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez departs following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., US, on July 22, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Through March 31, 2026, it had spent about $1.6 million and reported roughly $68,000 in cash on hand. The committee remains active, so those figures may change.

Contributions are not tax-deductible, the disclosure notes.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

#6007. Is Netflix’s ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ for Real?

Review: Is Netflix’s ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ for Real?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

I had to chuckle when I got the email. A PR blast announced “Netflix presents The New Stanford Prison Experiment.” Was this an attempt to one-up the satirically dystopian phrases in David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest? A “yes, and” to Wallace’s “Year of the Depend Adult Undergarment”? Alas, no. And for the streaming service that only became more ubiquitous after the global success of the gleefully sadistic Squid Game, it seemed apt.

The phrase “Stanford prison experiment,” like Lord of the Flies, is pretty much synonymous with violence, anarchy, and the bleakest confirmation of man’s inhumanity to man. Do we really need a “new” one?

I had to chuckle when I got the email. A PR blast announced “Netflix presents The New Stanford Prison Experiment.” Was this an attempt to one-up the satirically dystopian phrases in David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest? A “yes, and” to Wallace’s “Year of the Depend Adult Undergarment”? Alas, no. And for the streaming service that only became more ubiquitous after the global success of the gleefully sadistic Squid Game, it seemed apt.

The phrase “Stanford prison experiment,” like Lord of the Flies, is pretty much synonymous with violence, anarchy, and the bleakest confirmation of man’s inhumanity to man. Do we really need a “new” one?

Chances are you know about the original Stanford prison experiment. In August 1971, with the campus on break, a psychology professor at Stanford University named Philip Zimbardo offered a paying gig to students willing to run through an unusual and morally questionable exercise. The basement of a university building was made up to resemble a prison. Twenty-four students (all male, all white except for one Asian-American; “good boys,” Zimbardo called them) were randomly split into groups of inmates or guards and given appropriate uniforms. For two weeks, the professor thought, he would take notes on how unchecked power in an enclosed system would reveal itself. The experiment, funded by the U.S. Office of Naval Research, ended after six days, and that’s only because Zimbardo’s girlfriend stopped by and said, “Holy crap, what the hell is happening here?!”

Stanford professor Philip Zimbardo discusses the Stanford prison experiment on Aug. 20, 1971.Duke Downey/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images

At least that’s the lore. Zimbardo—a wonderful self-promoter later taken to wearing t-shirts with the letter Z resembling Superman’s logo—seemed eager not just to lean into his experiment’s findings, but to allow that he, too, lost his ethical mooring, suggesting that all closed institutions are incubators of depersonalization and madness.

You can watch this all play out in a pretty good fictionalized version of the experiment produced in 2015 called The Stanford Prison Experiment, adapted from Zimbardo’s 2007 book The Lucifer Experiment. In it, Billy Crudup plays Zimbardo, Michael Angarano plays a guard nicknamed John Wayne, and Ezra Miller and Tye Sheridan play the inmates who suffered the most, eventually quitting.

Indeed, the fact that the experiment went haywire and needed to be canceled surely aided in spreading its premise—that merely donning the costume of guard or inmate in a sealed-off environment would radically alter someone’s personality, and rather quickly. These findings, plus the inherent “wait, they let students do this?” question, made Zimbardo a notable and sought-after voice on cable news during the Abu Ghraib scandal.

But recent research and a three-part 2024 documentary that aired on the National Geographic channel, The Stanford Prison Experiment: Unlocking the Truth, offers firsthand testimony from the participants that they were coaxed to behave in ways that would conform to the experiment’s thesis. John Wayne, for example, wasn’t really a skull-cracking bully as the film clips suggest, but a pot-smoking theater kid who wanted to please his director. One of the kids who quit wasn’t on the verge of psychological collapse; he just thought the experiment was annoying and was told the only way to get out of it was to pretend he was losing it.

All these decades later, it’s hard to know which version is accurate. (As with so much in life, it is likely somewhere in between.) But the suspicion surrounding Zimbardo’s data is, I suppose, reason enough to call for a redo.

The punchline, of course, is that however bogus the original may actually be, this new iteration is a hundred times more manufactured.

Trymaine Lee and host Alison Wood Brooks in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

Enter television producers Jane Lipsitz and Dan Cutforth, whose previous work includes competition shows like Project Runway, Top Chef, Nailed It!, and my personal favorite, the ongoing Is it Cake? franchise, which has somehow managed to stretch the act of wondering whether something is cake for three seasons plus five holiday-themed specials. With that eternal question still lingering, they decided it was time to turn their reality TV lens to issues of crime and punishment. (One wonders how Rodion Raskolnikov’s life would have been different had he had access to fondant.)

“Does power corrupt?” is the big question laid out in the first of six episodes in The New Stanford Prison Experiment. Our host—the Ryan Seacrest of this affair—is Alison Wood Brooks, an associate professor of business administration at Harvard University and a behavioral scientist, and she assures us this experiment will answer this question once and for all. Her two associates offering color commentary are Trymaine Lee, a Pulitzer-winning journalist and author, and Michael Cantrell, a retired federal corrections officer and podcaster.

In a decommissioned wing of an actual county correctional facility in Georgia, the trio sit before a bank of monitors from their panopticon’s perch, which naturally includes a whiteboard featuring circled names, flowchart markings, and vague phrases like “test ourselves.” They observe the activity of the show’s willing participants as though they were Harry Lime on a Ferris wheel, strikingly detached from humanity.

And who are the participants? Unlike Zimbardo’s crew—kids looking for a summer gig—these are adults with a full understanding of what they are doing. If there is a financial incentive, it is never mentioned. What is mentioned is that everyone involved considers this is a test of their character, and that the experiment may lead to an important conclusion. What’s more, the show has intentionally kept the pool of applicants diverse in age, race, and class—CEOs and bartenders walk side by side in their civilian clothes before the selection begins.

Contestants wait to join the experiment in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

The original experiment left who would be an inmate versus a guard completely up to chance. Not so here. The producers have predetermined this, but the audience isn’t privy to how they made their decisions. (The three women are guards because someone must have wisely realized that mixing genders in a locked-down 24-hour quasi-jail was something no insurance company would cover.)

But there’s an elephant in the room. Unpleasant though this may be, no one is actually incarcerated or in anything resembling danger. There are cameras everywhere, and all anyone needs to do is say the safe word (“pineapple”) and they are free to go.

Also, all of the inmates have clearly been encouraged to give periodic first-person addresses (cleverly shot through glass to resemble a visiting room)—a very common reality show trope to add narration and assist in the editing process. Annoyingly, while watching the finished product, we have no idea how scripted these moments are, or when during production they were recorded. Also, everyone, from all walks of life, uses Instagram-friendly therapy speak phrases. Great for marketing clips.

This is the perfect project for the creator of ‘Adolescence.’

Vince Gilligan’s “Pluribus” asks whether an AI-led society would really be that bad.

Over time, some personalities begin to shine. One of the younger inmates, Pete, who has a Jesse Eisenberg-like quality, is a fifth-grade social studies teacher who feels compelled to instigate and push back against authority. His reasoning is hazy, but he seems to be working toward some poorly defined, somewhat utopian ideal. (The show works mostly in soundbites, not thorough arguments.) He quickly finds some teammates in the art of pushing back, one specifically who seems even more eager to be a thorn in the guards’ side, even though Pete is quietly calling the shots.

The guards, meanwhile, are split into a night and day shift, and an alpha male soon finds himself the unelected leader of each. On night shift, there is Chris, an entrepreneur with a coaching business and an intense desire to be liked. He enforces rules but does it with a smile. On the day shift, there’s Chet, a supervisor on an oil rig, who seems more than eager to carry the metaphorical big stick.

The guards get printed memos (not unlike directives from the Gamemakers in The Hunger Games) with certain tasks and directives. They are to vote for a head guard among them on their shifts (in one case reversing what seemed like natural selection) then each shift must elect what is effectively a shop steward from among the inmates. As the choices are made, our three observers titter and murmur in fascination.

Things move along largely as expected. There is discord. Much of this is due, so the experts conclude, from too much individuality, which is anathema in a prison. Chris and Chet have different styles, and this imbalance causes a rupture. When penalties (such as removing a common clock) aren’t enforced, it creates a mess.

On the seventh day of the show, longer than the original experiment ever went, there comes a new twist. Some of the guards and inmates are directed to trade places. Wouldn’t you know it, the troublemakers are now wearing the badges. How will this change things?

Naturally, the show milks this reversal for as much drama as possible, but it is ultimately quite anticlimactic. This isn’t a real prison, it isn’t even a rogue college experiment from the early 1970s; it’s a Netflix reality show. It’s meaningless! You keep waiting for a hockey brawl to break out, but nothing like that ever happens.

Guard and inmate contestants in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

At first, the new guards try to act like “good” guards but soon realize this makes them seem like hypocrites. Instead, they ease up on restrictions, leading to a bit of a party atmosphere. Meanwhile, many of the inmates realize this is all kind of dumb (as will a great number of home viewers, I’m sure!) and start saying “pineapple.” Others are determined to make it to the end, to fulfill some sort of promise they’ve made to themselves. (Does Netflix cut them a bonus check if they last 14 days? None of that is ever discussed.)

Finally (to risk spoiling things), a decision emerges from the ranks. If the inmates all decide to leave as one, as a collective instead of individuals who have had enough, then they will have “taken power” and used it in the name of righteousness. Beaming with pride, our three overseers are delighted to conclude that, wowee, power doesn’t always corrupt! What a relief! The world’s systems can stay in place now. Or something.

If all this sounds preposterous, just know I’m leaving tons of extra nonsense out. I watched this series in awe of its stupidity. I am not one who automatically dismisses all competition shows. The Great British Baking Show is charming and RuPaul’s Drag Race is chock full of puns and creativity. But The New Stanford Prison Experiment is a round peg in a square hole—a ludicrous scenario desperate to rationalize its own existence.

Zimbardo’s experiment may have been unethical, but this is just humiliating, both to the audience and to the people who had to spend nearly two weeks in uncomfortable conditions before landing on a milquetoast and meaningless conclusion. If I were forced to watch all six episodes again, it would feel like a jail sentence.

This post appeared in the FP Weekend newsletter, a weekly showcase of book reviews, deep dives, and features. Sign up here.

Jordan Hoffman is a film critic and entertainment journalist living in central New Jersey. He also publishes at Vanity Fair, Entertainment Weekly, and the Times of Israel. He is a member of the New York Film Critics Circle and co-author of The Star Trek Book of Friendship. X: @jhoffman
