#5986. How to watch critical 2026 midterm election races in TX, OH, MI, WI, GA, IA, NV, ME and FL

FOX Business' Grady Trimble and Republican Senate candidate Michele Tafoya join 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss tight Senate races in Iowa and Minnesota.

Control of Congress is on the line Tuesday as voters decide pivotal Senate and House races across the country, while closely watched contests for governor will shape the political landscape in key states during President Donald Trump's second term.

Republicans are fighting to defend their congressional majorities as Democrats seek gains in battlegrounds from Texas and Georgia to Michigan and Maine. Open seats, vulnerable incumbents and competitive statewide races have put nine states at the center of the fight for power in Washington and state capitals.

With races stretching across multiple time zones, here are the key contests to watch, when polls close and how to follow live results as Election Night unfolds.

Fox News Power Rankings on midterm seat losses under President Donald Trump's economy. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Texas voters face two major statewide showdowns, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton battling Democratic state Rep. James Talarico for the Senate seat held by outgoing Republican John Cornyn, while GOP Gov. Greg Abbott seeks a historic fourth term against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.

TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK

The Senate contest has emerged as an unusually competitive race in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988, pitting Paxton's conservative appeal and history of legal controversies against Talarico's campaign focused on political change.

Meanwhile, Abbott's reelection bid offers another test of Republican dominance, with border security, education and the economy shaping the fight over the state's future.

SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY

Ohio features a Senate rematch of sorts, with former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown seeking a return to Washington against Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vice President JD Vance's former seat. Brown is attempting a political comeback in a state that has shifted toward Republicans, while Husted seeks his first electoral victory for the Senate.

Husted's campaign also enlisted Ohio native and former NFL coach Jon "Chucky" Gruden for campaign appearances.

Voters will decide who succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy facing Democrat Amy Acton. Ramaswamy's campaign recently pulled a controversial ad featuring Acton's estranged mother after criticism from fellow Republicans, including DeWine.

Michigan's open Senate seat could prove pivotal to the balance of power in Washington, with former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers facing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the contest to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW

The Senate race has grown increasingly contentious as Rogers and Republican allies have raised allegations about El-Sayed's family's purported ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, citing old social media posts by his half-sister. El-Sayed has denied any connection to the organization and publicly disavowed it, while independent fact-checkers have found no evidence establishing his personal affiliation.

The state also features a gubernatorial showdown between Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican Rep. John James, testing whether Michigan voters will maintain Democratic control of the governor's office or turn to Republicans.

Wisconsin's open governor's race pits Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany against Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley as voters choose a successor to Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.

The contest centers on the state's political direction, including taxes, public spending and education, after Crowley defeated progressive state Rep. Francesca Hong in a crowded Democratic primary.

Georgia offers two major statewide contests, with Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defending his seat against Republican Rep. Mike Collins in a state Trump narrowly carried in 2024.

Georgia Republican Senate candidate, Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA) speaks alongside U.S. President Donald Trump during a midterm campaign rally at the Guardian Centers on October 24, 2026, in Perry, Georgia. Trump is speaking at a rally in support of Georgia Republican Senate candidate, Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA), who is trying to unseat the incumbent U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA), and Georgia Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson. (Alex Wong / Getty Images)

Ossoff's race will test whether Democrats can hold a Senate seat in a state that has delivered closely contested presidential and Senate elections, while the open governor's race between Republican businessman Rick Jackson and former Democratic Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will determine who succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp.

Iowa voters will decide whether Republicans can retain two major offices in a state Trump carried comfortably in 2024. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for the Senate seat being vacated by Republican Joni Ernst, while Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand faces Republican Zach Lahn in the open governor's race to succeed retiring longtime GOP Gov. Kim Reynolds.

Although the Hawkeye State has shifted toward Republicans in recent election cycles, Democrats previously enjoyed sustained statewide success through figures including former Sen. Tom Harkin and former Gov. Tom Vilsack.

The contests will test whether Democrats can regain ground, with affordability, agriculture and state economic policy among the central issues.

Nevada's marquee contest features Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo seeking another term against Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford.

The race will test whether Republicans can retain the governor's office in a state where Democrats have remained competitive in statewide elections, with housing affordability, education and public safety among the issues facing voters.

Lombardo, the former Clark County sheriff, defeated incumbent Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak in 2022, with Ford now hoping to hit the jackpot in Carson City.

Maine's Senate race pits longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins against former Democratic state Senate President Troy Jackson in one of the country's most closely watched contests.

Collins is seeking another term in a blue-leaning state that supported Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Meanwhile, Jackson is attempting to turn Maine's Democratic presidential voting pattern into a Senate pickup after replacing Graham Platner, who withdrew as the Democratic nominee following a sexual assault allegation that he denied.

Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, faces off against Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president and the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, in their fourth debate appearance together on Thursday evening. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images; Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

The contest will test Collins' longstanding crossover appeal and could have major consequences for the Senate's balance of power, as she remains New England's only Republican member of Congress.

Florida voters will choose a successor to term-limited Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, with Republican Rep. Byron Donalds facing former Republican congressman-turned-Democrat David Jolly.

The race presents a contest over the future of Florida's government, including affordability, immigration and the direction of state policy.

Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, appointed to the seat vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, also faces DSA-affiliated Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon in a special Senate election, while competitive House contests could affect the national congressional picture.

As polls close across the country's biggest battlegrounds on Tuesday, Nov. 3, Fox News Channel and Fox News Digital will deliver live results, race calls and analysis of the contests that could determine control of Congress.

Viewers can watch live coverage on Fox News Go with a participating television provider or stream Fox News Channel through FOX One.

On Fox News Digital, readers can follow a live Election Night blog featuring breaking developments, Fox News Power Rankings and Fox News Voter Analysis as polls close across the country.

The Fox News Elections Center will serve as a central destination for tracking results in Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Maine and Florida, as well as other key congressional and statewide races nationwide.

The Fox News app will feature a new "Midterms 2026" tab with interactive county-level election maps and an AI-powered "Election HQ" chatbot that answers questions about races and results using Fox News reporting.

More than 20 Fox News Channel and FOX Business correspondents will report from battleground states nationwide, while chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram will provide updates from Capitol Hill.

With control of the House and Senate at stake, Fox News Channel and Fox News Digital will provide continuing coverage as results emerge from the nine battleground states and beyond, including races that may remain undecided into Wednesday.

#5984. Brazil’s Economic Impasse

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MONICA DE BOLLE is Senior Fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, an Adjunct Professor at Georgetown University, and a co-author of The New Economic Nationalism.

Neither Lula nor Bolsonaro Can Solve the Country’s Problems

On October 5, the day after the first round of Brazil’s general elections, the country’s financial markets were euphoric. Brazil is struggling with high debt and low growth, and investors are eager for leaders to reduce budget deficits, deregulate, cut taxes, and perhaps even privatize state assets. After nearly four years under the left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, who has been slow to implement such measures, investors hope a right-wing government will create opportunities for bold reform.

Rule by the right might be exactly what Brazil gets. The far-right Liberal Party made substantial gains in the legislature, becoming the single largest party in both the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. Its presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the notorious former President Jair Bolsonaro, led the aging incumbent, Lula, by nearly two percentage points in the first round of voting. Lula has shown himself capable of impressive political comebacks, but Flávio Bolsonaro is still the favorite in the runoff vote scheduled for October 25.

Even if Bolsonaro wins, however, the prospects for the Brazilian economy are dim. The policies he has put forward are nothing close to the substantial fiscal consolidation program that will be necessary to bring down debt and stimulate private investment, and his determination to weaken Brazil’s political institutions creates the kind of uncertainty that scares investors away. Economic growth has been sluggish under Lula, whose administration has struggled to relieve the high debt burdens afflicting the public sector and households. What would truly doom the country to economic crisis, however, is the kind of authoritarian-inspired politics that a Bolsonaro government could usher in.

Brazil is in serious economic trouble. The country’s sovereign debt ratio has ballooned to 83 percent of GDP, fiscal deficits leave no room for additional government spending, and high interest rates are hurting consumers and investors. Meanwhile, the Iran war has raised the price of fuel and other goods, weighing on household balance sheets already strained by high debt and leaving many Brazilians desperate for leaders who can alleviate their daily hardships.

This predicament is years in the making. Before Jair Bolsonaro was elected in 2018, his predecessor, President Michel Temer, enacted a cap on public spending to contain Brazil’s runaway fiscal problems. Temer introduced the cap as a constitutional amendment to prevent future governments from changing the spending ceiling to suit their needs. Yet Jair Bolsonaro raised the cap several times anyway, which required convincing Congress to amend the constitution. In return, the executive branch effectively ceded control of the budgetary process to the legislature.

Lula therefore inherited a system in which he had little room for fiscal adjustment, and he made few attempts to fix the problem during his term. The result was high budget deficits and persistent inflation, which forced the central bank to raise interest rates substantially. In turn, high interest rates damaged household balance sheets and lowered overall investment and growth.

If Lula were reelected, he would find it incredibly difficult to introduce new fiscal reforms and other measures to support growth. He promised to reduce spending and has proposed a comprehensive overhaul of Brazil’s tax system, which would help increase the budget surplus and reduce public debt. Yet Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies now hold a majority of seats in the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies, allowing them to block any legislation Lula might pursue.

Yet it is overly optimistic, if not completely unrealistic, to expect that Bolsonaro would fare better. Neither candidate has provided much detail during the campaign about what he would do to fix the economy. Bolsonaro has instead spoken often about “institutional reforms,” which he has said would include amending Brazil’s 38-year-old constitution to make existing labor and environmental regulations more flexible, among other changes; meddling with the Supreme Court; and granting amnesty to his father, who is serving a prison sentence for leading a 2023 coup attempt. Those steps are likely to drive away investors because stable institutions are necessary for an economy to function well. A government that undermines the judicial system and the constitution will compromise the integrity of its economic policies, no matter what those policies are or how good the reputations of the officials making them may be.

Gathering support for such an overhaul of the country’s political institutions, moreover, would require compromises that could worsen Brazil’s economic troubles. To secure enough votes in Congress to advance Bolsonaro’s priorities—for example, two-thirds of the Senate would need to approve the removal of a Supreme Court justice, and three-fifths of both houses must approve a constitutional amendment—the government would have to bring legislators outside its coalition on board. Those politicians would almost certainly demand substantial funds for their constituencies in exchange for their support, adding to the budget deficit.

Bolsonaro’s far-right movement will also be focused on holding together its recently formed coalition of governors, mayors, and voters. Much of its constituency is lower-middle-class Brazilians who rose out of poverty during the boom years two decades ago, while Lula was serving his first two terms in office. After seeing their income growth stagnate in the years since, these voters have turned to the Liberal Party, but their loyalty is new. Most are self-employed and face economic precarity. Both Bolsonaro and Lula are now trying to appeal to these voters by promising initiatives that boost income and offer household debt relief, but delivering such programs—if it is even possible—would only exacerbate Brazil’s economic woes.

What Bolsonaro has shared about his economic policies does not inspire much confidence, either. His party has said it would reduce government spending by $40 billion, or 1.5 percent of GDP, and deliver primary budget surpluses—a measure of the budget balance that does not include interest payments. But it has not explained how it would accomplish this, nor has Bolsonaro elaborated on his vague plans for controlling the rise in public debt. Ultimately, it is unlikely that Bolsonaro can deliver on any of these promises, especially if he keeps his pledge not to cut pensions and key social programs.

Part of the problem is that the Liberal Party’s economic program lacks a viable plan for reducing costs. It proposes eliminating at least ten government ministries but has no estimate of the resulting cost savings. When Jair Bolsonaro took similar steps after he assumed office in 2019, removing cabinet positions and laying off public servants, those moves had little effect on fiscal outcomes. Other promised measures include reducing Brazil’s value-added tax, phasing out a tax on financial transactions, lowering taxes on electricity and fuel, spending $180 billion on infrastructure over four years, and building 2.5 million new homes. None of them would fix Brazil’s fiscal problems; they would only make those problems worse.

The same goes for the rest of Flávio Bolsonaro’s tax plan. His economic advisers have said they intend to reverse every tax created or raised under Lula’s finance minister, Fernando Haddad. Haddad’s tax increases were intended to shift the tax burden to high-income brackets, raise government revenue, and reduce inequalities in the tax system. These taxes have contributed to a modest increase in revenue but fell short of delivering budgetary surpluses. Bolsonaro has argued that the measures are impeding investment because they tax higher income brackets more heavily, but there is no evidence to support this idea. Instead, repealing all these tax increases would worsen Brazil’s fiscal situation. A simple calculation shows that Brazil needs to increase its primary budget balance by about six percent of GDP, either through increased revenue or decreased spending (or both), to keep its debt from rising further. That adjustment would have to be spread over at least three years, giving indebted households and firms time to change their consumption and investment patterns, to avoid a recession. Slashing taxes, however, would reduce government revenues, raising the debt.

Brazil’s high interest rates are another constraint. The central bank’s current rate is 13.75 percent, astronomical by Latin American standards, dictating interest rates everywhere in the economy. Public debt service payments alone consume some 8.7 percent of GDP. Bolsonaro would not be able to lower interest rates significantly without sparking a recession, so he would face the same problem that has plagued Lula during his latest term—few good options for containing a rapidly growing debt.

Neither Lula nor Bolsonaro is well positioned to solve Brazil’s economic problems. A decisive turn toward illiberalism under Bolsonaro, however, would all but assure economic disaster.

Flávio Bolsonaro has never disavowed his father’s championing of Brazil’s dictatorship, which lasted from 1964 to 1985, and his Liberal Party traces its lineage to the party that sustained the military regime. Moreover, he has pledged to release his father and his father’s associates who are in prison for staging an insurrection and a coup attempt in 2023. Flávio’s brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, a former member of Brazil’s Congress who would likely play a significant role in his brother’s government, has openly expressed his admiration for Viktor Orban’s illiberal regime in Hungary, claiming a desire to learn the “best practices” of a movement that rewrote Hungary’s constitution, reshaped its courts, silenced its press, and deployed other overtly authoritarian tactics. And the substantial far-right bloc in Brazil’s Congress supports policies to undermine institutions, including by impeaching members of the Supreme Court—a step these parties advocated even before corruption allegations emerged against several of the court’s justices. (Flávio Bolsonaro is also under investigation for his involvement in the same corruption scandal.)

Although Brazil is not at risk of returning to military rule, the former authoritarian regime serves as a warning of what could happen if a Bolsonaro administration follows its illiberal inclinations to their logical conclusion. During those two decades of military dictatorship, Brazil spent at unsustainable levels, mostly funding state enterprises, to preserve the regime’s hold on power. The country defaulted on its public debt, endured corrosive hyperinflation, and saw income inequality skyrocket. Six economic stabilization plans failed and growth stagnated. Brazil is not alone in this experience. No Latin American country that swung from democracy to authoritarian rule in the past century has benefited economically from the shift. Countries elsewhere in the world that prospered after such a transition, including some in East Asia, became less authoritarian during their economic ascent.

Brazil’s rightward shift fits a regional pattern. The common thread that unites Brazil with Argentina, Chile, and Colombia is the crude libertarian worldview that each of their far-right movements espouse. All of them talk about citizens becoming entrepreneurs free of the state. They tell voters who have unstable employment and little economic security that their policies will bring prosperity. But their populism rarely wins the confidence of investors. Like its peers, when the Brazilian far right says it can overcome the country’s substantial problems with institutional demolition and a threadbare economic agenda, what it really offers is empty promises.

#5983. The Biggest October Surprise of All

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: The Biggest October Surprise of All

It is unclear whether anything that happened over the past month will go down in the history books as an “October surprise.” Most of the big events did not seem to move the needle relative to existing issues of affordability, war in Iran, mass deportations, and political chaos. Although President Donald Trump announced an oil deal with Russia and federal agents raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, the underlying trends favoring Democrats seemed to hold.

The one possible exception is a late-breaking New York Times story about staffers connected to Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska poised to pull off a possible upset, who were part of a reported secret effort to recruit another Dan Sullivan to confuse voters and split the state’s Republican vote; Dan J. Sullivan now also appears on the ballot alongside the incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation. Although there is nothing illegal about “stacking,” an old partisan tactic, the story will feed the Justice Department’s effort to block the state from certifying the election results if the Republican loses. Whether it will have any broader impact, however, remains unclear.

It is unclear whether anything that happened over the past month will go down in the history books as an “October surprise.” Most of the big events did not seem to move the needle relative to existing issues of affordability, war in Iran, mass deportations, and political chaos. Although President Donald Trump announced an oil deal with Russia and federal agents raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, the underlying trends favoring Democrats seemed to hold.

The one possible exception is a late-breaking New York Times story about staffers connected to Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska poised to pull off a possible upset, who were part of a reported secret effort to recruit another Dan Sullivan to confuse voters and split the state’s Republican vote; Dan J. Sullivan now also appears on the ballot alongside the incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation. Although there is nothing illegal about “stacking,” an old partisan tactic, the story will feed the Justice Department’s effort to block the state from certifying the election results if the Republican loses. Whether it will have any broader impact, however, remains unclear.

The ambiguity over the October surprise should not itself be surprising. Since 1980, every election cycle has generated speculation about the possibility of one. The term refers to the emergence of earth-shattering news, whether generated by individuals associated with a campaign or by unfolding events, that could dramatically influence the electorate. It was popularized during the 1980 election, when William Casey, Ronald Reagan’s campaign manager, feared that President Jimmy Carter might announce a breakthrough agreement to free the 52 U.S. hostages being held in Iran before Election Day. No such deal materialized before voters cast ballots. Iran ultimately released the hostages minutes after Reagan was inaugurated in January 1981, a dramatic split-screen moment that has fueled longstanding allegations, never conclusively proven, that members of the Reagan campaign interfered with the negotiations by signaling that Tehran would receive more favorable terms under a Republican administration.

Most anticipated October surprises never occur. As in 1980, the fears usually prove greater than the reality. Even when such surprises have emerged—such as the indictment of former Secretary of Defense Caspar Weinberger over the Iran-Contra affair days before the 1992 vote or the revelation of George W. Bush’s 1976 drunk driving arrest shortly before the 2000 election—other factors appear to have been more consequential in shaping the outcome.

Sometimes, however, major developments, particularly foreign policy, have significantly altered the political environment in the final weeks of the campaign. One of the most dramatic took place in October 1962, when President John F. Kennedy confronted the Soviet Union over the placement of nuclear missiles in Cuba, about 90 miles from the shores of the United States.

Since Kennedy’s inauguration in 1961, Republicans had attacked the young president as incapable of dealing with the threats posed by the Soviet Union. The spectacular failure of the Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba in April intensified that criticism. In early June 1961, Kennedy met with Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev in Vienna, and Khrushchev treated the U.S. president with little respect and brazenly intimidated him.

Of all the difficult foreign policy challenges that Kennedy confronted in his first two years of office, few were as explosive domestically as Cuba. Vice President Richard Nixon had been hurt in his 1960 presidential run by the fact that Cuba had fallen to communism on Republican President Dwight Eisenhower’s watch in 1959. Meanwhile, Kennedy had successfully positioned himself as more hawkish than Nixon, particularly through claims that a so-called missile gap had left the Soviet Union with a strategic advantage.

Domestic tensions over Cuba escalated in the summer of 1962 as reports of a Soviet military buildup on the island hit U.S. politics. As the debate over Cuba heated up, Democrats anticipated the losses normally suffered by president’s party in midterms. With the exception of Democrats in 1934, such losses had been a constant in political life since the Civil War. The economy added to the party’s worries. The stock market had declined, with the steepest one-day drop since 1929 taking place on May 28, while the president clashed with steel industry executives over price increases. Violent struggles over civil rights were occurring in the Deep South. All of this occurred as much of the president’s domestic agenda, including Medicare, was stalled in Congress. Republicans hoped to reduce the size of the large majorities that Democrats enjoyed in the House and Senate.

Republicans believed that Cuba was a winning issue. Evidence of Soviet activity in Cuba first emerged in August, when a U-2 reconnaissance flight captured images indicating the presence of Soviet military equipment, though the president told reporters that there was no indication of any Soviet combat troops. CIA Director John McCone warned Kennedy that Soviets were likely shipping some sort of missiles into Cuba, but many administration officials dismissed his claims as those of a hardline anticommunist Republican.

Two Republicans, Sens. Kenneth Keating of New York and Homer Capehart of Indiana, spent much of August criticizing Kennedy for ignoring Soviet intervention in Cuba and placing the United States at risk. Keating, who was considering a presidential run at a time when liberal northeastern Republicans remained an influential force within the party, ridiculed the president’s claim that the Soviets were only sending defensive weapons that did not require a response. “Who is to say whether a weapon is offensive or defensive?” Keating asked. “It depends on the direction in which it is aimed.” Capehart was far more conservative than his counterpart, having opposed the liberal internationalism of Presidents Franklin Roosevelt and Harry Truman. In Cuba, however, he demanded force, once asking, “How long will the President examine the situation … until the hundreds of Russian troops grow into hundreds of thousands?”

Worried about the political situation, Kennedy told Secretary of State Dean Rusk and National Security Advisor McGeorge Bundy that he wanted to remain in close contact with Republican leaders, the “key gasbags and others,” to calm the growing storm. On Sept. 7, he also tried to demonstrate his resolve by requesting from Congress stand-by authority to mobilize 150,000 men from the Ready Reserve. Arizona Sen. Barry Goldwater, a right-wing Republican who was preparing to run for president in 1964, was not satisfied. “The American people will not be satisfied with the President’s reiteration of a ‘do nothing’ policy toward Cuba,” he said. Keeping a close eye on Capitol Hill, Bundy reported to the president that “[t]he congressional head of steam on this is the most serious that we have had.”

The crisis broke on Oct. 16, just three weeks before the midterms. U-2 reconnaissance flights, which Kennedy had stepped up earlier in the month, returned with photographs of Soviet missile sites being built in Cuba. Military officials understood that the Soviets could strike the U.S. within minutes. Before seeing the photographs, advisor Kenneth O’Donnell had assured the president that “voters won’t give a damn about Cuba.” After revealing the photographs to O’Donnell, Kennedy said, “You’d better believe it. We’ve just elected Capehart in Indiana and Ken Keating will probably be the next president of the United States.”

After being briefed on the situation, Kennedy formed the Executive Committee of the National Security Council to deliberate over the available options. Its members debated everything from a full-scale military strike to an intensive diplomatic effort. Kennedy pushed back against the hawkish recommendations of military leaders, wary of how quickly the crisis could spin out of control.

On Oct. 22, Kennedy addressed the nation on television to announce his middle ground solution. The U.S. Navy would impose a quarantine around Cuba to prevent additional military material from reaching the island. At the same time, he demanded that the Soviet Union remove the offensive weapons that had already been installed.

From the moment Kennedy made his announcement until Oct. 28, the nation waited with bated breath to see what would happen, terrified that nuclear war might be imminent. After years of school children doing “duck-and-cover” drills in the classroom and suburban families building bomb shelters in case of war, an actual crisis was unfolding. Americans watched anxiously as Soviet ships approached the quarantine line. Those living in dense cities mapped out escape routes and made emergency plans in case of a nuclear attack. Years later, archival material revealed that Soviet commanders in Cuba had been granted authority to deploy certain weapons without direction from the Kremlin.

The first political result of the crisis was to neutralize Cuba as a Republican campaign issue, producing a classic “rally-around-the-flag” effect. Although 8,000 conservative activists gathered at Madison Square Garden to criticize the president for his reluctance to use military force, most Republican leaders vowed to avoid stumping on the issue. At the same time, Kennedy had been on the campaign trail before his address, in part to hide the fact that a major crisis was unfolding.

One day after Soviet forces shot down a U-2 reconnaissance plane over Cuba, killing its pilot, the crisis ended. Through an exchange of letters between Kennedy and Khrushchev, as well as secret talks between Attorney General Robert Kennedy and Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin, the two sides reached an agreement: The Soviets would remove the missiles from Cuba, while the United States would pledge not to invade Cuba. In a secret side agreement, Kennedy vowed that the United States would remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey.

The second political effect of the crisis was to bolster the standing of Kennedy, and the Democratic Party. The president left the crisis perceived as a highly effective leader on foreign policy—a sharp contrast to the image after the Bay of Pigs—and Republicans had avoided one of the most fraught issues for weeks: The claim that Democrats were “soft on communism,” a staple of GOP rhetoric since the fall of China to communism in 1949, lost some of its force for the time being. Kennedy’s approval rating increased by 13 percentage points, reaching 74 percent.

Democrats did well in the elections, avoiding the normal cycle of loss. They gained four seats in the Senate and only lost a few seats in the House. While Republicans scored some important victories, such as George Romney’s election as Michigan governor, Democrats generally thrived. A new generation of talented liberal senators, including Indiana’s Birch Bayh and South Dakota’s George McGovern, entered the upper chamber, where they would leave their mark over the decade. (Capehart, who was seeking reelection, lost to Bayh.)

Although scholars debate the precise electoral impact of Kennedy’s handling of the missile crisis, one thing is sure: The confrontation dominated the news and boosted Kennedy’s standing in an area where he had been viewed as weak. “It must be assumed that the Democratic party gained rather than lost by its leader’s well-dramatized action,” concluded the chairman of the Republican Congressional Campaign Committee.

The midterm also laid the foundation for even bigger gains in the 1964 election. The neutralization of national security as an effective partisan issue made it more difficult for Goldwater to attack Lyndon Johnson, who became president after Kennedy’s assassination, on this front.

While October surprises have often failed to materialize, there have been moments when unexpected effects dramatically reshape the political playing field. This was the case in 1962.

Today, a consequential October surprise is even less likely to alter the course of an election. Hyperpolarization has rendered much of the electorate resistant to change, even in the face of extraordinary events, such as a pandemic. The fragmentation of the media environment has made it harder for single issues—or even presidents—to command public attention for very long. Meanwhile, the spread of disinformation has made it more difficult for candidates to persuade voters of almost anything. High levels of political disengagement and distrust have also reduced the chances that disaffected citizens will vote. Finally, in both terms, Trump has gone so far to normalize the unpredictable that it is hard for anything to create shock and awe anymore.

Still, history is full of surprises. In early October 1962, very few Americans imagined that the final weeks before the elections would be dominated by a crisis that brought the United States and the Soviet Union to the brink of nuclear war. Sometimes the unpredictable forces of history are the one factor strong enough to break through the political gridlock that constrains the possibility of major change.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. In 2027, Norton will publish his new book, Rumble on the Promenade: The Clash of Justice and Power at the 1964 Convention. X: @julianzelizer

#5979. What Israel’s Election Won’t Change

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ALUF BENN is Editor in Chief of Haaretz and a Senior Fellow at the Bill Graham Centre for Contemporary International History at the University of Toronto.

The Constraints and Costs of the New Security Consensus

When Israelis go to the polls on October 27, much of the world will be rooting for the defeat of the country’s longtime prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Under his nearly two decades of rule, Israel has become steadily more aggressive. It has abandoned any pretense of supporting a two-state solution; started constructing hundreds of new Jewish settlements in the West Bank; and, following Hamas’s cross-border attack on October 7, 2023, laid waste to the Gaza Strip, occupied parts of Lebanon and Syria, and launched war against Iran, its archnemesis. Meanwhile, its democratic institutions have faced endless attacks by Netanyahu and his allies, who have proposed laws that would, among other things, greatly curtail the power of Israel’s courts. Should he return to power for an unprecedented seventh term, many fret that the country will permanently transition into a rogue theocratic actor.

To many voters, this election thus marks a crucial turning point in Israeli domestic policy. The prime minister’s main political opponent, former Israel Defense Forces Chief Gadi Eisenkot, holds a more liberal worldview than his competitor. He supports an independent judiciary, a free press, and a professional civil service. Should he win, he will likely try to reverse Netanyahu’s efforts to curtail each institution’s independence.

But an Eisenkot victory is unlikely to change Israel’s foreign policy or approach to the Palestinians. Almost all of Israel’s Jewish political parties, Eisenkot’s included, are opposed to Palestinian statehood, not just Netanyahu’s Likud. They all believe that Israel’s brutal war on Gaza was morally just and practically necessary. And almost all of them think that Israel was right to attack Iran and to establish and create what its government and military call “security zones”—occupied territory—in Lebanon and Syria. In fact, the only real disagreement between Eisenkot and Netanyahu on matters of security is whether the latter made the right tactical decisions in each of these conflicts, such as when Netanyahu rejected a cease-fire in Gaza that would have freed Israeli hostages earlier.

That is not to say he will follow exactly the same course. Eisenkot and Netanyahu differ in important ways on the barrage of West Bank settler attacks against helpless Palestinians, which are aimed at driving them out of their land. The prime minister, committed to his far-right allies, shrugs off the issue, whereas his competitor calls their behavior “Jewish terror.” Even if Eisenkot has little pity for the Palestinian victims, he realizes that the West Bank is on the verge of a bloody explosion and that Israel is at risk of even greater international opprobrium because of its reckless policy there. But overall, no matter what happens in the elections, Israel will continue to repress the Palestinians and strike its enemies. It will thus face diplomatic and economic costs, as the country’s frustrated partners begin cutting off aid and perhaps even enacting sanctions.

There are many issues at play in Israel’s election. Politicians, for example, have debated ultra-Orthodox exemptions from the draft, Netanyahu’s corruption charges, and what, if anything, the government should do about Jewish terrorism. But on the whole, the contest has been focused on who is to blame for failing to stop Hamas’s October 7 attack, which killed 1,200 Israelis and resulted in 251 more being taken hostage in one day. The opposition has argued that Netanyahu is responsible for the country’s worst-ever security failure, pointing out that he sustained Hamas with Qatari money, ignored intelligence warnings about Hamas plots, and then blocked an independent investigation into what happened. Eisenkot, who lost a son and two nephews to fighting in Gaza, has been particularly unsparing in his criticism, repeatedly hammering Netanyahu for refusing to take any accountability for the calamity. The prime minister and his supporters, for their part, have brushed off these accusations. Instead, they have blamed October 7 on the military and security services. They have also promoted conspiracy theories that there is what Netanyahu’s cronies and supporters call “treason from within”—or that someone inside Israel helped facilitate Hamas’s brief invasion.

But despite this blame game, both sides agree on the tragedy’s primary lessons: that Israel is surrounded by diehard merciless enemies and that the Palestinians can never be trusted. This attitude is, in part, a raw expression of anti-Arab racism, which is more visible in Israel’s post–October 7 Jewish society. But it is also an electoral play. If the polling is correct, Eisenkot will need the support, however tacit, of Israel’s two Arab parties to put together a government. Netanyahu is thus trying to win over voters who, much as they hate him personally, cannot stand the idea of a government propped up by Palestinians.

This strategy is unlikely to work on liberal Israelis, who view this election as the last chance to save their homeland from sliding into dictatorship. Many Israelis who live abroad, including immigrants who left the country because of Netanyahu’s leadership, thus intend to come home and vote for his replacement. But these election day visitors and likeminded liberal voters are rallying to protect and preserve their way of life in a country that is becoming more religious and nationalistic. And even many of the anti-Netanyahu voters would be unhappy about partnering with the Arab parties to replace the current government. Few would bother to think about the two-state solution, viewing the idea as a relic from the overly optimistic 1990s. Eisenkot, the current leader of this electorate, has declared his personal opposition to a Palestinian state, as have Israel’s other centrist and conservative opposition figures. Only Yair Golan, the leader of Israel’s sole left-wing Jewish party, supports what he calls “separation from the Palestinians” and a return to diplomacy—and even he lacks a plan for how to make that happen.

In one sense, the country’s rejection of a two-state solution is not new. The last detailed negotiations over Palestinian statehood took place in early 2001. Most Jewish Israelis turned against the idea following the second intifada and Hamas’s 2007 takeover of Gaza. Netanyahu has railed against Palestinian sovereignty for his entire political career. (His brief ostensible endorsement of such a state, in 2009, was heavily conditioned and widely considered insincere.) And after October 7, opposition to the notion has become far more resolute. Before the attack, some major Jewish parties would still pay lip service to the notion of making peace with the Palestinians, and their politicians expressed tentative openness to a settlement. Now, they either reject it out of hand or simply dismiss the issue altogether.

Israeli officials have also become far more aggressive. The country may have turned against Palestinian independence years ago, but for most of the last two decades, it avoided full-scale wars and preserved the low-cost status quo. That restraint, even if disrupted by periodic rounds of fighting with Hamas, endeared Netanyahu to mainstream Israelis, who could pretend that the conflict was a thing of the past and all but forget about the Palestinians. Yet this attitude changed when Hamas crossed the border. Afterward, Israel adopted its current policy of destruction and occupation—which Netanyahu’s election campaign is bragging about, since it knows that bombing Iran and invading Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria have been extremely popular among the population at large. The prime minister’s main opponents all endorsed these tactics—criticizing him only for failing to achieve his pledge of “total victory.”

Netanyahu, in turn, blamed Eisenkot for being soft on Hamas when he served in the country’s war cabinet. Eisenkot then said that he had voted for a more aggressive invasion than what the prime minister ultimately undertook. Eisenkot later pledged to “end Hamas rule in Gaza within 18 months” if elected. This line is not necessarily as hawkish as Netanyahu’s posture, since it suggests a willingness to consider diplomatic means of removing the group from power. Eisenkot has also strongly criticized Netanyahu’s campaign pledge to overthrow the Iranian regime. Instead, he supports measures to take the enriched uranium out of Iran and to put its nuclear program under a verification regime. “You can’t overthrow a government from the air; it’s a delusion,” he said. But he nonetheless backed bombing the country to weaken its military and nuclear program, even if he disagreed with the ultimate end.

The rest of the world, of course, does not share Israel’s view. Quite the contrary—in the wake of the destruction of Gaza, polls show that Israel’s international approval ratings have hit new lows. Politicians in every region are arguing that Israel is guilty of major human rights violations, with many claiming that the country has committed genocide. Even some of Israel’s friends are warning that the state has gone overboard. In July 2025, for example, U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer declared that although Israel “has a right to defend itself and end Hamas’s brutal rule,” the “reporting and images out of Gaza—depicting the devastating levels of hunger, starvation, suffering and death—are wholly unacceptable.”

Outside countries are also particularly furious about its settlement expansion in the West Bank, which cannot be justified as a reaction to October 7. As a result, sanctions have reached Israel’s shores. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband declared on September 8 that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank is unlawful and announced a sanctions regime against the settlements and companies involved in their financing and construction. Given that London is a major financial center, Israeli banks—which are financing the major settlement projects—are now in trouble.

Across the Atlantic, Israel still has the support of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Netanyahu’s reelection campaign. But most of the Democratic Party’s politicians—and even many Republicans—now want to stop or limit U.S. aid and technology transfers to the Israel Defense Forces, citing the use of American munitions in the destruction of Gaza. Many prominent Democratic Party officials want to sanction the country, too. If Democrats take control of at least one house of Congress in the midterms, the United States could stop sending blank checks to Israel.

Israelis generally attribute such rising international anger to anti-Semitism instead of sincerely held concerns about the rights of Palestinians, Middle Eastern stability, or the proper allocation of military resources. But they are nonetheless aware of their growing isolation and fear that, after the election, they might get hit by what former Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak has called a “diplomatic tsunami.” This assessment is widely accepted in the mainstream media and by Netanyahu, who argues that only he—with his superior English skills—can stop such an onslaught, much as he maneuvered to stop the Biden administration from ever imposing real consequences on the country for its war in Gaza. The Israeli right wing has been arguing for many years, with justification, that Israel can continue its occupation and denial of civil rights to the Palestinians while manipulating the international community with hasbara (public diplomacy and lobbying). Eisenkot, by contrast, will try to win the world back by being upfront about what his country is willing to accept and then negotiating honestly—two things that Netanyahu has rarely done.

Eisenkot’s approach would likely win over more international partners, at least for a time, as did the leaders of two other former military chiefs, Barak and Yitzhak Rabin, who unseated Likud governments. Netanyahu has burned so many bridges with his parade of lies that Eisenkot would probably get an international grace period simply by virtue of his relative honesty. And Eisenkot might indeed make changes that please Israel’s partners, such as slowing settlement construction. He opposes the controversial E1 settlement project, which is aimed at slicing a future Palestinian state by half, and has pledged to tackle Jewish terrorism.

But eventually, Eisenkot would disappoint any overseas Israel supporters who expect a thorough reversal of Netanyahu’s foreign and Palestinian policies. And even if he somehow changed his own mind on Palestinian statehood—which he insists he has never supported—his freedom of action would be severely restricted by his governing coalition. Eisenkot’s power bloc relies on two right-wing parties whose leaders strongly oppose the two-state solution and mistrust the Palestinians. One of them, Avigdor Lieberman, even wants to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and bring in Jordan to rule over the Palestinians who reside in the West Bank (an idea that Amman rejected decades ago). They would bring Eisenkot’s government down if he expressed openness to a Palestinian state.

Polling shows that the October 27 election will be extremely tight. In fact, if the surveys are right, neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu will win an outright majority. The country is thus likely to experience a period of horse-trading, as both politicians jockey to peel off the other’s partners. Netanyahu might even try to lure Eisenkot himself into a kind of unity government, promising to put his judicial overhaul or other culture-war campaigns on hold in return. (Eisenkot has adamantly rejected the idea of serving under Netanyahu, even for a rotation, but about-faces have been a staple of Israeli coalition politics.) Alternatively, negotiations could fail, and the country would almost immediately return to the polls. It would not be the first time that an Israeli contest failed to produce a lasting government: the country held five general elections from 2019 to 2022 before its political leaders established a coalition that could hold on to power for more than 12 months.

But no matter the outcome—a Netanyahu caretaker government, a Netanyahu majority government, a unity government, a minority Eisenkot cabinet supported by the Arab parties, or even an Eisenkot majority government—Israel’s next prime minister will keep occupying parts of its neighbors and brutalizing the Palestinians. He will thus have to contend with Israel’s increasing isolation from the rest of the world. The government might end up spending even more on local arms production to replace U.S.-funded systems, working hard to bypass export controls on military and dual-use items (as sanctioned Iran and Russia do today, and as Israel did in its early years). Israel might face its ultimate fear—losing the United States’ veto at the UN Security Council, which has protected its occupation since 1967 from international censure, even under critical Democratic presidents such as Jimmy Carter and Barack Obama.

This may not be the outcome that Israelis actually want. But without a sea change in how they think about their problems, it is the one they are careening toward. The odds, however, are particularly pronounced if Netanyahu and his partners stay in power. In that case, more liberal Israelis will not wait to see how badly the world punishes their country. They will instead flee to pursue their way of life in a quieter place.

#5978. Don’t Read Too Much Into These Midterms

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Don’t Read Too Much Into These Midterms

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

If there’s one truism in U.S. politics, it’s that voters don’t vote on foreign policy. Eggheads like me in Washington might go back and forth on what we believe the American people want from foreign policy, complete with polls that reflect our own opinions. But it is rarely, if ever, the case that foreign policy is a salient enough issue to drive voting behavior.

With his Iran war, however, President Donald Trump has made a foreign-policy choice so destructive and toxic that it has raised the ire of voters—and likely cratered his party’s chances heading into the midterm elections on Tuesday.

If there’s one truism in U.S. politics, it’s that voters don’t vote on foreign policy. Eggheads like me in Washington might go back and forth on what we believe the American people want from foreign policy, complete with polls that reflect our own opinions. But it is rarely, if ever, the case that foreign policy is a salient enough issue to drive voting behavior.

With his Iran war, however, President Donald Trump has made a foreign-policy choice so destructive and toxic that it has raised the ire of voters—and likely cratered his party’s chances heading into the midterm elections on Tuesday.

Despite this, we should be cautious about overinterpreting these results. As the horse race for the 2028 presidential election kicks off in the coming weeks, you’ll hear about the ways in which the election is a wholesale rejection of the Trump administration’s foreign-policy choices. This would be an oversimplification. What voters are incensed about is the war with Iran, not necessarily Trump’s broader rejection of the old bipartisan foreign-policy consensus.

Honestly, it’s not clear from polling or focus groups what it is that American voters want from foreign policy, other than perhaps less of it: a reduced role in the world and a policy that focuses on the needs of Americans. For Democrats in particular, then, overreading these midterms as a wholesale rejection of change in foreign policy is a mistake; just because voters have rejected one disastrous foreign-policy choice does not mean that they’re ready to return to the pre-Trump status quo.

There are, in fact, several truisms about U.S. politics that one could apply to this midterm. Parties rarely do well in midterms when they hold the White House, for example; governing is harder than campaigning. Or take lame-duck presidents. Even though they are not on the ballot—and never will be again—midterm results are usually more indicative of voter discontent with the incumbent than how they feel about actual candidates.

And then there’s the truism that voters don’t vote on foreign policy. Certainly, there are marginal cases where foreign-policy opinion can swing votes: Florida’s Cuban exile community, for example, or the marginal impact of Arab American abstentions on Kamala Harris’s electoral chances in Michigan in 2024.

But, in general, though voters will happily express their views on foreign policy when polled, experts say they don’t prioritize it. In 2020, for example, no single foreign-policy issue cracked the top 10 concerns in one Pew Research Center poll; foreign policy overall ranked below the economy, healthcare, Supreme Court appointments, and violent crime as top issues for voters. Perhaps the only time in recent memory where foreign policy took center stage in a midterm election was in 2002, when the “rally around the flag” effect of 9/11 allowed President George W. Bush’s Republican Party to retake control of the Senate.

Yet despite this apparent rule, polling shows that the war with Iran is a top three issue for voters in this election, with 77 percent of respondents in one Gallup poll saying that it’s an extremely or very important issue for them. Gas prices—the most obvious knock-on effect of the conflict for the economy—also rank highly, with 72 percent of voters saying it’s important. (A related foreign-policy issue also cracks the top 10: the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.)

Two reasons for this break from routine explain why the Iran war has resonated so strongly with voters. The first is that the war is not a purely foreign-policy issue. It has made life less affordable for many Americans in concrete and visible ways. Indeed, though some other Trump policies, such as tariffs, have contributed to the higher cost of living faced by Americans today, much of the pain from inflation has been driven by higher energy costs, which jumped only after the start of the war.

Secondly, the Iran war has been a hot-button topic for voters because Trump himself made it one. One of his primary campaign pledges to voters in 2024 was that there would be “no new wars.” He also committed to improving the cost of living; the latter was a priority for many voters following several years of COVID-induced high inflation. The war with Iran is an open and clear betrayal of these promises.

Foreign policy is not the only factor in this election. Trump voters have soured on his tariffs, on the excessively violent immigration crackdowns, and against the blatant corruption of some parts of his administration. Republicans would likely have lost ground in Congress regardless of the war with Iran. But it’s increasingly looking as if they may lose bigger as a result of it.

Despite this, it’s not clear how much we can really learn from these election results. When the polls close on Tuesday night, media attention will quickly turn to the presidential primaries, which are likely to be highly competitive on the Democratic side and at least somewhat competitive among Republicans.

Polls suggest Democrats will retake at least one chamber of Congress. And with tariffs and the Iran war raising prices, foreign policy is a powerful force at the ballot box. What will Democrats do with power? How will the world react? Susan Glasser joins FP Live to analyze the results.

Is the United States destined for a repeat of Jan. 6 every election now?

We can expect that foreign policy—given its high salience in the midterms and the likelihood that the war with Iran will continue for some time yet—will remain a key topic of discussion. If Democrats take the Senate, they may well initiate impeachment hearings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Those hearings will examine not only the Iran war but also U.S. military actions in the Caribbean. Some congressional Democrats are also pushing for a confrontation with Trump over arms for Ukraine.

There will be a tendency, particularly among congressional Democrats, to see these midterm results as voters rejecting Trump’s foreign-policy promises writ large or—more worryingly—as a vote by the public for a return to the pre-Trump foreign-policy status quo. But they would instead be wise to see this more as a single-issue vote: a rejection of the Iran war and of a president who promised one thing and did another.

Americans remain deeply divided about what they want from their foreign policy. Many voters are unhappy with the Trump administration on tariffs, on Iran, on Venezuela, on Trump’s apparent rejection of long-standing U.S. alliances.

At the same time, many of Trump’s discrete policies are not unpopular. Americans generally express support for alliances such as NATO, but a sizable proportion do want Europeans to contribute more to defense; 49 percent of Americans want to cut military aid to other nations. Voters tell pollsters that they disapprove of the shuttering of the U.S. Agency for International Development, but only 17 percent of Americans want to expand humanitarian aid. And in direct contrast to the more hawkish views prevalent in Washington, Trump’s détente with China is popular. Only 40 percent of those polled believe that the United States should actively work to limit the growth of Chinese power.

In short—as the racers climb onto the starting blocks for the 2028 presidential primaries—they would be well advised not to overread the lessons of the midterm elections on foreign policy. Democrats in particular would be wise not to spend the next few years picking fights on issues such as arms to Ukraine, which is only popular with a minority of voters—and only important to a superminority. Instead, candidates and Congress alike would be wise to hold Trump’s feet to the fire on issues that are broadly unpopular with the electorate, such as the Iran war, and even perhaps to co-opt the “America First” language popularized by Trump in his first term.

After all, if there is one lesson we can take from these midterms, it is that voters do not believe that the war with Iran puts Americans first. They want a foreign policy that does.

Emma Ashford is a columnist at Foreign Policy and senior fellow with the Stimson Center’s Reimagining U.S. Grand Strategy Program. She is also an adjunct assistant professor at Georgetown University and the author of Oil, the State, and War. X: @EmmaMAshford

#5976. Michigan Dem claims Stevens shot down Rogers endorsement rumor hours before turning on El-Sayed

Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., said Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., had told her that reports she would support Republican Mike Rogers were "a rumor" and "not true." Stevens endorsed Rogers hours later. (Credit: WJBK)

The decision by Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., to endorse Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers was apparently a sudden change of heart, and tied to the Abdul El-Sayed campaign's stay-away order this weekend.

Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., said Stevens told her Saturday night that reports of an impending Rogers endorsement were not accurate.

"It's very hard," Dingell told local FOX 2 on Sunday night. "Haley Stevens told me at midnight last night this was all a rumor and was not true."

DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP SENATE NOMINEE MIKE ROGERS AT DETROIT CHURCH

Democrat Rep. Haley Stevens appears alongside GOP rival Mike Rogers at a Detroit church on Nov. 1, 2026. (Courtesy of Rogers for Senate)

Five hours later, Stevens was standing shoulder to shoulder with Rogers at a Detroit church service.

"She texted me at 7:45, watching you on MS NOW, heart, heart," Dingell continued. "And by the way, I talked to her. Look, I'm just upset. I'm very concerned. It's sad, but I don't want to be distracted anymore."

The Detroit church event was intended to bring unity for El-Sayed's campaign, because Stevens had won the Black vote, but instead, after being told by the Democratic nominee to stay away, she unified with Rogers.

FORMER RIVAL DODGES FULL-THROATED EL-SAYED ENDORSEMENT AFTER BITTER SENATE PRIMARY

"We got a phone call this morning and, you know, there's been a lot of unfortunate activity, I think," Rogers told FOX 2 Detroit. "Abdul discarded Haley Stevens, was rude to Haley Stevens, has been rude, I think, to many in the African-American community. At least that's what they're telling me. And I think this just boiled over when he dis-invited her to the campaign event that was supposed to happen today. And basically said don't need you and don't need your supporters."

Rogers welcomed the early November surprise with just two days to go before Tuesday's Election Day in a race that could flip the Democratic Senate seat red and help President Donald Trump's party keep control of the upper chamber.

HALEY STEVENS RIPPED BY FELLOW DEMS FOR REFUSING TO EXPLICITLY BACK EL-SAYED: 'STAY THE F--- OFF TELEVISION'

"I think she picked up the phone today after having lots of, apparently, conversations with a lot of people and picked up a phone and said, 'Hey, I heard you’re going to church, you want some company?'" Rogers added. "And so that was, I mean, we were very welcome for her, I’m very welcome to have her support."

The unity event became divisive for the former Democratic Senate primary combatants after Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blamed Israel for high grocery prices. Stevens' fiancé Jason Turkish, a Democratic donor and Jewish lawyer, said earlier in the week that he was going to vote for Rogers, raising concern from El-Sayed's campaign and other Democrats.

ROGERS OPENS DOOR TO DEMOCRATIC VOTERS AFTER EL-SAYED’S PRIMARY VICTORY: ‘THERE IS STILL HOPE’

El-Sayed’s campaign then asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day to avoid distracting from the race, sources said.

In a social media video, Stevens said, "I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign."

Rogers said Democrats were "veering off into the virulent hate" directed at a group of people, while Stevens’ mother, Maria Marcotte, told Reuters her daughter was concerned about rhetoric she believed frightened constituents.

BLACK VOTERS, JEWISH DEMOCRATS IN MICHIGAN WARY OF VOTING FOR EL-SAYED, SAY 'HE'S TAKING ADVANTAGE'

Despite the rift, El-Sayed’s campaign said it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens’ endorsement, its second-best fundraising day since the August primary.

Fox News Power Rankings' latest projection rates the race as a Toss Up. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority.

While midterm election history tends to deliver power back to the party in the minority, Trump and Republicans have put added emphasis on retaining Senate control to hold back what is expected to become a Democrat-controlled House.
