Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the key issues in the U.S. midterm elections, cyberattacks targeting Russia and Ukraine, and Iran’s proposal to end the war.

Democrats and Republicans made their final pitch to voters on Monday in the run-up to Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. Early polling suggests that Democrats will likely win back control of the U.S. House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate in what would be a crushing blow to President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement. According to experts, the White House’s poor handling of the Iran war could be to blame.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the key issues in the U.S. midterm elections, cyberattacks targeting Russia and Ukraine, and Iran’s proposal to end the war.

Democrats and Republicans made their final pitch to voters on Monday in the run-up to Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. Early polling suggests that Democrats will likely win back control of the U.S. House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate in what would be a crushing blow to President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement. According to experts, the White House’s poor handling of the Iran war could be to blame.

In the eight months since U.S. and Israeli forces first launched strikes on Iran, fuel prices have skyrocketed, energy infrastructure has come under fire, and fighting has upended critical supply chains. Products from batteries to medical supplies to sulfur have borne the brunt of the U.S.-Iran war. And the wallets of U.S. voters are far from immune to the fallout.

The cost of living for the average American household has grown by around $2,000 since the war began, according to economists at Moody’s Analytics, or roughly $265 billion for U.S. consumers in total. Coupled with Trump’s continued tariff war with Canada, dissatisfaction with high inflation rates has dropped Trump’s approval rating to 38 percent, per NBC News’s polling average.

Democrats are capitalizing on these figures to try to win control of one or both chambers of Congress. Doing so would give them more leverage to challenge Trump’s foreign-policy agenda, such as by blocking Trump’s national security nominees, cutting off further military funding for the Iran war, investigating alleged corruption within the president’s inner circle, and even trying to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Republicans, meanwhile, tried to distance themselves from Trump’s Iran policies on Monday and instead focused on tried-and-true conservative talking points, such as the need for immigration crackdowns, low taxes, and the (unsubstantiated) threat of Muslim lawmakers in office.

Trump echoed a few of these arguments during a speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday. “We have to keep our Congress strong, free, a little bit of apple pie,” Trump said, adding, “We’re not looking to have a jihadist be in our Senate,” in a thinly veiled reference to Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is vying to represent Michigan.

Yet Trump spent the bulk of his remarks—originally advertised as a closing midterms campaign speech—discussing topsoil, graffiti stains, piping, algae, limestone, and other construction elements of his capital renovation projects.

It is unclear if these issues will be enough to convince voters to back the Republican Party.

Trump has already vowed to “veto everything” if Democrats take back Congress. In an interview with the New York Post published on Monday, the U.S. president did not rule out issuing preemptive pardons to his aides and allies, such as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company recently came under heavy criticism after the Trump administration reportedly cut off Ukraine from military-grade Starlink internet services. And the administration has already asked the U.S. Supreme Court to temporarily block around 20,000 mail-in ballots from counting in California as part of its growing bid to sow distrust in the U.S. electoral system.

Tuesday, Nov. 3: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung hosts Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni hosts Chilean President José Antonio Kast.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosts Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda.

Wednesday, Nov. 4: Israeli President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with party leaders.

Friday, Nov. 5: Chinese President Xi Jinping hosts Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.

Saturday, Nov. 6: New Zealand holds a general election.

Pope Leo XIV begins a multiday trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru

Monday, Nov. 8: Turkey begins hosting the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference.

G-7 foreign ministers hold a two-day meeting in France.

Phony alerts. Residents in Ukraine and Russia received phony emergency alerts late Sunday and early Monday that warned of high radiation levels, chemical threats, ballistic missile attacks, and on-the-ground fighting. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of hacking the Ukrainian emergency alert app and said his country had hacked Russia back in response.

The messages, some of which were riddled with spelling errors, did not appear to worry many locals. However, the cyberattacks did cast new uncertainty over the security of both nations’ emergency alert systems. It also highlighted the very real and ongoing threat of Russian ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine. On Friday, the United States unveiled a $2.1 billion deal to supply 500 more Patriot interceptors to Ukraine; however, sources told Reuters that it could take years for the missiles to arrive, even though Kyiv currently has inadequate air defenses.

This week’s incident occurred just as a limited cease-fire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky expired on Monday. U.S. first lady Melania Trump had negotiated the six-day truce to allow humanitarian aid to reach the devastated city. However, on Monday, Kyiv accused Moscow of using the pause to strengthen its military position in the area. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov responded that any troop movements there were “standard practice” and that Ukraine likely did the same thing.

Last-ditch negotiations. Iran announced a two-day plan on Monday that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the United States. The deal, which could be implemented within a week, would only occur if Washington agreed to meet Tehran’s seven conditions for ending the war. Those include an end to the U.S. military blockade on Iranian ports, a U.S. waiver on Iranian oil sales, and the cancellation of new U.S. sanctions on Tehran, among other concessions.

“The basis of dialogue ​and talks between Iran and the U.S. via mediators is still Iran’s seven-step proposal, which is now condensed, making it possible to implement it within two days,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said. Trump, however, rejected that deal in September and has since repeatedly threatened to launch fresh strikes on Iran.

“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice,” Trump said on Sunday at a campaign rally. “But at some point, we’re going to have to give them [Iran] the hammer.” Whether such a resumption of fighting will ultimately happen—and if so, when—remains anyone’s guess. Asked on Monday if he’s considering striking Iran after the U.S. midterms, Trump simply said, “No.”

Meanwhile, Persian Gulf nations are preparing themselves for a possible return to heavy fighting, which they expect could trigger Iranian retaliatory strikes on their civilian infrastructure. Alongside deadly Houthi strikes on Saudi energy facilities, experts fear that the region is not ready to absorb renewed warfare. “Gulf producers spent five decades persuading the world that their supply could withstand regional wars,” Amir Handjani wrote in Foreign Policy. “Eight months of fighting on two fronts have badly weakened that case.”

A win for Moscow? Acting Bulgarian President Iliana Yotova won the country’s presidential runoff on Sunday, making her Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state. According to the Central Election Commission on Monday, Yotova clinched 57.6 percent of the vote, putting her in double digits ahead of former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who secured 39.5 percent. She will be inaugurated on Jan. 22.

Yotova’s win marks a larger victory for the country’s ruling Progressive Bulgaria party. The Russia-friendly group, led by Prime Minister Rumen Radev, secured 131 seats during parliamentary elections in April. Yotova retaining power means that the party’s agenda will now have even less resistance, as Radev and Yotova are united in their support for lifting international sanctions on Moscow as well as their opposition to providing Ukraine with further military assistance.

At the same time, Yotova and Radev have both sought to maintain Bulgaria’s European friendships. Being a member of NATO and the European Union has forced Sofia to exercise a delicate balancing act of fostering closer relations with Russia while also not angering Bulgaria’s traditional allies. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Yotova on her win on Sunday, writing on X, “From security and defence to our competitiveness and energy independence, I look forward to continuing our joint work.”

Four continents, 30 countries, 31,000 miles. English adventurer Karl Bushby completed his 28-year journey around the world on Monday, walking from Punta Arenas, Chile, to his mother’s home in northern England. During that time, he dodged war in the Darién Gap, was airlifted to safety while crossing the Bering Strait, and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel. Visa struggles, the 2008 financial crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic came close to sapping his resources for good, but the now 57-year-old explorer remained adamant on completing his odyssey entirely on foot. “They say it takes a village, but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said.

#5950. Mamdani, Hasan Piker among radical left-wing voices erupting over Haley Stevens' endorsement switch

Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers for Senate, saying Abdul El-Sayed made it clear she wasn't welcome in his campaign.

Prominent Democrats and left-wing voices nationwide exploded with fury after Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in the final stretch of Michigan's U.S. Senate race over the weekend.

In her video posted to social media on Sunday after attending church service with Rogers, Stevens noted how Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed told her to "stay away" from his campaign and slammed him for embracing radical steamer Hasan Piker — who was among those criticizing the endorsement.

"Working class people’s lives are on the ballot on Tuesday—their healthcare, their rent, their bills," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in an X post. "Haley Stevens just betrayed them by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against."

Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said on X shortly after the endorsement: "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."

Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., speaks with media after a debate at WoodTV studios on July 7, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Kristen Norman)

EL SAYED'S LEFT-WING ALLIES ATTACK 'EVIL' STEVENS AFTER BOMBSHELL ROGERS ENDORSEMENT

Stevens, who will leave Congress in January, lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed earlier this year. She was widely viewed as the moderate, establishment candidate compared to the more progressive, left-wing policies of her opponent.

On Sunday, Stevens abandoned the party in the final hours of the Senate campaign as Democrats seek to win back control of the upper chamber.

"This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said on X. "Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors."

DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP SENATE NOMINEE MIKE ROGERS AT DETROIT CHURCH

"Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic caucus," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. "We will have a discussion about appropriate next steps upon our return."

Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., called Stevens "clearly disturbed," and said she "has thrown her constituents under the bus" on several key midterm issues.

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed takes questions from reporters after a campaign rally on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

HALEY STEVENS RIPPED BY FELLOW DEMS FOR REFUSING TO EXPLICITLY BACK EL-SAYED: 'STAY THE F--- OFF TELEVISION'

"Too many people live off their 15 minutes of fame," Pocan continued. "In this case, she threw away an entire career because she couldn’t get over a loss and needed attention. Pathetic. Sad. Clearly she has some serious issues. But no one will take her seriously ever again."

Outside of her own colleagues condemning her endorsement, Stevens also saw an immediate staff exodus after she posted the video.

After the endorsement, a visibly upset El-Sayed demanded the media focus their questions on political issues, rather than Stevens' endorsement.

EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS

"I'm going to ask that when we take questions, you keep your questions focused on the issues that Michiganders really care about. Now that might not drive clicks for you. I get it. I understand your business, right? But they're the issues that Michiganders are paying attention to," he said.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican from Michigan and U.S. Senate candidate, during the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 10, 2026. (Mark Felix/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

FORMER RIVAL DODGES FULL-THROATED EL-SAYED ENDORSEMENT AFTER BITTER SENATE PRIMARY

Stevens drew an official condemnation from the Democratic Party at a national level, too.

"Haley Stevens’ disappointing decision to endorse Mike Rogers, a Trump ally who would join Republican efforts to sell out working families, is a betrayal of the values of the Democratic Party," Democratic National Committee (DNC) chairman Ken Martin said in a statement on behalf of the organization.

"At a moment when Democrats are united in fighting for Michigan families and standing up to Trump’s agenda, we reject these efforts to sow division within our party. We will not allow last-minute political stunts to derail our momentum and we will triple down on our efforts to elect Abdul El-Sayed on Tuesday."

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), chaired by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., lashed out at Stevens' decision, too.

MICHIGAN SENATE RIVALS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ALLEGATIONS AS ROGERS DOUBLES DOWN ON EL-SAYED

"The stakes of this election could not be higher: Mike Rogers is a rubber stamp for Donald Trump, and together they plan to continue sowing chaos and making life unaffordable for families while prioritizing their billionaire donors at the expense of Michigan families," the DSCC statement said, adding the group will "reject any efforts to divide Democrats ahead of Tuesday’s crucial election."

DEMOCRAT RIPS HASAN PIKER AS 'HACK WHO THRIVES ON HATE' OVER HIS WARNING TO AMERICAN JEWS ABOUT ISRAEL

Piker, who was partly the reason for Stevens' break from El-Sayed, simply wrote: "i [sic] condemn haley stevens."

Piker has caused major controversy in the Michigan race due to his proximity to El-Sayed. Since his primary win, the progressive candidate has sought to distance himself from the streamer.

"This is the single most unproductive, selfish thing a Democratic candidate has done all cycle and likely many cycles before that," Jon Favreau, Pod Save America cohost and speechwriter to President Barack Obama, said on X. "Having misjudged candidates in the past myself, I hope everyone who tried to recruit, support, and defend Haley can now admit what a mistake it was."

HALEY STEVENS URGES EL-SAYED TO DITCH HASAN PIKER AFFILIATION AFTER MICHIGAN PRIMARY

Fellow PodSaveAmerica cohost Jon Lovett called Stevens a "sleaze."

"Not to downplay Haley Stevens' vermin-like betrayal of her party and her constituents and her nation... But given her track record as a clownish loser, do we really believe any who will now follow her weren't already going to vote for the Fascist?" podcaster and former television sports personality Keith Olbermann said in an X post.

Former President Barack Obama, Abdul El-Sayed and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson raise hands during a campaign event at Cass Technical High School on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)

Stevens, who was narrowly defeated by El-Sayed in Michigan's Aug. 4, 2026 primary election, crossed partisan lines after saying for months that she would support El-Sayed.

It all devolved after Stevens expressed concern last week over an ad aired in El-Sayed's favor that was widely viewed as antisemitic. She said she would appear at a weekend campaign event with El-Sayed on the condition that he denounced the ad. El-Sayed, whose support among the Michigan Jewish community is already tenuous, disinvited her from the event instead.

The ad that sparked the controversy was released by the Rebellion PAC, which is operated by The Young Turks co-founder and bombastic leftist commentator Cenk Uygur, who is Piker's uncle. Piker, whom El-Sayed invited onto the campaign trail in Michigan during primary season, has been a headache for El-Sayed during the general election.

Piker said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11." He has also praised Mao Zedong and Communist China, said capitalists should be murdered in the streets, and is known for making antisemitic comments.

El-Sayed has refused to denounce Piker, brushing him off as a "streamer from California" who he says shouldn't be the focus of the campaign in Michigan.

#5949. Only the Gulf Can End the Iran War

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ALLISON MINOR is a Senior Fellow in the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and served as Deputy U.S. Special Envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2023.

NATE SWANSON is a Resident Senior Fellow and Director of the Iran Strategy Project at the Atlantic Council. He served as Director for Iran at the National Security Council from 2022 to 2025. In the spring and summer of 2025, he served on the Trump administration’s Iran negotiating team.

The Arab Monarchies Must Help Washington and Tehran Save Face

For everyone involved, the war in Iran has been a strategic failure. The United States and Israel have shown that they can achieve a few military objectives, such as sinking Iran’s navy. But after eight months of fighting and pressure, they have also proved that they cannot forcibly realize their main ambitions, including regime change, destroying Iran’s nuclear program, or even reopening the Strait of Hormuz—a waterway that was not closed when the war began. The Islamic Republic, for its part, has demonstrated that it can survive intense bombings. Yet it cannot break the American military’s economically suffocating blockade and has thus far failed to achieve its goal of putting an end to indefinite threats of war against Iran.

In theory, the war’s descent into a painful stalemate should open the door to diplomatic outcomes. But both sides have proved incapable of making the concessions necessary to strike a deal. Instead, they appear to prefer a mutually destructive status quo that maintains the delusion of achievable victory and which they can justify with the continued pain they inflict on their adversaries. As a result, rather than moving toward a settlement, both sides are threatening renewed attacks.

But there is a face-saving way for Iran and the United States to extricate themselves from this conflict: a cease-fire brokered and managed by the Gulf Arab states. The deal would begin with Gulf countries providing economic relief to Iran in exchange for Iran lifting its restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz. This would, in turn, allow the United States to lift its own blockade. The Gulf states would also need to commit to taking steps to deter Washington from resuming strikes on Iran in the future. But neither the United States nor Iran would need to make direct concessions to the other, and each would avoid the most painful compromises. The United States, for example, would not have to lift its “maximum pressure” campaign, and Iran would not have to agree to limit its nuclear program. Gulf states could then use their leverage to sustain the cease-fire until conditions permit a more comprehensive agreement.

Serving as the guarantor of a cease-fire comes with real costs and risks for the Gulf, but its countries have good reason to accept them. They are part of the battlefield on which the Iran war is being fought, and should the conflict continue indefinitely, it could pose a threat to the very economic and political models on which they are built. The Gulf depends on oil and gas exports to sustain itself, and there is no way it can completely bypass the Strait of Hormuz in shipping its energy resources abroad. Its efforts to diversify away from hydrocarbons, meanwhile, are also vulnerable to renewed attacks from Iran.

Securing a cease-fire will not be easy. It requires that the Gulf countries overcome their own lack of cohesion, that Iran prioritize economic recovery and forgo explicit guarantees about U.S. behavior, and that the United States gives Gulf countries the space necessary to reach a deal. Even if successful, the resulting agreement will not address the underlying issues driving the war. But with scant alternatives on the horizon, it is the best—and perhaps the only—way to ease the pain for everyone.

In theory, a U.S.-Iranian agreement should be straightforward. There is a historical template for deals between Iran and the United States—Tehran agrees to constrain or give up a specific behavior, and Washington agrees to give it money and recognition—that could apply neatly to the current conflict. In the Algiers Accords of 1981, for instance, Iran agreed to release American diplomats it held hostage in exchange for frozen funds and a commitment by the United States not to intervene in Iran’s internal affairs. In the 2015 nuclear deal, Tehran accepted strict limits on its nuclear program in return for sanctions relief and an implicit acceptance of its right to enrich uranium. Today, Iran could stop impeding maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz (and perhaps eventually make concessions on its nuclear program), and Washington could grant it some combination of sanctions relief, cash, and acknowledgment of Tehran having a formal role in the waterway.

In practice, however, reaching this understanding will be extremely difficult. One reason is technical: Iran won’t make the nuclear concessions that U.S. President Donald Trump wants, and the United States will not provide the upfront, irreversible financial incentives that Tehran demands. But the bigger problem is reputational. To justify his quixotic war and decision to withdraw from the 2015 nuclear deal, Trump wants sweeping concessions from Tehran. Iran, for its part, is loath to settle for fewer benefits than it received from the United States in their ill-fated June memorandum of understanding, in which Washington pledged significant relief. As a result, both sides feel compelled to sustain the confrontation, even though doing so is mutually detrimental.

The Gulf states cannot resolve the dispute over Iran’s nuclear program. But they can bring about relative peace by helping address other essential issues. The United States may not be willing to pay Iran for merely opening the Strait of Hormuz, but its Gulf partners have the wealth and the motivation to offer the regime immediate economic concessions. Those partners could, for instance, give Iran some form of humanitarian and reconstruction funding. Iran, in turn, would stop attacks on ships transiting the strait and on Gulf states themselves. In response to Iran ceasing its attacks on commerce, the United States would lift its own blockade, and the Gulf states and Iran would establish a temporary deconfliction mechanism for shipping that acknowledges Iran’s role in the waterway without establishing unacceptable precedents for international commerce. This mechanism could require that ships use Iran’s preferred traffic pattern but would not formalize Iranian control over the passage.

This particular arrangement would not resolve Iran’s other core objective—prohibiting the United States and Israel from launching a renewed military campaign. This concern is harder to address. The United States may lack a credible military endgame, and the war might be unpopular domestically, but that has not stopped an erratic Trump from drawing up plans for renewed military action. But the Gulf states can provide Iran with assurances that they would use their leverage with Washington to help deter future attacks. For example, in May, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia temporarily paused U.S. access, basing, and overflight—the approvals that allow the United States military to use Gulf countries’ territory and airspace—because of concerns about the United States’ plans for escorting merchant ships through the Strait of Hormuz. The tactic worked: the United States paused the operation.

The United States might bristle at handing Iran negotiations over to the Gulf countries. But ultimately, U.S. officials should be able to spin this deal as a win. Trump, for instance, could exit the war while telling Americans that he saved the world from high energy prices without making the kind of economic and nuclear concessions to Iran that the Obama administration did under the 2015 agreement. He could likewise boast about the steps he took to weaken Iran, and, in the absence of a nuclear deal, point out that his self-proclaimed “maximum pressure” sanctions remain in place. In fact, in some ways, a Gulf-brokered deal is exactly the kind of “America first” foreign policy Trump promised. It would let the region take on the burden of managing a bad actor, including responsibility for providing most of the necessary concessions. Trump would have stumbled into the outcome. But he would still leave office with an empowered set of allies more capable of managing their own security.

Iran, for its part, would not only get significant economic benefits. It might also advance its goal of reducing the United States’ influence in the region. After all, if Israel or the United States undermines an arrangement down the road, it will only accelerate the decline of Washington’s credibility and influence with its Gulf partners. The United States has already placed its relationship with these countries under stress by going to war with Iran, something they did not ask for and for which all have suffered serious consequences. A Gulf state deal would thus allow Tehran to leverage any future U.S. military campaigns against Iran to further drive a wedge between the United States and its regional partners.

Iran has repeatedly made clear that its top war-related priority is to end the war on terms that reduce the likelihood of a future conflict. To some extent, Iran has already achieved this benchmark with the pain it has inflicted on the global economy. Assuming this war eventually ends, the next time an Israeli prime minister asks an American president to approve an attack on Iran, that president will have to weigh global economic instability against Israeli security interests. The threat posed by Iran, in the absence of a nuclear breakout or massive terrorist attack, may not outweigh the risk to the global economy. Israel might act independently of the United States, but doing so would risk further damaging the U.S.-Israeli relationship and invite Iranian retaliation without American protection.

But this deterrent is effective only once the current iteration of the war ends. If the war continues, Iran will forfeit the future de facto security guarantee that the Strait of Hormuz and geography provide. The longer this conflict goes on, the more it favors those in Israel or the United States advocating for regime change or endless war. Unless there is a solution to high energy prices that allows Trump to disengage from Iran, he will continue grasping, and it could eventually lead him to adopt aggressive kinetic options that have not yet been tried—and for good reason.

Iran and the Gulf countries are already exploring regionally led solutions to the conflict. On October 26, Saudi officials traveled to Tehran to meet with their Iranian counterparts, alongside leaders from Pakistan and Turkey. Gulf countries had also planned to meet with Iran in Salalah, Oman, on September 14 to discuss the Strait of Hormuz. But that gathering never happened, and unless there is a broader regional solution, Gulf countries will instead mostly pursue private, bilateral deals with Iran to help forestall future attacks on their ships or territory. These agreements might help lessen the pain for individual Gulf countries in the short term, but they fail to address the overall risk of Iranian escalation or resolve the global consequences stemming from disputes related to the Strait of Hormuz. Furthermore, they allow Iran to stoke division and distrust between Gulf countries while driving up its own demands.

To get a workable deal, the Gulf states will thus need to improve internal cohesion. This is easier said than done, particularly in light of continued tensions between two of the major Gulf players—Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. But fixing this issue is wholly within the power of Gulf states, and the Salalah effort demonstrates there is some interest in doing so. Improving cohesion among Gulf states also does not require resolving the larger bilateral tensions and competition among the region’s capitals; it only requires an agreement to isolate the Iran issue from those tensions and address this shared imperative. The Gulf states must therefore collectively agree on redlines for Iranian behavior and coordinate on how to enforce them. If Iran seeks to test the agreement or demand more concessions from Gulf governments, they must collectively push back by pausing economic aid or cooperation—even if it means risking Iranian retaliation.

The Gulf states and Iran will also be tested by the Houthis. Saudi Arabia understandably holds Iran accountable for Houthi attacks on its territory because Iran helped build the group’s capabilities, continues to provide it with significant technical and material support, and helped trigger the re-escalation of the Yemen conflict in July. But Iran does not control the Houthis, so the group is not going to stop attacking Saudi Arabia or call off its campaign inside Yemen simply because Iran says to. Tehran will thus need to extend an olive branch to Riyadh by showing that it is willing to limit its direct involvement in the current Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia. For instance, Iran could credibly promise Riyadh that Tehran-backed Iraqi militias will stop attacking the kingdom. It was, after all, Iraqi militia attacks that took the kingdom’s valuable East-West oil pipeline offline on September 10, and defending against attacks from both the north (where Saudi Arabia borders Iraq) and south (where it borders Yemen) greatly complicates Riyadh’s already strained air defenses.

These efforts to craft a deal might still come up short. Even if the Gulf states overcome their internal divisions and sideline concerns about Houthi activity, Tehran and Washington could refuse to sign on. Iran could conclude that control of the strait and the ability to throttle energy markets are its best security guarantee, whereas the United States might struggle to even implicitly acknowledge that the war will not achieve the outcome its leaders promised. And even if the cease-fire agreement does work, the result will be far from ideal, for both the United States and its Gulf partners. It could encourage Iran to increase its control over the strait, and it could weaken U.S.–Gulf state partnerships. Worse yet, it fails to address the underlying issues driving the U.S.-Iranian conflict and the tensions between Iran and its neighbors: Tehran’s nuclear program and support for armed groups, respectively.

But a comprehensive Iran deal is not feasible today. A Gulf-brokered outcome on the Strait of Hormuz is. In fact, it may be the only way to stop a mutually hurting stalemate that is poised to last years and cause mounting damage to global markets. The strategies that states have employed to blunt the consequences of global oil and gas shortages will likely start wearing thin in 2027, as governments deplete their strategic reserves, Chinese demand increases, and alternative supply routes out of the Gulf come under Iranian attack. The economic consequences of the conflict could even undermine the domestic stability of the most vulnerable Gulf states or reignite old conflicts, as happened in Yemen this year. A Gulf-brokered deal, then, is the least bad outcome. Such is the irony of this conflict: the bystanders that have already lost the most will need to save the warring parties from themselves.

#5947. Supreme Court denies Trump admin request to reverse block on segregating 20K California ballots

Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter joins 'Saturday in America' to weigh in on the Justice Department investigation into alleged illegal voting in California.

The U.S. Supreme Court (SCOTUS) on Monday rejected a Trump administration request to temporarily block lower-court rulings that denied requests to segregate more than 20,000 California mail-in ballots cast by people it says are likely not U.S. citizens.

Justice Elena Kagan denied the appeal on the eve of the midterm elections without comment, and did not refer it to the other justices.

The administration argued that the limited injunction would preserve the ballots while their eligibility is investigated, without canceling any votes. California and the federal government dispute whether the ballots are unlawful.

"Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm is impossible to remedy," the Department of Justice (DOJ) wrote in a court filing.

JUDGE REJECTS DOJ REQUEST TO BLOCK CALIFORNIA FROM IMMEDIATELY COUNTING BALLOTS LINKED TO ALLEGED NONCITIZENS

California has a heavy Democratic registered voter edge over Republicans and has the highest representation in the House with 52 seats, mostly Democratic. (Christina House/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images; Emily Elconin/Reuters)

The SCOTUS appeal came about after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the request Friday, with Judge Patrick Bumatay dissenting, as did a federal judge in Los Angeles last week.

The DOJ sought relief while the matter proceeds. California says its safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and argues the federal list may contain errors that could disenfranchise eligible voters.

The lower courts also cited the state’s authority over election procedures and warned that granting the request could jeopardize the election.

On Monday evening, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., said it was "likely" the Trump administration violated the Constitution by taking over responsibilities for elections from the states and Congress.

Chief Judge James Boasberg issued an injunction blocking the administration from making requests from California over its mail-in ballots.

DOJ HAS VERIFIED 20,000 NONCITIZENS ON CALIFORNIA VOTER ROLLS, FEDERAL PROSECUTOR SAYS

The case stems from an Oct. 15 DOJ lawsuit alleging that California is impeding enforcement of a federal law barring noncitizens from voting in federal elections.

The administration says the state violated the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, which generally gives federal law precedence over state law.

The dispute comes amid the administration’s broader push to influence how states run elections, including demands for access to voter rolls and warnings that officials could face prosecution for knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote.

California, the nation’s most populous state, has 52 House seats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.

Fox News' Shannon Bream and Bill Mears and Reuters contributed to this report.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

#5945. Don’t Go Backward on China Policy

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ALI WYNE is Senior Research and Advocacy Adviser for U.S.-China Relations at the International Crisis Group.

RYAN HASS is Director of the John L. Thornton China Center and Chen-Fu and Cecilia Yen Koo Chair in Taiwan Studies at the Brookings Institution.

Nearly halfway through his second term in office, U.S. President Donald Trump has undercut both the United States’ capacity to protect its interests related to China and its role as a provider of regional security in Asia. His undisciplined approach to dealing with Beijing, in which he has focused on building warm personal ties with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and discounted or ignored long-standing sources of tension between the two countries, has reduced Washington’s leverage to shape the relationship. At the same time, Trump’s sustained attacks on allies and partners have driven them to hedge against the United States and strengthen their ties with China. Beijing, in turn, has successfully cast itself as a steady counterweight to an erratic Washington: in 25 of 36 countries that the Pew Research Center surveyed in the spring of 2026—among them Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and Mexico—more respondents had a favorable view of China than of the United States.

Given the failures of Trump’s second-term strategy, many Democrats and even moderate Republicans may try to strike more hawkish postures on China after the midterm elections and during the 2028 presidential campaign. This temptation is understandable: there is a strong desire to provide a contrast to a flailing approach and correct what Trump has gotten wrong. But succumbing to it would be dangerous. If Congress and future presidential candidates reflexively adopt a more aggressive stance toward China, they could both undercut a future administration’s capacity to preserve vital diplomatic space with Beijing and further disquiet allies and partners that do not want to be trapped in a new twilight struggle. Overcorrecting Trump’s China policy would also be unlikely to help candidates get elected or boost their public profile in the run-up to 2028. Recent polling shows that only a small share of Americans in seven battleground states view China as an enemy or consider it to be one of the top threats to U.S. security.

The goal for the next Congress and, eventually, Trump’s successor, should be to prioritize steady competence over performative toughness in dealing with China. Political point scoring and wistful nostalgia for strategies that discount Beijing’s mounting power, and growing domestic support in the United States for great-power calm, would compound Trump’s mistakes rather than mitigate them. A smarter, more coherent China policy—one rooted in disciplined competition with Beijing, patient efforts to build goodwill with anxious allies and partners, and vigorous efforts to refresh the domestic sources of U.S. strength—can make life safer, healthier, and more affordable for Americans.

Trump’s views on China are iconoclastic in Washington, and even at odds with other members of his own administration and party. Whereas most policymakers agree that China is the United States’ foremost strategic competitor, Trump has embraced a narrow conception of competition focused primarily on the size of China’s trade surplus and its export of chemicals used to make fentanyl. He also sees Xi less as a determined geopolitical foe than as a transactional business rival with whom he can negotiate to stabilize bilateral ties.

This judgment—that dealing with China can and should be nonideological and transactional—was also present in Trump’s first term in office. It even survived the COVID-19 pandemic, during which Trump, believing that Xi had exported the virus, empowered senior advisers to implement a hard-line approach to China that included challenging the legitimacy of Chinese Communist Party rule and openly calling for political change. But Trump’s core views did not dictate U.S. policy as greatly then as they do now because he had less command over his own administration during his first term and was less dominant over the Republican Party as a whole.

Trump has also been chastened into a more realistic appreciation of Beijing’s power. China is the only country in the world that stared down Trump’s April 2025 tariff barrage and forced him to retreat. In 2026, Beijing used Washington’s fear of a fresh economic rupture to deter Trump from targeting major Chinese banks as part of his global efforts to squeeze Iran’s economy. Even as the president claims to be ushering in a new era of U.S. dominance, he has had to acknowledge China as a “near peer”—a designation that his administration codified in its 2025 National Security Strategy. Similarly, he has touted the prospect of a “G-2” of the United States and China, making allies and partners worry that he is privileging Beijing’s sensitivities over their concerns.

In some discrete areas, the Trump administration continues to view China through a competitive lens. For example, it is reducing U.S. dependence on Chinese rare-earth exports through initiatives such as Project Vault, an effort to stockpile critical minerals, and pressuring countries to forswear participation in Chinese-led artificial intelligence initiatives. And even as Trump lambastes allies and partners, alleging that they exploit U.S. beneficence, Washington is deepening its security cooperation with treaty allies in Asia, including Australia and the Philippines, and stepping up its training of troops in Taiwan.

Yet on balance, the president has been more conciliatory than competitive toward China. And with his other foreign policy goals—dominating the Western Hemisphere, pushing for regime change in Iran, and ending the war in Ukraine—vying for priority, Trump has devoted far less attention to the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship than many observers had expected when he retook office. His various retreats on China have left the United States worse off: he has undermined Washington’s leverage over Beijing while causing U.S. allies and partners to question whether they should align with a country that prefers a veneer of stability with China to coordinated efforts to address Chinese assertiveness abroad and repression at home.

Because Trump’s China policy places him at odds with much of the foreign policy bureaucracy and the vast majority of lawmakers, including those within his own party, there will likely be pent-up pressure to resume intense strategic competition with China. Candidates seeking the 2028 presidential nomination, in particular, will be tempted to pledge to take a tougher approach to Beijing, potentially including calls to curtail high-level diplomatic exchanges between U.S. and Chinese officials or adopt more expansive measures to limit China’s technological progress. But attempting to restore or make minor updates to the status quo that existed before Trump’s second term—or to go even further in an effort to project ostensible strength—would be misguided.

Most obvious, the nearly decadelong U.S. effort to slow Chinese innovation through sanctions, tariffs, and export controls is foundering. In AI, for example, Chinese companies are finding workarounds to such efforts and advancing their capabilities alongside those of their U.S. peers. Any sustainable attempt to limit technology access also requires multilateral cooperation; as Washington’s ties with many of its closest allies and partners fray, questions are mounting about whether any coalition can thwart Beijing’s technological strides and would be willing to bear the costs of trying to do so.

At the same time, China is widening its lead in sectors such as electric vehicles, advanced robots, and life sciences. Attempting to construct a technological moat around the United States is unlikely to help it regain its competitiveness. Instead, Washington will need to strike a better balance between mitigating the security risks of Chinese investment and collaboration and securing commercial benefits from Chinese knowledge and industry. The United States could gain from using the same technology transfer practices that China employed against U.S. companies starting in the late 1970s, when Washington led in many cutting-edge technologies. In battery manufacturing, for instance, U.S. firms would benefit from acquiring know-how from their Chinese competitors, and both countries would gain if their laboratories pooled capabilities to accelerate the discovery of cures to diseases such as cancer.

The United States also may not be able to pick up where it left off before Trump retook office because even its well-wishers no longer can treat his foreign policy as an aberration. He won a second term after losing in 2020, and he did so more decisively than in 2016. Although U.S. allies and partners would welcome a more multilateralist administration after Trump, they will find it difficult to overlook the possibility that aggressive unilateralism will periodically shape Washington’s foreign policy. Merely eschewing Trump’s crude bullying will not be enough to rebuild trust; his successor must avoid treating allies and partners as instruments of strategic competition.

Paradoxically, though, Trump’s mishandling of China policy has opened the political space for a new, more durable strategy to emerge. Previously, proponents of sustained high-level diplomacy between the United States and China were often dismissed as shortsighted, Chinese investment in the United States was seen as a Trojan horse, and critiques of zero-sum conceptions of bilateral relations were considered naive. But Trump’s actions have shifted the Overton window of what is possible, creating room for a wider variety of ways to work productively with China.

Both Republican and Democratic members of Congress have gradually resumed bipartisan visits to China. Even Secretary of State Marco Rubio, one of the foremost hawks during his time in the Senate, said in September that it would be “outrageous” for top U.S. and Chinese officials to avoid each other. Respected voices in Washington, including former senior Biden administration officials, are calling for some joint ventures with Chinese companies to help U.S. companies develop. And there is a growing recognition in both Congress and the White House that China’s steady accrual of power necessitates a more focused approach to competition.

There is also public support for a new China policy. Although many policymakers frame relations with Beijing as a competition to be won, most Americans regard it as a reality to be managed. In a July 2025 survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, 53 percent of Americans wanted the United States to pursue “friendly cooperation and engagement with China”; it was the first time since 2019 that a majority of respondents had expressed that view. Young people are driving this shift. A January 2026 Pew poll found that only 32 percent of Republicans and ten percent of Democrats between the ages of 18 and 49 called China an enemy, compared with 55 percent and 18 percent, respectively, of those age 50 and older. A March 2026 survey by the Searchlight Institute, a center-left think tank, found that 62 percent of respondents between 18 and 34 wanted the United States to “cooperate with China and improve U.S.-China relations.”

A better China policy will begin by abandoning hollow admonitions to “win” the strategic competition with Beijing. Although China faces numerous internal challenges, including slowing productivity, an aging population, and mounting government debt, it also has powerful advantages, two of which have become undeniable in Trump’s second term: China’s dominance of supply chains that provide vital commodities to Americans and its stranglehold on rare earths that the U.S. automotive industry and defense industrial base need to function.

The next president should neither understate nor exaggerate Beijing’s trajectory; rather, as we have previously argued, Washington should consider it “an enduring yet constrained competitor.” The inescapable reality is that neither country can deliver any knockout blows against the other without doing grievous damage to itself. Both countries will remain interdependent and have to operate with awareness of their vulnerabilities to each other.

If the world’s two foremost powers are fated to compete over the terms of coexistence, they must redouble efforts to avoid a catastrophic confrontation. Washington will have to build trust with rightfully wary allies and partners if it is to shore up deterrence in Asia. It will also have to continue signaling to Beijing a willingness to take reciprocal steps to reduce the risk of incidents that could spiral out of control, such as accidental air or naval collisions. Such signaling will become ever more essential as AI rapidly advances. Protecting the U.S. homeland against AI misuse and misalignment will require Washington to coordinate with Beijing on guardrails for frontier models and reject the argument that such efforts are inimical to securing a decisive strategic advantage over China. The need to work together on AI safety is already shaping U.S.-Chinese relations: at September’s summit between Trump and Xi, the two countries agreed to establish an incident alert system, and many members of Congress have publicly supported broader bilateral efforts with China to reduce the risks of AI-enabled security crises.

Reindustrialization will also be a major project for Trump’s successor. Progress on that front will be essential if the United States is to reduce its vulnerabilities to China and put itself on firmer footing to pursue a favorable coexistence. The next Congress and potential 2028 candidates could outline realistic plans for reducing dependence on China for active pharmaceutical ingredients, rare earths, and potential future chokepoints. They could also prioritize key industries on which U.S. security depends, such as AI-powered robotics and shipbuilding, and explain how they would deploy funding and talent to those sectors. Elsewhere, with public support for the president’s tariffs sagging, his successor could narrow or place sunset provisions on—or, through executive order, rescind—protectionist policies toward China that lower productivity and increase the costs of inputs for American producers. Such efforts would be broadly politically popular at home and would better position the United States to work with allies and partners to push back on China’s unfair economic practices, including extensive subsidies, undervalued currency, and suppressed domestic demand.

Ultimately, the United States must remember that its external competitiveness will flow from its internal vigor. Leaders in Washington should accordingly embed policy positions on China in a hopeful vision: helping the United States realize its potential as a pluralistic, self-correcting democracy. Framing U.S.-Chinese relations around the United States’ capacity to steer its ties with China in productive directions is more likely to produce a resilient approach than casting Washington as a victim or reasserting a policy framework that no longer meets the moment.

Observers can and should debate specific policy positions vigorously. But another harsh swing in the United States’ approach to China would create more policy instability while also discounting the extent to which Beijing’s rise is transforming the geopolitical balance. Taking advantage of the political space that Trump has generated, however ineptly, the new Congress taking office after the 2026 midterms and presidential aspirants looking to run in 2028 will have an opportunity to present a steadier approach, articulating a clear focus on national renewal and a balanced posture toward Beijing that reflects the mood of the American public. Approaching China’s challenge with this sensibility would not only be more prescriptively sound; it would also be more politically sustainable.

#5944. California is still without a functioning community solar program

California, the state with the most installed solar capacity in the country, has spent years trying, but still doesn’t have a community solar program. That means residential solar and storage systems are often still only accessible by the affluent, and low-income residents and renters continue to experience the country’s second-highest electricity rates without any self-generated relief.

A community solar project in Colorado, developed by Pivot Energy.

Despite the California Legislature mandating that the state create a community solar program in 2022, nothing yet has been established. Solar and community advocates have been battling with the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) and investor-owned utilities to establish a working community solar market, but talks have reached a stalemate. Outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed the latest community solar legislation in September, and the state continues to lose out on this new solar market development.

In 2022, Newsom signed AB 2316 into law, which aimed to create a community renewable energy program that would support both solar and storage projects. The bill required large utilities serving more than 100,000 customers to create and implement programs that “enable ratepayers to participate directly in offsite electrical generation facilities that use eligible renewable energy resources.”

In 2024, the CPUC rejected a proposal from solar advocacy groups that would support community solar in the state, instead putting more decision-making power into local utility hands. State legislators then attempted in 2025 to pass a new bill (AB 1260) designed to strengthen and expand the initial framework for California’s community solar-plus-storage program, guaranteeing affordability to low-income customers, among other stipulations. AB 1260 was never fully adopted.

Instead, community and solar advocates threw their support behind AB 1813, the Community Renewable Energy Program Act. Groups like Californians for Local, Affordable Solar and Storage (CLASS) said AB 1813 was a workable community solar and storage program that could overcome the CPUC’s “built-to-fail” program outline.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom Photo credit: Gage Skidmore

The California Legislature passed AB 1813, which directed regulators to value community solar and storage using the CPUC’s own Avoided Cost Calculator, an existing tool the state has declined to apply, and required paired battery storage so projects deliver power when the grid needs it most. Ultimately, Newsom vetoed the bill in September, and community solar development in California is still stalled.

“With Gov. Newsom’s veto of AB 1813, California continues to fall further behind other states who are aggressively moving forward with successful community solar programs. Unfortunately, the voices of community leaders, environmental justice organizations, ratepayer advocates, labor, community choice aggregators, the building industry and so many others were denied a solution they have long fought for,” said Derek Chernow, executive director of CLASS. “Study after study demonstrates the benefits of community solar-plus-storage to households, businesses, our environment and the grid. We are committed to working with the next administration to make community solar and storage part of the solution to California’s growing affordability crisis.”

Newsom, whose gubernatorial term ends in January 2027, stated in his veto that AB 1813 “would effectively require an administratively set price for the generation of power that exceeds the value that generation provides to the grid. This would result in significant upward pressure on consumer energy bills without delivering reliable, high-performance capacity to the grid at the times we need it. Fundamentally, this bill would shift costs and work counter to the state’s energy affordability and reliability goals. For these reasons, I cannot sign this bill.”

Without an approved process for bringing community renewable energy efforts online, project developers will focus on opportunities outside the state.

A Renewable Properties solar + storage project in California. Credit: Renewable Properties

Aaron Halimi, founder and CEO of Renewable Properties, a community solar developer headquartered in San Francisco, said Newsom’s veto relied on outdated cost assumptions and would hurt local rate payers looking for utility bill relief.

“Twenty-two other states have workable community solar programs that are attracting investment, creating local economic benefits and expanding consumer access to clean energy,” he said. “As a result of this veto, Renewable Properties will invest more of our resources into those 22 community solar states instead of our home state of California.”

There’s not much else advocates can do until the next legislative session begins in December. Then a new governor would have until September 2027 to sign any community solar legislation into law. Chernow said CLASS will continue putting pressure on legislators to build a successful community solar market in California.

Kelly Pickerel was a long-time reporter with Solar Power World before leaving her post as editor in chief in 2026. You may find her on LinkedIn.

I think there is something in bill, A1813 that sets prices. This article does not say enough about that section of the bill which Governor Newsom objects to and paints a bad picture of his actions. Knowing his bent to renewable energy development in the state, I can’t help but think some information is missing, information that would make him veto the bill.

#5943. Talarico campaigns alongside Democrat who called ICE 'new KKK' and demanded its abolition

Fox News host Will Cain discusses accusations from James Talarico’s former classmate Mike Garcia about the Democratic Texas Senate candidate's honesty on 'The Will Cain Show.'

James Talarico, a U.S. Senate candidate in Texas, briefly praised Frederick Haynes III, a Democratic congressional candidate who compared President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts to the KKK, at a get-out-the-vote event on Thursday as part of his Clear Eyes Full Hearts tour.

"Give it up for your next congressman, Dr. Freddy Haynes. Thank you, Dr. Haynes, for those kind words and for your service to this community," Talarico said, following an introduction and speech from Haynes.

Although Talarico has not issued a formal endorsement of Haynes, the moment is notable for Talarico as he pitches himself as a Democrat who can represent the values of the Republican-leaning Lone Star State — and as he tries to distance himself from controversy over past remarks Republicans have characterized as woke.

TALARICO RALLY WARMUP ACT CALLS FOR ABOLISHING ICE, CONTRASTING SENATE HOPEFUL'S MESSAGE

State Representative James Talarico addresses the crowd during a campaign rally after launching his Senate campaign for the seat currently held by John Cornyn in Round Rock, Texas, Sept. 9, 2025. (Callaghan O'Hare for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Haynes, the pastor of Friendship-West Baptist Church, has framed many of his political views in the context of race and did so again on the event with Talarico.

"You transformed ICE into the new KKK and brought about terror in this nation," Haynes said of Trump's use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

"It’s time to melt ICE. It’s time to abolish ICE," Haynes added.

Haynes is running to fill the seat of Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, the incumbent in Texas' 30th Congressional District who gave up her seat in a Senate bid she ultimately lost. During his campaign, Haynes has framed his support for climate policy as a fight against "environmental racism." He has also accused conservatives and the Trump administration of benefiting from fears of Black advancement.

"They have used Black people and perceived Black progress as the boogeyman. We have not witnessed this kind of corruption, this kind of blatant corruption," Haynes said in an October interview.

"We are witnessing the demolishing of what democratic infrastructure was built by the gains of the civil rights movement," Haynes added.

Even before his congressional run, Haynes made political commentary that relied heavily on a racial lens.

After the death of Charlie Kirk, a conservative political commentator who started Turning Point USA, Haynes described Kirk as a man with views "rooted in White supremacy" and contrasted it with the deaths of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X.

"A White Christian gets killed, murdered — not assassinated. We going to tell the whole truth today. Martin King got assassinated. Malcolm X got assassinated. Medgar Evers got assassinated. Don’t compare Kirk to King," Haynes said in a September 2025 address to his church.

UN PUSHES NATIONS TO CONSIDER SLAVERY REPARATIONS BUT LEGAL GROUP SAYS IDEA 'NOT GOING TO FLY IN THE US'

Rev. Frederick Douglass Haynes III, a Dallas megachurch pastor and social activist, is running to replace Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, in Texas Congressional District 30. (Fox News)

Haynes would go on to condemn Kirk's death and political violence.

Haynes has also said he was a personal supporter of reparations.

"America, you owe us. What you done to us has been immoral. It’s been evil. It’s been unjust. It’s been downright wrong and the only way to bring salvation to America — you gotta pay us what you owe us," Haynes said at a Solidarity for Reparations event at a San Francisco church.

"I've come by to say, San Francisco, California, Texas, United States of America, if you want salvation to come to this house, you've got to engage in reparations."

For his own part, Talarico has also supported the idea of reparations, framing it as an outflow of his religious convictions.

"Reparations, repairing past harms, is part of my faith tradition. It’s part of the values I was raised with," Talarico said in a town hall meeting in July. "We have to correct the injustices of our past."

In the closing days of his campaign, Talarico has argued that, despite some of his views on race and gender which run counter to conservative stances, he could still represent Texas as a moderate.

TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS

Frederick Haynes III is running to replace outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas. He is a megachurch pastor in Dallas who Crockett has cited as "my pastor." (Haynes for Congress)

"Our campaign has been able to show that you can be a more moderate, reasonable candidate and still be exciting," Talarico said in October.

Talarico’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment if his comment about Haynes should be viewed as an endorsement of his platform or his views on race in politics.

#5940. Union boss stuns with major Republican endorsement as election nears

Teamsters general president Sean O'Brien discusses supporting Sen. Markwayne Mullin’s, R-Okla., nomination for DHS Secretary despite their past dispute on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

The leader of one of the nation’s oldest and largest unions stunned political observers by issuing a surprise endorsement for a Senate Republican stalwart over the weekend.

Teamsters General President Sean O’Brien, who famously nearly came to blows with now-Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin during a Senate hearing before ultimately becoming acquaintances, issued a ringing endorsement of Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., signaling a major break from national union sentiment that has tended to favor Democrats.

"Just voted in the State of Florida for the first time, and very proud to have cast a ballot for Sen. Ashley Moody," O’Brien, whose 123-year-old union is about 1.3 million-strong, announced Sunday.

"Sen. Moody has been extremely helpful working with the Teamsters to protect workers’ pensions, defend good-paying jobs, and support well-funded union apprenticeship programs."

"The Teamsters look forward to working with Sen. Moody in her role on the Senate HELP Committee to pass the Faster Labor Contracts Act and get this critical legislation signed into law to protect American workers," he added.

FRUSTRATED BLUE-COLLAR UNION BOSSES RIP SOCIALIST POLITICIANS, WARN OF LABOR EXODUS FROM DEM PARTY

O’Brien, a self-described "lifelong Democrat," previously spoke at the 2024 Republican National Convention, but emphasized at the time that the Democratic Party had snubbed his request to speak at its convention.

"If the far-left want to criticize me and attack me, that’s OK. If the far-right wants to do the same, that’s great. I represent 1.3 million hardworking men and women," O’Brien said at the time.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Teamsters as well as Moody’s campaign for comment.

Moody, a former state attorney general, said in a statement that she was proud to have O’Brien’s endorsement:

"I’ll always fight to protect hardworking Americans, strengthen good-paying jobs, and ensure resources are available to train our next generation. It’s been great to deliver for Florida’s working families," she said.

After O’Brien endorsed Moody, the lawmaker’s Democratic opponent responded by posting a photo she once took with O’Brien and writing that "Ashley Moody never walked the line with you."

Sean O'Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, speaks during a press conference outside the West Wing of the White House on Oct. 30, 2025, in Washington, D.C., flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. (AFP via Getty Images)

"But ok brother. Shout out to all the rank and file Teamsters that are voting for me. I will always stand with you," Democratic nominee Angie Nixon, a state lawmaker from Jacksonville whose platform is considered DSA-aligned, wrote on X.

O’Brien also caught heat for voting in Florida, which appeared to signal a move from his hometown of Boston.

DSA candidate Angie Nixon advanced to a high-profile November Senate matchup against Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla. (Nixon: Joe Raedle; Moody: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)

"Be union leader — move to a famously anti-union state — vote for a famously anti-union candidate — Brag about it — really cool stuff man," a top commenter on O’Brien’s post said. Other critics characterized O’Brien as a "scab", union jargon for someone who crosses a strike picket line to return to work for the company with which they are at odds.

The Teamsters leader’s announcement marked a noteworthy development with polls set to open nationwide in a matter of hours.
